We investigate the generalization capability of two-layer neural networks, comparing dense and sparse architectures, and analyzing the effects of different overparameterization levels, activation functions, and data samples. Our analysis focuses on networks with $d$ input, $d$ hidden, and $d$ output units, and we show that the generalization error in two-layer networks can achieve the same level of decay as in linear models, particularly when the data lies on or within a hypercube of radius $R$. Notably, for dense two-layer networks with sigmoid activations and $d = \Omega(\log^3 N)$, where $N$ represents the number of data samples, we demonstrate near-optimal generalization performance, even in the presence of adversarial label noise. Our results also highlight the significance of sparsity, as dense networks may exhibit improved generalization. Furthermore, we illustrate the generalization gaps through numerical examples, and provide open-source code for these experiments. Additionally, our analysis includes theoretical and empirical comparisons with other neural network architectures, revealing the robustness of two-layer models in achieving generalization. These findings are backed by extensive numerical experiments, along with code available at https://github.com/alex-hathaway/generalization-studies. Based on these results, two-layer models appear to offer a suitable choice for achieving good generalization with moderate overparameterization. Our study presents an in-depth analysis of the arrival directions of extremely energetic cosmic rays, exceeding 4 x 10^18 eV, based on eight years of data from the Telescope Array experiment. Our findings reveal significant anisotropies in the distribution of these cosmic rays, featuring two distinct patterns: one resembling a millipede, observed at lower energies, and an oval-shaped dipole, evident at energies exceeding 4 EeV. We quantify the anisotropies by comparing the anisotropic cosmic ray flux to a corresponding isotropic component, finding that the amplitude of the dipole enhances with increasing energy. Additionally, we identify a notable anisotropy in small circular regions, centered at (1.78, -1.22) in galactic coordinates, and verify that the anisotropies do not correlate with the characteristics of nearby active galactic nuclei. Our research further indicates that the anisotropies do not exhibit a clear connection to the locations of extensive air showers. We discuss possible explanations for these findings, including the hypothesis that these anisotropies originate from the nearby M87 galaxy and the galaxy SSC 0838+513, located at 125 Mpc and 3.4 Mpc distances respectively, both members of the Virgo cluster. We also examine an alternative scenario involving a more widespread "Galactic-Type" source, encompassing a larger area and energy output. We used the Auger Anisotropy Approach to quantify the likelihood of our observations given these hypotheses, and found that the data on anisotropies is more likely (by a factor of 4) explained if the sources include M87 and are skeptical towards extended sources at higher energies. We also found that the isolated sources such as SSC 0838+513, located at 3.4 Mpc distance, is unlikely (by a factor of 10) to explain the data on anisotropies. This study examines the long-term behavior of solutions to the Klein-Gordon equation within a specific Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker spacetime, characterized by a single time-dependent factor. We identify two distinct cases: one where solutions scatter to a set of free solutions and another where they remain confined. The solutions in the first case can be generalized as the product of an initial, localized function and a set of expanding, oscillatory wavefunctions. The solutions in the second case either remain steady or vary oscillating around a constant value, depending on their frequency relative to the spacetime's expansion rate. The general solutions are classified into three categories based on their correlation with the spacetime's expansion rate and the solutions are analyzed through linear superposition, revealing that the scattering case arises from superposing solutions with frequencies above the spacetime's effective mass. The validity of these solutions is confirmed through conservation of energy and by comparing our results with those from flat spacetime, the Minkowski model. The approach employed in this study is versatile and can be applied to more complex spacetimes, such as those featuring multiple time-dependent factors or spatial variations. The methodology is also adaptable for use in computational methods, like finite element analysis, to determine the long-term behavior of solutions in complex spacetimes. The techniques developed can be utilized in modeling cosmological scenarios where a Klein-Gordon field is embedded in either a Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker spacetime or a more complex spacetime setting. The methods presented can serve as a framework for an analytical or computational investigation of such a field's long-term behavior. The analytical techniques can also inform the construction of finite element spaces for numerically solving the Klein-Gordon equation in these spacetimes. The relationship between the spacetime's scalar curvature and the Klein-Gordon equation's coefficients is explored, revealing how the curvature influences the equation's properties and, by extension, the properties of the finite element spaces. The relationship between the finite element spaces serves as a basis for developing an inf-sup condition, which in turn can be used to determine whether the discrete formulation is stable and solvable. The techniques employed are general and can be utilized for modeling a Klein-Gordon field in any spacetime setting, provided the metric coefficients are specified. The methods presented can be applied in both analytical and computational studies of the Klein-Gordon equation, and our findings can be extended to various physical scenarios. The shift in cancer research towards digital methodologies has led to the application of digital image analysis for extracting comprehensive information from tissue sections. This shift is particularly evident in the study of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, a critical indicator of cancer prognosis and treatment responsiveness. Nevertheless, digitally analyzing lymphocytes in tissue sections poses a significant challenge due to their sparse distribution and complex microenvironment. This review summarizes the most recent advancements in digital tissue analysis, specifically focusing on single-cell detection, segmentation, and tracking within tissue sections, as well as the incorporation of contextual information for accuracy enhancement. It also highlights the necessity of making research methods accessible and reproducible, and we will demonstrate this by illustrating a fully automated pipeline for detecting and segmenting lymphocytes using H&E-stained tissue sections. This pipeline is implemented in the Fiji distribution, an open-source platform, and comprises a collection of well-documented macros that can be easily shared and modified. This approach promotes transparency and understanding in digital image analysis. A supplementary paper will be published, detailing the underlying assumptions and explaining the steps of the pipeline in greater depth. Both papers are part of a larger collection focusing on digital image analysis in pathology, available online at https://digitalpathologyhub.org. A groundbreaking technique in studying magnetic properties of 2D magnetic materials has emerged through cavity magnomechanics. This method achieves this by leveraging a membrane made from a 2D magnetic material placed above a mirror in an optical cavity, causing it to vibrate when exposed to light and thereby driving a specific mechanical response. This interaction enables the precise engineering of quantum states, particularly in the mechanical system, to the point where it reaches a quantum-squeezed condition. Furthermore, this method offers a highly sensitive means of detecting ultra-weak magnetic fields, giving it significant potential for application in magnetic-field detection. We have conducted in-depth research on the fundamental principles and applications of cavity magnomechanics in 2D magnetic materials, including the analysis of vibrational modes, the exploration of new materials, and the examination of the influence of environmental factors. Additionally, we have created a set of educational resources and a user-friendly database that enables users to easily identify and study the characteristics of various 2D magnetic materials. This comprehensive study and these supporting tools are intended to facilitate further research in the field of cavity magnomechanics in 2D magnetic materials. The database can be accessed through the following link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spmi.2022.100995. An alternative can be found at the following email address for download: [s2dmdb@ustc.edu.cn](mailto:s2dmdb@ustc.edu.cn).

This research presents a novel method of generating gaits for quadrupedal robots in difficult terrain using reinforcement learning. By utilizing a reinforcement learning approach, our system trains a policy to produce dynamic gait patterns tailored to the specific objectives of walking in challenging environments, eliminating the need for a pre-defined cost function. To validate our method, we tested it on the Hydra quadruped in a simulated environment and compared the results to a traditional optimization approach. The outcome revealed that our reinforcement learning-based method yielded superior performance, particularly in steep inclines and narrow pathways, due to its capacity to produce more dynamic and adaptive gait patterns. Additionally, we observed that the training of the policy enabled the detection of the robot's limits of stability in the simulated environment. To facilitate real-world application, we also extracted a set of static poses from the optimal gait trajectories and employed them to inform a controller using joint space resolution, which demonstrated strong alignment with the desired trajectories in both the simulated and real-world environments. The resulting framework exhibits great potential for generating effective gait solutions in a wide range of challenging scenarios. Further details can be found in the paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11149. A video showcasing the method's performance is available at https://youtu.be/6Q4Q4e4Q4e. A study of a nearby low-luminosity active galaxy, located 35 million light-years from us, has been carried out using data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory. The analysis covers a 10-year period during which the galaxy's central black hole's active state and surrounding winds could be observed. The observed X-ray flux from the galaxy changed slightly over time but showed significant variations in 2013, corresponding to a change in its state. The data also indicate the presence of two separate hot plasmas with temperatures of 0.65 and 5 keV, respectively. One plasma is likely powered by the galaxy's central black hole, while the other is thought to be associated with the galaxy's nuclear star cluster. The winds, however, are responsible for the majority of the galaxy's energy output, influencing a region of over 10 kiloparsecs in diameter, potentially feeding back into the galaxy's interstellar medium. The data suggest that the galaxy's hot winds, powered by the galaxy's central black hole, are the primary mechanism driving galaxy evolution through feedback. The study also indicates that the galaxy's hot winds, although variable, remain relatively stable in terms of their overall power output, averaging 2.0 × 10^43 erg/s. This stable power output, in turn, powers the winds that maintain the galaxy's hot phase gas, averaging 2.4 × 10^43 erg/s. The study suggests that the variability in the galaxy's X-ray flux, observed in 2013, may have been the result of a change in the galaxy's accretion rate, potentially linked to the disruption of a dust torus due to the galaxy's winds. The data also indicate that the galaxy's central black hole, with a mass of 700 solar masses, has an accretion rate of approximately 0.01 times the Eddington rate, averaging 0.013 times the Eddington rate over the 10-year period. The SiD Detector, one of the two validated detector designs for the ILC, has a sensitive precision silicon tracker with a sensitive precision calorimeter system. These combined subsystems work together to achieve precise overall performance. In this report, we specifically examine the contribution of the precision silicon tracker and the precision calorimeter system to the resolution of jet energy across various energy ranges. Precise energy measurement is essential for many physics analyses at the ILC, such as Higgs discovery and top quark detection. In this study, we investigate the precision of jet energy achieved by the SiD Detector using Monte Carlo simulations of jet formation, accounting for fluctuations in particle shower formation, and track contributions from the silicon tracker. The precision of jet energy is remarkably high, with a goal of reaching 1% precision for jets with energies below 50 GeV and 10% precision for jets with energies above 200 GeV. In this study, we specifically examine the precision of jet energy achieved by the precision silicon tracker and the precision calorimeter system separately, highlighting their individual contributions to the overall precision. The precision silicon tracker significantly improves jet precision by accounting for subtle inner tracking details. The precision calorimeter system, composed of a forward and a central system, works together to achieve high precision in high energy regions. By combining these contributions with an electron reconstruction algorithm previously reported, we verified that the SiD Detector meets its goals for precise jet energy measurement. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the precision silicon tracker and the precision calorimeter system in achieving the precise jet energy goals for the SiD Detector. This letter presents recent findings regarding the contribution of two-pion interactions to the muon anomalous magnetic moment, with our calculation covering the range of 0 to 1 GeV. A novel, all-orders technique is utilized to compute the two-pion contribution, with the results being entirely consistent with the predictions of quantum electrodynamics. By combining this new calculation with our previous derivation of the three-pion contribution, the total hadronic correction in the $q^2$ range of 0 to 1 GeV is provided. Our all-order, hadronic calculation yields a value of $(494.3\pm 1.4)\times 10^{-10}$ for the anomalous magnetic moment, with this estimate aligning with the data from Experiment 1 and being in concordance with the findings of Experiment 2. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the hadronic corrections for the tau magnetic moment and the shift in the mass are $(18.2\pm 0.6)\times 10^{-14}$, with the ratio of these values to the corrections for the muon anomalous magnetic moment being approximately 0.037. Our study also reveals that the contributions from the two-pion and three-pion interactions are 0.944 and 0.056, respectively, in the range of 0 to 1 GeV. With the results being fully consistent with the predictions of quantum electrodynamics, our calculations provide valuable insights for future calculations involving the hadronic corrections in the range of 1 to 3 GeV. A detailed numerical analysis is provided in the tables and figures accompanying this letter. Moreover, our study paves the way for the derivation of the hadronic contribution at fourth order in the fine structure constant, with the results being fully documented in the accompanying tables and an accompanying paper. A brief overview of our previous work is also included in this letter. A more comprehensive review of our past research is available elsewhere. Additionally, our study is in concordance with the findings of the Hadron Loop contribution to the muon anomalous magnetic moment publication. Recent advances in pre-trained models have yielded significant gains in performance for downstream applications, and the programming domain is no exception. In this study, we explore the utility of pre-trained models in code completion, and our findings indicate that pre-trained models can learn essential code patterns, enabling them to be leveraged for improved performance in a range of downstream tasks. Building on the success of pre-trained models in natural language tasks, we introduce a method for fine-tuning pre-trained models on code datasets, and our results reveal substantial enhancements in code completion accuracy and overall model efficiency. Additionally, our experiments highlight the importance of using large, high-quality datasets for fine-tuning pre-trained models, and the potential for such models to be used in combination of code generation techniques to achieve superior outcomes. Using the GPT-3 framework, our results show that pre-trained models can accomplish several code-related tasks with nearly perfect accuracy when given sufficient context, and our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/pretrain-code. Conversely, for tasks requiring fewer code snippets or less context, neural code models still outperform traditional approaches. Furthermore, in a task involving code summarization, pre-trained models exhibit superior performance compared to models specifically designed for code, and our results suggest that pre-trained models may be used to bypass the need for specialized code models in downstream applications. Ultimately, our research indicates that pre-trained models present an appealing option for addressing programming-related tasks. By fine-tuning pre-trained models, developers can create effective code-completion tools without needing to invest in training custom code-generation models. This study introduces a novel method of determining the vertical aerosol optical depth at night using a broad field photometry technique, separated from stars. The approach leverages the extinction of which-way light due to interstellar dust, enabling the calculation of extinction without the need for absolute photometric calibration. We also derive a relationship between optical depth and colour, obtained from observations made with a 1-square-degree field of view over 40 minutes. Although the observations are limited to a single vertical layer, the analysis suggests that the aerosol optical depth can be modelled as a layer at a height of approximately 0.1 kpc. Finally, the method offers a promising means of studying the aerosol patterns over various latitude locations, and their possible connections to the atmospheric transport models. The approach is also compatible with future space missions that may involve the global monitoring of aerosol effects using the global network of small satellites. The Graphical Lasso has been widely utilized to infer undirected graphical models represented as Gaussian graphical models, yet this model is limited in its ability to account for unobserved variables, leading to inaccurate estimations and potentially incorrect graph structures. To address this limitation, a new method is proposed, Graphical Lasso for Latent Variables, which incorporates both observed and hidden variables to estimate a Gaussian graphical model represented as a Gaussian graphical mixture model. By introducing a matrix that compactly represents the relationships among latent variables, this model is able to relax the assumption of complete data, making it suitable for large datasets. Through mathematical proofs, it is shown that this model is still identifiable under certain conditions and converges to the optimal solution as the number of samples increases. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this model in inferring correct graph structures and revealing latent variables, outperforming the standard Graphical Lasso in many cases. An implementation of this method is available through the GLLV R package. We have developed a novel, efficient algorithm for estimating pitch values in a speech signal, capable of withstanding significant background noise. Traditional high-frequency signal extraction methods are compromised by background interference, while more advanced algorithms requiring extensive parameter tuning are impractical for noisy conditions. Our proposed algorithm, the Adaptive Harmonic Ratio-based Pitch Estimation Algorithm (AHR-PEA), employs an adaptive approach to signal extraction and harmonic ratio calculation, enabling pitch estimation in noisy speech signals without manual adjustment. Experimental results on the NTT-NAQUST NOISEUSED database and DB usd database demonstrate AHR-PEA's superiority over existing pitch estimation algorithms, particularly in noisy environments. In the field of Neural Architecture Search (NAS), researchers have discovered that
the performance of neural networks is correlated with specific properties of the
program representing the network. This study investigates whether this
performance-Program-Property relationship also exists when considering programs
derived from multiple-source code. By examining the source code of various deep
learning models, which can be represented as programs consisting of multiple
components, the study reveals that specific program properties emerge to
determine each model's performance on benchmark datasets. Furthermore, the study
links these program properties to structural features of the models, indicating
that there is a connection between the source code, program properties, and
performance. The study's findings suggest that targeted program modifications
can improve model performance, which can be an efficient approach in comparison to
the exhaustive search typically involved in NAS methods. The study's code is
available at: https://github.com/ProgrammNas/multi-source-program-properties.

This study investigates whether there is a relationship between the performance of these models and their program properties, but instead of using source code derived from a single source, we use program representations derived from multiple sources. The results of our study reveal that there is a correlation between the performance of these models and specific program properties, but the characteristics of these properties differ significantly from those found in single-component systems. Moreover, we discovered that there is a connection between the program properties, the structure of the model, and its performance, indicating that targeted modifications to the program can improve performance more efficiently than exhaustive searches in the program's search space. Overall, this study contributes to the existing body of research by showing that program properties can be used to predict performance, while also highlighting the differences between program properties used to predict performance in single-component systems and those used to predict performance in multiple-component systems. This research explores mmWave multicasting with multiple antennas at both the transmitter and receiver, and derives lower and upper limits for the total transmitted power to maintain a specified level of reception quality for each user. We find that using multiple receiver antennas allows for a reduced transmit power while achieving the same level of service to each user, and this power reduction grows as more receiver antennas are added. Close-to-optimal performance is achieved through a combination of beamforming and power allocation based on hierarchical coding. The proposed scheme first uses hierarchical coding to split the transmitted data into different layers, and then assigns power to each layer based on an iterative algorithm that maximizes throughput, considering both beamforming and power allocation. Simulation results show that this combination of beamforming and power allocation outperforms traditional methods in terms of system performance, particularly when there are many receiver antennas. Additionally, most of the transmitted power can be concentrated on the lowest layer of the hierarchical codeword, and using multiple receiver antennas allows for a significant reduction in transmit power while maintaining the same level of service to each user. As a result, this combination of beamforming and power allocation is a good choice for mmWave multicasting when there are many receiver antennas. Communicational requirements in Federated Learning pose significant challenges, 
leading to efficiency limitations in current techniques such as Federated Averaging 
and Federated Federated Distillation. To address these issues, a novel approach 
called Compressed Federated Distillation is presented, incorporating dataless 
learning and weighted average aggregation. Compressed Federated Distillation 
overcomes previous difficulties by providing accurate models with reduced 
communication needs. Notably, it surpasses both Federated Distillation and 
Federated Averaging in terms of efficiency while staying competitive in terms of 
accuracy. Moreover, it outperforms other compression methods without relying 
on lossy data transmission. The system's effectiveness is demonstrated through 
experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets. The code is 
available at https://github.com/stevenm299/CFD.

In modern networks, the increasing complexity of service delivery requires more sophisticated techniques than traditional fixed routing methods can provide. To address this challenge, the SDADO method optimizes service delivery performance by efficiently discovering available services and directing traffic to them. Compared to other service discovery approaches, SDADO achieves better results for both delay and throughput in scenarios involving multiple service delivery points. The method's performance improvements are due to its dynamic orchestration of service discovery, which adapts to varying network conditions and prioritizes available services based on traffic volume. While SDADO excels in scenarios with multiple service delivery points, it may experience slightly lower results in simple scenarios with a single point. To address this, a modified version of SDADO, SDADO-R, has been developed to perform nearly as well in all scenarios by using a more efficient algorithm to find the optimal service discovery point. The results show that SDADO-R is very similar to SDADO in its performance, but requires much less computational power. Therefore, SDADO-R is recommended as a more practical solution for achieving the best possible results in service delivery. The recommended approach is to use SDADO-R for its general applicability and SDADO for specific scenarios with complex network conditions. This study examines the exponential stability of a star-shaped metric graph with non-uniform edge properties, specifically focusing on the edges that lack elasticity at its vertices. We investigate the exponential stability of the closed-loop system, depending on the vertex weights and edge parameters, without making any specific assumptions about these parameters in relation to each other. Interestingly, our analysis reveals that exponential stability is achieved when all edge parameters are identical, but unique or randomly distributed parameters lead to stability only if a certain condition is met. However, when all parameters are infinitely varied, the absence of elasticity on the slopes of the edges becomes the determining factor for exponential stability, which is not the case when these parameters are uniformly distributed on a finite range. To confirm our theoretical findings, corresponding numerical examples are provided. Ultimately, our research contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of non-uniformly weighted star-shaped networks, paving the way for further generalizations to more complex metric graph structures. Additionally, the study identifies challenges and opportunities for exploring the stability of nonlinear controlled dynamic systems in diverse and unpredictable environments. As a bonus, our analysis offers a connection to the study of planar graph representations, specifically in relation to the star-shaped graph's equivalent planar representation, which consists of three edges that intersect at a common point. This connection may hold potential for further research in graph theory, motivated by our findings in this study. Finally, the study delves into the unknown dynamics of a quantum particle hopping on a graph, which serves as the primary motivation for our mathematical analysis, and our findings are translated into the context of this particle's behavior. By confirming the exponential stability of the closed-loop system, we demonstrate the existence of an invariant neighborhood of the origin, which represents the particle's position on the graph, when subjected to a suitable feedback control. This achievement is a crucial step towards understanding the particle's asymptotic convergence to a specific point on the graph, which corresponds to the origin in this context, under the influence of optimal control. This research is a key component of our broader investigation into the controllability of this particle's dynamics, motivated by a fundamental question in mathematics and graph theory, which seeks to identify the necessary and sufficient conditions for a graph to be controllable. This controllability condition is closely related to the concept of hypervisibility, as postulated in a previous study, and our findings in this area have the potential to significantly impact the development of new control strategies for complex systems, which are essential for a wide range of applications in controlled dynamics. By considering a background with two spatial momenta, we analyze the correlation functions of different channels and find that only the $T_{3J}|0\rangle$ correlation exhibits instability. This instability is characterized by a dip in the invariant mass spectrum of the decay chain $\rho$ and $a_1$ and is dependent on the momentum of the decay products. This behavior is distinct from the instability observed in the $T_{1J}|0\rangle$ correlation with zero spatial momenta. As a consequence, we generate unique, twisted distribution amplitudes for the $a_1$ meson with a particular momentum structure. This result may lead to observable effects in $e^+e^-$ annihilation into three pions when the momentum of the decay products is high enough. This paper explores the concept of learning an optimal utility function in real-time optimization problems, but with a twist: instead of relying exclusively on pairwise preference data, we also tap into expert knowledge of the underlying utility function, but with it wrapped in noise. Our goal is to uncover the underlying utility function offline by utilizing the expert's not-too-bad estimates and pairwise result preferences, which are acquired through an interactive learning process. Notably, we identify two distinct offline learning settings, each requiring a different approach, and we develop the first regret bounds for these scenarios. Interestingly, the difference between these settings highlights a trade-off between utilizing expert knowledge and pairwise preferences, and this distinction is likely to be relevant in various real-world applications. To illustrate the practical applicability of our findings, we apply our theoretical results to two specific optimization problems: learning the parameters of a Gaussian utility function and identifying the best result in a finite set, which are both accompanied by empirical evidence validating our analysis. Overall, our work provides significant insights into offline learning of utility functions, and it paves the way for further research in this domain. A significant unaddressed question in reinforcement learning involves using sequence-to-sequence models to forecast the future actions of trained agents. Our research addresses this query by exploring the capacity of future action prediction as a supplementary objective to reinforcement learning training. We utilize a Future Action Prediction module, which is trained to predict action sequences for future timesteps, leveraging the given sequence length and output size. The results indicate that incorporating this module enhances the performance of reinforcement learning agents, as evidenced by accelerated training and improved long-term rewards in diverse environments. The code for this module is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexeyguz/fap. Additionally, our research has been integrated into the established environments provided by PyTorch Marina (https://marina.pytorch.org/). Specifically, the demonstrated results pertain to navigation in maze worlds (https://marina.pytorch.org/envs/Maze-v0/) and driving on a track (https://marina.pytorch.org/envs/Drive-v0/). It is worth noting that the performance of the Future Action Prediction module is most pronounced when the temporal differences between predictions are substantial (i.e., predicting actions far in the future). Consequently, it is most beneficial when the time horizon for reinforcement learning is extended. For instance, in the driving task where the time horizon is limited to 20 time steps, the performance gain from using the Future Action Prediction module is relatively minimal. Nevertheless, in the maze navigation task with a time horizon of 100 time steps, the module yields a 43% increase in long-term rewards. Overall, the findings suggest that utilizing sequence-to-sequence models to forecast future actions can serve as a supplementary objective to accelerate reinforcement learning within environments with prolonged time horizons. It is worth noting that the incorporation of this objective may have varying implications for different environments, with predictions far in the future generally yielding greater gains. Consequently, the potential benefits of employing the Future Action Prediction module could be maximized by extending the time horizon of reinforcement learning in a wide range of temporal environments. It is worth noting that the results presented in this abstract are based on the evaluation of a Future Action Prediction module that is trained to forecast action sequences up to timestep 20 in the driving task and up to timestep 100 in the maze navigation task. Specifically, the module was trained on data from the first 10 time steps in both tasks and was tested on data from timesteps 11 to 20 in the driving task and timesteps 51 to 100 in the maze navigation task. We examine an effective Hamiltonian representing a two-dimensional Herringbone Lattice, variant of the Kitaev model, with quantum spins of magnitude s. By altering the exchange and Zeeman terms, the model's characteristics can be altered without the lattice's geometry changing. For spins with unit magnitude, a phase transition occurs when the exchange and Zeeman terms are equal, where a quantum spin liquid transforms into a classical Herringbone Antiferromagnet. Our research investigates this transition through analysis of finite spin systems and the calculation of the model's ground state through the Quantum Monte Carlo method. Additionally, we demonstrate that the two-phase coexistence region can be determined by calculating the free energy of the classical Herringbone Lattice model. Our findings are further validated by simulating larger systems of spins up to s=3/2 and the results are compared with the model's predictions for this case. The research also extends to the study of finite-size effects and the behavior of the susceptibility in systems of varying size. The results show that the susceptibility in these systems increases with the size of the spins, the size of the systems, and the ratio of the exchange to Zeeman terms, ultimately reaching a maximum at the point where the two phases meet. The research concludes by comparing the results with the research on the Quantum Spin Hall effect and the Kitaev ladder, highlighting the similarities and differences between these systems and the Herringbone Lattice model. The final section discusses potential future research directions on the model. The appendices contain additional information, including the derivation of the effective Hamiltonian, the Heisenberg model, the Kitaev ladder model, the phase diagram of the model for spins of magnitude s, and the magnetic phase diagram of the model for spins of s=3/2. To effectively tackle rapidly changing situations, we need agents that can adapt quickly and make wise decisions rapidly. Yet, reinforcement learning algorithms often struggle with dynamic environments, particularly those that aren't part of a Markov Decision Process (MDP). To overcome this limitation, researchers have incorporated restart mechanisms into existing policies, allowing the agent to restart from a common point after each episode. While restart-based algorithms have shown promise in certain settings, their performance is highly dependent on the choice of restart point. In our research, we examine how these algorithms can be applied to risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in changing environments. By analyzing the variability in the reward distributions of these environments, we propose a method to select the most suitable restart points and demonstrate its effectiveness through theoretical validation and experimental results. This approach not only improves the performance of risk-sensitive reinforcement learning but also offers a valuable tool for adapting to unexpected shifts in other types of reward functions. Ultimately, our goal is to leverage this knowledge to develop more robust reinforcement learning algorithms capable of navigating uncertain and unpredictable environments. DT-RL is the first restart-based algorithm to achieve sublinear regret in a wide range of non-stationary environments. As a result, this contribution has significant practical implications, as it moves us closer to creating reinforcement learning algorithms that can effectively navigate real-world scenarios where uncertainty is inherent. By building on the success of restart-based algorithms in certain risk-averse reinforcement learning applications, we expand upon this concept and show that risk-sensitive versions of these algorithms can be just as powerful. In particular, we examine the existing risk-sensitive variants of DT-RL and explore their potential benefits and drawbacks. By applying a restart-based approach to a broad class of risk-sensitive reinforcement learning problems, we develop an innovative algorithm that outperforms existing methods and achieves nearly linear regret in non-stationary environments. Notably, our research focuses on RND-RL, a risk-sensitive variant of DT-RL, and proves its ability to achieve sublinear regret in a wide range of non-stationary environments. By generalizing this result, we identify a new family of non-stationary environments and establish the challenges associated with risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in these scenarios. Ultimately, our research contributes to the development of reinforcement learning algorithms that can effectively navigate uncertain and unpredictable environments. To generalize our results, we apply a restart-based approach to a broad class of risk-sensitive reinforcement learning problems and prove the existence of a new family of non-stationary environments in which RND-RL achieves linear regret. In modern distributed machine learning, the weighted power-p mean (WPM) aggregation function is increasingly used to combine gradients or models from parallel workers. While its application has been widespread, a fundamental issue arises when handling outliers, as WPM can be heavily influenced by anomalous data. This problem is particularly prevalent in big data analysis, where outliers are not uncommon. This paper presents a new aggregation method called Quadrant-weighted Power-p Mean (QPMM), an improvement over WPM. Under specific conditions, QPMM is mathematically equivalent to WPM, yet it is better equipped to handle outliers by dividing the data into quadrants and using a more robust aggregation technique for the anomalous sections. Our results show that QPPM is more resistant to outliers than WPM, and this advantage is maintained across various error measures. To validate our findings, a comprehensive experimental evaluation was conducted, which supports our claims. This study offers a new solution for a pressing issue in distributed machine learning aggregation, providing a more reliable alternative to WPM. Our code is available for public access at the provided link. Future research could focus on further optimizing our proposed method. Additionally, a potential area of study is how to dynamically adjust the quadrants to improve the method's reliability. Lastly, an intriguing possibility for investigation is whether this approach can be applied to other aggregation functions. With further refinement, these potential areas of research have the potential to significantly contribute to the field. Until then, our current results remain a significant achievement. We suggest a novel optical device that serves as a near-zone superfluid dark matter detector, capable of sensing the gravitational wave background and other parabolic scalar fields, in addition to single-atom quantum physics research. The device acts as an ultra-high sensitivity single-photon detector for gravitational wave signals, similar to the concept employed in dark matter detectors, but can also utilize Ising-like interactions between adjacent atoms to amplify signals. Such a device has the potential to contribute to single-atom quantum technology advancements and has various applications, including enhanced single-photon emission, quantum memory utilization, and the realization of artificial spin baths, making it a versatile tool for single-atom research. Furthermore, we propose an innovative method for reconstructing the shape of dark matter particles based on the detected atomic arrangements in our device. Lastly, we investigate the potential of our device to detect exotic parabolic scalar fields, setting up parameter boundaries for such fields and outlining their implications for our understanding of the universe. Overall, the dark matter photon detector offers a groundbreaking opportunity for single-atom research and has far-reaching implications for our understanding of the universe.

Our innovative approach represents a polymer as a discrete collection of its constituent monomers, allowing for the reconstruction of entire polymers through the connection of identified monomers. This method, which we refer to as the "core-OM" technique, first identifies a core monomer within a polymer through comparison with a extensive database of known monomers in a solution. If additional core monomers are detected in close proximity to the initial core, the shape and connectivity of the resulting polymer can be inferred. Notably, this method requires only one core monomer to accurately reconstruct a linear polymer and multiple core monomers for representing more complex topological structures. This strategy has been demonstrated effective in simulating various conditions, such as different concentrations of monomers in a solution and the presence or absence of light, to build an extensive library of known polymers. Ultimately, our "core-OM" technique offers a powerful new tool for the computer-based modeling of polymers. During the COVID-19 pandemic, intensive care units were overwhelmed, leading to a critical shortage of ventilators. In this crisis, using a single ventilator for multiple patients became a necessary life-saving measure. However, this setup presents a significant challenge: ensuring each patient receives their individualized tidal volume. Our study proposes a real-time control system to achieve this goal by using a model of the ventilator and the airway pressure sensor. The model is based on a parallel connection of two pneumatic circuits, which allows for the distribution of gas to each patient. The system identifies and responds to changes in flow rate, airway pressure, and patient volume within seconds. The results of our simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed control system in providing each patient with their desired tidal volume under various ventilator settings. The next step is to validate this model through clinical trials. The developed algorithm can be applied in two main configurations: when the flow source and pressure gauge are connected to one patient, and when they are connected to neither. In both cases, the system remains functional and accurately regulates the air mixing chamber to ensure each patient receives their desired tidal volume. The study also explores the impact of dead spaces, flow source characteristics, and pressure regulators on the ventilation system. The developed model is versatile and can be applied to different ventilator models with modifications based on their specifications. In conclusion, the proposed control system successfully uses a single ventilator to provide individualized ventilation to multiple patients under various operating conditions. In addition to critical care applications, this study has implications for research in airflow dynamics and engineering design of ventilators. The developed model can be used in future studies to explore other aspects of ventilator function. The model's simplicity and accuracy make it an excellent example for engineering and medical students to learn about pulmonary physiology and ventilator function. In terms of limitations, the study assumes a perfect seal between the ventilator and the patients' and ventilators' airways. Future studies can investigate the effects of air leaks on the ventilation system. The study also assumes that the patients' lung compliance and resistance remain stable. In cases where this parameter changes, the system can adapt through online identification of the patients' and ventilators' characteristics. Finally, the study suggests future applications of the developed algorithm in other medical devices, such as oxygen concentrators and continuous positive airway pressure devices. In conclusion, the proposed control system effectively uses a single ventilator to provide individualized ventilation to multiple patients under various operating conditions, making it a valuable tool during medical emergencies and a useful educational

The study finds that, assuming a linear regression model, a normal prior distribution, and a Gaussian error term with a minimum possible error variance, the posterior can contract at the optimal rate when the regression coefficients are estimated. However, if the error variance is unknown and only known to be greater than a certain value, a loss function that takes into account this additional information leads to a posterior contraction rate that is suboptimal. This result highlights a limitation of using such a loss function in other Bayesian models with unknown error variance. This research investigates the correlation between surface roughness in CNC machining, influenced by tool roughness and cutting conditions, using a statistical approach. An initial study with 27 experiments revealed that tool roughness has a more significant impact on surface roughness compared to cutting parameters. Building on this, a total of 81 additional experiments were conducted, confirming the initial findings. The resulting dataset of 108 experiments was analyzed using a statistical model to identify the interactions between factors and their effects on surface roughness. The results show that tool roughness has the greatest impact, followed by the interaction between feed rate and tool roughness, then cutting speed, and finally depth of cut, with the weakest effect belonging to radial approach rate. Furthermore, tool material and cutting tool geometry were found to have a substantial influence on tool roughness. This knowledge can be utilized to optimize cutting conditions for a specific tool to achieve a specified surface roughness level. Additionally, a predictive model was developed to estimate surface roughness based on cutting conditions and tool characteristics. This model can be applied to two different machining operations, with the condition that the tool is used within its valid speed and feed rate range. However, it is essential to note that surface roughness is highly dependent on tool geometry and these effects can vary between operations and materials being machined. Consequently, the model may require recalibration for different materials, even when using the same tool. This research successfully developed a predictive model for a CNC machining operation, specifically turning with a titanium alloy, using a specific tool set. The resulting model has an R-squared value of 0.94 and provides a reliable means of estimating surface roughness within the tested cutting conditions and tool characteristics. However, it is necessary to note that surface roughness is an inherently complex and non-repeating phenomenon. As a result, the accuracy and applicability of the model could be improved by increasing the number and variety of experiments conducted. This could potentially involve incorporating simulation tools, such as finite element analysis, to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms influencing surface roughness. Furthermore, the model could be refined to account for any systematic discrepancies between simulated and actual surface roughness values. In conclusion, this research has made significant contributions in understanding the effects of cutting conditions on surface roughness, as well as tool characteristics, through a combination of experimental and analytical methods. This study examines the Ahlfors regular conformal dimension of graph distance spaces and relates it to the conformal dimension of the underlying metric measure space. We demonstrate that for graphs with bounded degree and bounded vertex connectivity, the conformal dimension of their graph distances is equivalent to the conformal dimension of the underlying space. The proof relies on a novel translation technique and further extends to graph directed sets, yielding insights into their structural properties. Consequently, this leads to the discovery of certain conditions that imply the existence of unique directed paths between any two points in the graph, thereby shedding light on when directed path distances are equivalent to the original graph distance. We present numerical examples to illustrate the validity of our findings and the complexity of certain conditions, such as the relationship between the bounded connectivity number and the spectral dimension. Moreover, our work provides an alternative proof that the conformal dimension of graph distances is greater than or equal to the Lebesgue dimension of the underlying space, a fact previously observed by many researchers. The main results of this study can be extended to more general group actions and related phenomena, and we provide a specific illustration involving Cayley graphs. The study also provides an application to the directed path distance of infinite graphs with bounded connectivity, showing that this distance is conformally equivalent to the original graph distance. To conclude, we provide an example of a directed path distance that is different from the original graph distance, but shares the property of being Ahlfors regular with a conformal dimension of 1. This contrasts with the transitivity theorem, which states that for graphs with a conformal dimension of 1, the directed path distance and original graph distance are conformally equivalent and transitive, respectively. However, we note that the last statement requires the graph to have a connected underlying topological space, and does not hold for the Sierpinski graph or its directed version. Instead, the conformal dimension of these graphs is 2, which is the minimum possible value for conformal dimension. Moreover, these graphs exhibit unique properties, such as being directed tree graphs with bounded connectivity and infinite directed path connectivity. Finally, we note that the transitivity theorem also holds for graphs with a conformal dimension greater than 1, such as the dyadic tree and its directed version, as well as directed graph directed sets with bounded connectivity and infinite directed path connectivity. This concludes our study, which provides a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between graph distances, conformal dimension, and structural properties of graphs and group actions. This research introduces a novel living biometric framework, incorporating real-world living human body parts, specifically human hair, to create a functional and interactive authentication mechanism. The study delves into the development of a live person-based, pseudo-subjective intelligence (PSI) fingerprinting system, utilizing a distinct and unique characteristic, or signature, created from real-time live hair samples. The aim is to establish a link between a legitimate source and digital data, preventing unauthorized access and forgeries. To establish the legitimacy of a particular source, the proposed system employs a comparison of the extracted features from the obtained hair samples with a reference database. The effectiveness of the proposed system is evaluated using various metrics such as distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability of the signature templates, as well as the performance of the legitimate source authentication and whole area coverage in the reference database creation. The research also involves an experimental investigation of the proposed approach, applying it to real-world scenarios to determine its applicability and efficiency in real-time living biometric fingerprinting. The results demonstrate that the proposed method is both unique and repeatable, offering a practical solution for a functional and interactive living biometric fingerprinting system. The proposed approach has the potential to be adapted for various presentation attack (PA) modes, such as digital, analog, and live presentations, to prevent and detect forgeries effectively. Moreover, the study explores the use of hair samples in a PSI-based fingerprinting system, highlighting its potential and limitations as a real-time living biometric solution. Based on the findings, it is recommended to use a combination of distinct and unique characteristics, such as hair color and style, to create a more effective and repeatable living biometric fingerprint. The proposed system has the potential to be implemented in real-time, presenting a practical solution for a living biometric fingerprinting system. Finally, the study suggests future research directions, including the integration of multiple biometric sources and the development of more effective presentation attack detection methods. The theoretical framework presented in this study can be applied to various biometric systems, offering a useful reference for future research. The integration of the proposed method with existing biometric systems, such as face and voice recognition, has the potential to enhance their performance and effectiveness in a living biometric fingerprinting context. Maintaining private images is crucial, and graph models can effectively address this issue by representing images as undirected graphs, where image pixels are transformed into nodes and edge weights. To preserve image privacy, it's essential to identify the minimal subset of critical nodes that, when removed, renders the graph disconnected. Traditional graph models, however, have limitations in image privacy classification and do not adequately account for visual cues. To address this, a new approach, the Graph Privacy Advisor, utilizes a transformer-based model to predict node removal from graphs with varying structures. The approach comprises two key components: a pre-training stage using generic graphs and a fine-tuning stage using classified graphs. The assessment reveals that the Graph Privacy Advisor significantly outperforms the best existing methods, improving classification accuracy by up to 13.6% across different metrics. Moreover, the approach demonstrates superior robustness and flexibility in dealing with diverse graph structures. In this study, we focus on the challenges and opportunities presented by approximate arithmetic in the context of computational methods. We began by assessing the effects of approximate arithmetic on a basic matrix multiplication example and analyzed the outcomes in terms of relative error. The results showed that for a given level of approximation, the error can be mitigated by increasing the number of iterations. This insight led us to investigate whether we could exploit approximate arithmetic in a series of matrix multiplications, such as those involved in the solution of linear systems or the construction of probabilistic binary matrices. In this process, we demonstrated how the choice of approximate multipliers can influence the error and provided a theoretical framework for the relationship between matrix structure, approximate arithmetic, and relative error. The study also led to the creation of a new family of probabilistic binary matrices, which exhibit lower relative error compared to standard constructions, thereby demonstrating the potential for low-precision hardware utilization in future computational methods. The research was conducted using single-node CPU systems, with the prediction that similar behavior will occur on parallel architectures, where the benefits of approximate arithmetic may be more pronounced due to its potential to optimize communication costs. Searches for the pair production of charged Higgs bosons, particularly rare cases where both bosons decay into leptons of the same charge, have been conducted using comprehensive datasets, collected by the CMS experiment at CERN's LHC between 2016 and 2018. Multiple experimental findings, including seven events observed versus three anticipated, remain inconclusive in terms of standard model predictions. Additionally, searches for the standard model's most probable outcomes, such as charged Higgs bosons resulting from top quark decays and subsequently combining into boson pairs, have been carried out, yielding data that aligns with expectations in all scenarios examined. In contrast, a scenario involving charged Higgs bosons, resulting from the decay of top quarks, and subsequently combining into boson pairs, shows a slight discrepancy with standard model predictions with a significance of 1.4 standard deviations. Our research presents the results of a thorough study of the binary star system BD And, which had been initially identified as a unequal mass binary with nearly equal orbital periods. Recent observations by our team and additional data from the All Sky Monitor revealed an unusual, irregularly shaped dip in the light curve of the system, specifically a profound minimum in 2018 that wasn't present in previous years. We discovered that this peculiar feature recurred at precise times related to the system's orbital period, and further analyzed the phenomenon to rule out any feasible astrophysical explanations other than its likely connection to a third component in the system. To describe the data, we employed a generalized theoretical model for systems having three distinct components and applied a statistical method to assess the likelihood of various configurations. Our analysis suggests that a hierarchical system consisting of two close binaries orbiting around a common center provides the most probable explanation for the available data, with however, some residual discrepancies remaining unexplained. We also explored the possibility of a test particle influencing the system's motion, yet this concept didn't receive strong support. Given the presence of an eclipsing binary within the system, further research via high-resolution imaging and high precision spectroscopy could potentially reveal a physically connected, co-orbital relationship between the two binaries and their suspected companion. Moreover, our study emphasizes the significance of long-term observations in understanding complex celestial systems. To enhance user preference learning in recommendation systems, we have developed a novel module, referred to as the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement module (GAPE). This innovative module is designed to improve the performance of models by identifying the user's preferred aspects of items and incorporating a more precise preference learning outcome. The GAPE module is comprised of two primary components - a preference feature extraction module and a preference feature enhancement module. The preference feature extraction module leverages multiple item aspects to extract relevant preference features, whereas the preference feature enhancement module employs a user-independent transformer to refine these extracted features. The GAPE module is adaptable to various recommendation models through a fusion mechanism that seamlessly integrates it into the existing model. The effectiveness of GAPE in enhancing user preference learning has been demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets, which reveal significant improvements over the baseline models. Notably, our findings show that GAPE achieves an average boost of 11.6% in MRR and 6.3% in Hit@1 over the baseline models. Similar to the case of symplectic resolutions, the first obstruction group resides in the sheaf cohomology of the sheaf's soft locus. It also allows for the identification of a strong vanishing theorem for a particular condition, which implies that the obstructions can be reduced to the second hypercohomology space for that case. Recent research has focused on the role of the X(3872), a particle whose internal structure remains unclear, in these studies. In this contribution, two theoretical models of the X(3872) - a tightly bound state and a compactly bound state with significant orbital angular momentum - are examined. The hadronic interactions and initial conditions in the early stages of these collisions are computed for both scenarios. Mathematical expressions and numerical results for important reaction rates and initial conditions are provided. Our analysis reveals that the internal structure of the X(3872) significantly affects both the hadronic phase and, by extension, its earlier history. As a result, findings based on the particle's properties may be misleading unless the influence of its internal structure is taken into account. This study's results can be applied to a range of topics, including the particle's production, spectral function, and elliptic flow in both $pp$ and $PbPb$ collisions. These terms, typically found in the Lagrangian, can be represented by a matrix ($K_{ij}$) that links the U(1) currents to the scalar fields' derivatives. In such situations, even though the U(1) conservation law holds formally, it is impossible to find an operator that accurately represents the conserved current. Deep reinforcement learning has made significant advancements in resolving the classic planning stage vs prediction stage debate in motion planning. Our contribution addresses the former by employing a planning stage that leverages a pre-trained policy optimized via asymptotic optimization, as opposed to the conventional experience replay method used in the prediction stage. A novel, yet efficient, policy-based asymptotic optimization method is developed, along with an accompanying actor-critic framework tailored to this optimization setting. Theoretical models of supermassive black hole growth through gas accretion often struggle to reach the required masses before galaxy formation begins. A specific accretion mechanism, where a gas disk feeds a central black hole in a manner analogous to an Eddington accretion rate, has been proposed as a potential solution. A key aspect of this process is the rate at which gas is fed into these disks, and previous models have made unrealistic assumptions about this rate in relation to the overall mass of the gas within a galaxy. A more accurate representation is needed, one that takes into account how the gas within a galaxy is distributed and how it interacts with the central black hole. In a new study, a more detailed analysis of this process is explored, and it is found that the gas disk accretion rate is lower than previously estimated, and primarily accounts for a small amount of black hole growth over the course of a star-formation event. This growth, while relatively small, is sufficient to explain the massive black holes at the center of galaxies. Deep neural networks are highly effective classification tools, but they often fail to take account of their own limitations, resulting in overly confident outcomes all the more frequently as their prediction accuracy improves. Nevertheless, for tasks involving classification and critical decision-making processes, it is crucial to identify and account for the uncertainty inherent in their results. In this research, we combine the benefits of Monte Carlo dropout and Bayesian deep learning by employing a simplified approach to the variational inference method developed by Graves et al., aiming to apply uncertainty quantification to deep learning models without requiring substantial computational resources. We apply this framework to the challenging task of segmenting and detecting retinal vessels, a complex visual task, and compare its performance with other uncertainty quantification methods, such as MC-dropout, also accounting for the impact of hyperparameters on the model's performance. Our experiments demonstrate that this simplified approach yields comparable results to the original method in terms of predictive performance, while requiring significantly less computational resources. We further show that it is possible to leverage the uncertainty inherent in deep learning models by employing them as a prior for conventional stochastic gradient descent, a technique that is not reliant on MC-dropout or other uncertainty quantification methods. Our results indicate that models trained with this method exhibit improved performance, particularly in terms of predictive accuracy, compared to traditional deep learning models. We observe a significant reduction in the weight variance, from an average of 93% to 34%, indicating a substantial decrease in the reliance on uncertainty quantification. Furthermore, our approach has the added benefit of allowing the integration of prior knowledge into the model, a feature that is not available in standard deep learning methods. We verify this by comparing the average mean weights of models trained with and without uncertainty, observing a significant discrepancy of 94.8% between the two groups, indicating a substantial reduction in reliance on prior knowledge. In conclusion, our research demonstrates the efficacy of our simplified approach to variational inference, which yields results comparable to the original method in terms of predictive performance, while requiring significantly less computational resources. Additionally, we show that integrating this method into the traditional deep learning training process can improve the models' predictive accuracy, reduce their reliance on uncertainty quantification, increase their reliance on prior knowledge, and result in better generalization capabilities. Our approach has far-reaching implications for the use of deep learning models in classification tasks and can be applied to a wide range of domains, including the challenging and important task of retinal vessel segmentation and detection. The ever-growing information age has led to an immense accumulation of digital data. Consequently, the fields of machine learning (ML) and data science have gained significant prominence in the scientific community. Recently, researchers have leveraged ML techniques to tackle complex problems in materials science, including predicting phase formations and mechanical properties. Advanced simulations have also contributed substantially to understanding materials behavior. To further augment these methods, ML-based prediction coupled with simulations shows great promise. ML-based approaches can expedite simulations by identifying crucial atomic interactions and reducing required computational power. Additionally, simulated data can be used to train ML models, providing a supplementary means for evaluating algorithm effectiveness. This review explores the intersection of ML, data, and simulations in materials science, highlighting successful applications and potential avenues for future research. It also examines the challenges inherent in using ML and discusses the importance of integrating these methods in predicting materials behavior. Ultimately, the future of ML-based simulation-driven prediction appears bright, but it is crucial to acknowledge the existing limitations to guide research toward developing more accurate and efficient ML algorithms.

By leveraging these merged frameworks, known as GNN-DRL, we can tackle a range of difficult machine learning challenges including large-scale subspace learning, semi-supervised classification on complex graphs, and data representation on massive networks. In the area of subspace learning, our method surpasses state-of-the-art performance, exhibiting improved convergence speed and accuracy. For semi-supervised classification tasks, our framework exhibits exceptional generalization capability and high prediction accuracy. Furthermore, our model exhibits great potential in learning concise and interpretable data representations on large and intricate networks. Given its remarkable capabilities, we believe GNN-DRL will have a significant impact on graph-related learning tasks in the future. Experimental evidence strongly supports the claim that the synergy between graph neural networks and agent-based decision-making models significantly contributes to improved performance. Therefore, we anticipate GNN-DRL to be a vital tool for working with large and complex graph data in the future. The Sidon set problem, a well-known issue in harmonic analysis, has been reexamined in the context of the finite affine plane. Initially, this study confirmed the completeness of hyperbolas and ellipses regarding Sidon sets. Furthermore, it demonstrated the sufficiency of complete graphs and rectangles in relation to Sidon sets, while also identifying a lower bound for the complete graphs and rectangles in terms of the number of points in the affine plane. Notably, a counterexample to the completeness of squares was found. Additionally, the maximum number of Sidon sets that can be derived from complete graphs and rectangles was determined, along with a characterization of complete graphs and rectangles that are also dual Sidon sets. While the completeness of ellipses was confirmed, a counterexample to the completeness of triangles was discovered. The relationships between complete graphs, rectangles, ellipses, and hyperbolas in terms of Sidon sets were also explored, leading to the conclusion that complete graphs and rectangles are mutually exhaustive. Finally, a lower bound for the number of Sidon sets that can be derived from complete graphs and rectangles was found. This research partially answers an inquiry from Evans and Vsemirnov regarding the Sidon sets of ellipses and hyperbolas, while also raising further questions about the complete graphs and rectangles. As a result, this study significantly contributes to the field by providing significant progress on the Sidon set problem. Moreover, many of the techniques employed in this research are applicable to more general affine spaces. Consequently, this study offers valuable insights into the harmonic analysis of finite affine spaces. In addition, connections to the finite projective plane were also explored, leading to the identification of complete graphs and rectangles as dual Sidon sets in this context as well. Ultimately, this research provides an extensive understanding of the Sidon set problem in the finite affine plane. While the study does not resolve the problem in its entirety, it makes significant progress by confirming the completeness of ellipses and hyperbolas, identifying a lower bound for complete graphs and rectangles, and characterizing dual Sidon sets. Moreover, this research is significant because it is one of the few studies to contribute substantially to the Sidon set problem. As a result, this research marks an important milestone in the field by providing valuable insights into the Sidon set problem in the finite affine plane. Consequently, this research is likely to have a lasting impact on the field of harmonic analysis. Moreover, many of the techniques employed in this research are applicable to more general affine spaces.

This study investigates how various sampling methods on binary matrices are affected by different parameters. We find that matrices generated at random from a uniform distribution over all possible binary matrices conform to a specific exponential distribution. However, this property is utilized to create an optimal non-uniform probability distribution for sampling which yields a testable conjecture regarding the optimal solutions. Our findings also demonstrate that sampling matrices from this optimal distribution lead to a substantial improvement in our experimental results, with this enhancement being noticeable even when the probability distribution is approximated by a discrete non-uniform sampling method. In particular, we observe a notable improvement when approximating the optimal distribution by assigning a large probability to a single dominant eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix, resulting in a significant average running time of our algorithm. Even when the probability distribution is only slightly skewed towards the dominant eigenvalue, we notice a substantial improvement in our experimental results. These outcomes suggest that non-uniform sampling methods can be highly effective, offering potential benefits in various random matrix models. Moreover, the insights gained from this study may be applicable to other probability distributions as well. Lastly, the results of our experiments indicate that the average running time of our algorithm is typically very close to the optimal cases, even when the probability distribution is not known or not approximated well. This observation implies that the expected performance of our algorithm may be close to the optimal values even for general instances of the problem, making sampling a promising approach to finding efficient solutions. In addition to these theoretical findings, we also provide a new and efficient algorithm for solving systems of linear equations in nearly optimal time, further highlighting the potential benefits of sampling in combinatorial problems. Overall, the outcomes of our studies suggest that sampling could be a valuable tool for solving a wide range of combinatorial problems, potentially offering new avenues for efficient solutions. We hope that our results and findings will contribute to the development of novel sampling algorithms for various applications in the future. Additionally, we present an intriguing open problem for further research. Based on our experimental results, we propose a testable conjecture regarding the optimal solutions, offering a potential direction for further investigation in theoretical computer science. In line with this theme, we also discuss how our findings relate to the broader fields of algorithms, probability theory, and linear equations, ultimately contributing to the ongoing discussions in these areas. In conclusion, the outcomes of our studies offer significant insights into the capabilities and limitations of sampling, while also highlighting the vast potential of this approach for solving various combinatorial problems and potentially leading to new breakthroughs in algorithm design

We've developed a novel approach to solving the DGLAP equations that allows
solving the PDF evolution at different scales in a single step, rather than
incrementally. This method utilizes a matrix-vector multiplication concept,
treating the parton distribution functions at the lower scale as vectors and
the relevant coefficients (including anomalous dimensions) as the corresponding matrix.
This approach not only simplifies the PDF evolution but also makes it more efficient,
especially when accounting for uncertainties by solving the corresponding
transfer matrix. This enables a straightforward fitting procedure at various scales
using a least-squares minimization technique and a data covariance matrix.
This method can be applied to both PDFs and parton distribution functions (PDFs)
and is illustrated with a mock data simulation, showcasing its effectiveness. 
This technique will be incorporated into the cxxpdf C++ library as an alternative to
existing DGLAP solvers. Further, we've developed a Python interface, also named
pdfasym, to facilitate the use of this method, along with an extended version of
the NNPDF fit procedure. This approach is utilized to obtain a new NNPDF fit, named
pdfasym, utilizing data up to next-to-next-to-leading order with various data sets. 
This pdfasym fit demonstrates improved behavior at higher Q^2 when compared to
the NNPDF4TIS fit, utilizing a four-flavor scheme and fitting uncertainties at
the NLO level. Additionally, we've analyzed various biases in DGLAP-evolved PDFs
at lower scales and found significant corrections in quark and gluon distributions
at Q=0.1 GeV, underscoring the importance of proper evolution to extract PDFs
at commonly used lower scales like Q=0.01 GeV, relevant for a range of processes
including the study of charm hadronization in various environments. Finally,
we've examined the relevance of power-assisted uncertainties in the DGLAP
evolution, demonstrating their magnitude in comparison to the uncertainties
associated with the anomalous dimensions and the transfer matrix. This has the
potential to reduce the total uncertainties in the PDFs at lower scales by up to
25\%, as shown for the u and s quark PDFs at Q=0.01 GeV. This pdfasym fit,
along with an accompanying pdfasym fits webpage, as well as the cxxpdf and
pdfasym code repositories, are available for reproduction and further analysis.
