Protecting applications from malicious libraries has been the primary focus of recent research, but ensuring the security of those using interpreted languages like PHP and Python remains challenging due to the ease of modifying system calls in these languages. Our solution, Timeloops, addresses this issue by creating specialized guards for each system call that can detect and prevent the loading of malicious libraries in C. By employing timing-based authentication, Timeloops verifies the origin of system calls and prevents potentially harmful API calls, all while maintaining a lightweight footprint and minimal performance impact. In experiments using PHP and Python, Timeloops demonstrated a high detection rate for known attacks and showed promise in preventing unknown attacks, all while limiting false positives to less than 1%. Furthermore, Timeloops requires significantly fewer system calls than existing solutions, reducing the overhead by a factor of 5 to 10. The project is open-source and can be found at https://timeloops.org. Our ongoing efforts involve integrating Timeloops with additional security features such as memory protection and network filtering. Additionally, we are exploring more sophisticated techniques, like machine learning, to further improve Timeloops' capability to block unknown malicious library attacks. As a next step, we aim to expand Timeloops' applicability to languages with user-defined memory management, such as Java and C#. In this context, the primary challenge will be designing effective memory auditing mechanisms to detect memory-related vulnerabilities like buffer overflows, heap-based buffer overflows, and use-after-free attacks. We are also investigating ways to integrate Timeloops with existing memory protection systems to enhance its functionality and improve the detection of complex attacks that involve code injection and data tampering. Ultimately, our ultimate goal is to create a comprehensive security framework that can effectively detect and prevent both system call-related and memory-related vulnerabilities, making it possible to evaluate the security of applications more efficiently. In this regard, we plan to conduct a thorough study on the types and frequency of vulnerabilities in real-world applications to determine the most critical threats to target. In the short term, we aim to enhance Timeloops' ability to block unknown malicious library attacks by integrating memory and network auditing mechanisms. In the long term, we aspire to expand our research to user-defined languages, focusing on developing effective mechanisms for detecting memory-related vulnerabilities and integrating Timeloops with existing memory protection systems. In this study, we analyze a voter model where individuals are labeled as members of two species, representing coordinates of a unit square, with species corresponding to grid cells in this space. The model is asymmetric, with species competition influenced by a grid-based structure, but subject to random factors. The random element is controlled by a parameter that can be adjusted to understand the model's dynamics. We show that, under certain conditions, the competition results in coexistence, whereas other scenarios lead to dominance by one species. Furthermore, our research indicates the possibility of outcomes other than species coexistence or extinction. These may include patterns of periodic and complex behavior as well as the emergence of spatial structures. To confirm our theoretical findings, we present numerical simulations validating our predictions. Additionally, we establish a link between the model's dynamics and the model's degree distribution, revealing the significance of homogeneity in grid cells. The model's simplicity and accessibility make it an ideal teaching tool to illustrate complex biological and environmental phenomena using a geometric representation of species competition. Notably, at the point of maximum entanglement, the reduced density matrix's diagonal elements resemble a pure state, thereby facilitating near-perfect quantum teleportation. Our findings are further validated by both analytical calculations and numerical simulations. Specifically, analytical calculations employ a combination of exact and perturbative treatments, while numerical simulations utilize a Romberg integration method to analyze long-time behaviors. We have extended Greenberg's strong approximation theorem beyond one-dimensional local rings, encompassing all finitely generated abelian group stages of arithmetic for G-algebras, where G is a finite group with trivial square subgroup. Moreover, this generalization is expressed through the use of Euler products. By comparing algebraic and adelic representations of G-algebras, we have formulated a framework that is based on partial Hasse invariants. Within this context, our definition of strong approximation is satisfied by G-algebras that are either reduced or have a specific height exception. Notably, this theorem applies to G-algebras representing arithmetic manifolds with non-trivial square shear. This work is further illustrated by examples, including those related to modular curves and non-reduced G-algebras. Additionally, we have derived an application of this generalization, which confirms the strong approximation property for G-algebras of height less than or equal to 2. This result is particularly relevant to arithmetic manifolds with non-trivial square shear. Specifically, this applies to the case of G being the cyclic group of order 2. This generalization also shares connections with other theories, including the Kolyvanov-Shafarevich height formula and the G-algebraic version of the Manin-Mumford conjecture. Lastly, we have outlined possible directions for future research, including the possibility of extending our findings to G-algebras with an infinite group structure. One such scenario involves considering the case of G being the additive group of integers, in which context the theorem may be related to the arithmetic pure motive theory proposed by Kahn-Lebacque. Ultimately, this motivates the proposal of a more extensive arithmetic pure motive framework that incorporates strong approximation at all finite stages of group G. This could serve as a foundation for a unified approach to arithmetic geometry involving motivic and adelic aspects, as initially suggested by Borel's "motifs arithmico-algebriques". This research introduces a modified DED2D scheme, referred to as TFIET, designed to address the lack of user data and energy in a two-tier wireless communication system. To resolve this issue, TFIET enables direct data and energy transfer from the base station to users through two separate channels, while ensuring that the transferred data and energy are coupled in time but not mutually dependent. Building on a recent study that established the fundamental limits of any adaptive TFIET strategy, this work focuses on developing an optimal TFIET policy utilizing the Bollabos-Love-Thomas framework. To formulate this problem, two distinct optimization problems were defined, one to maximize the total information transferred and another to maximize the total information transferred per unit time. Analysis of these optimization problems revealed that an optimal TFIET policy results in either purely forward or purely backward transmission modes, with data and energy transferred exclusively in one direction. To achieve this optimal policy, a novel algorithm was created, requiring only a single iteration and yielding performance within 0.78 dB of the maximum possible transmission rate. When compared to suboptimal TFIET and DED2D schemes, this algorithm provided 0.78 dB and 1.32 dB improvements in transmission rate, respectively. Furthermore, this work established a lower bound on the optimal transmission rate, showing that any adaptive TFIET strategy can have a maximum transmission rate no more than 0.78 dB below the best possible rate. Lastingly, this research found that any suboptimal TFIET strategy can have a maximum transmission rate within 1.32 dB below the best possible rate. These findings provide valuable insights into the performance of TFIET, DED2D, and general adaptive TFIET schemes. With these results, it is now possible to measure the closeness of any TFIET or DED2D scheme to optimality. If an TFIET or DED2D scheme achieves a transmission rate within 0.78 dB or 1.32 dB of the maximum possible rate, respectively, it must be operating at or near optimal performance. Otherwise, there exists a better adaptive TFIET or DED2D strategy. With these benchmarks in place, future research can focus on developing closer approximations to these optimal performance limits. We conducted a dynamical study of a massive diffuse globular cluster, Westerlund 2, to understand its mass loss pattern over time. A 200 kiloparsec journey by a 3000 solar mass star allowed us to estimate the cluster's mass ejection efficiency at approximately 50%. This efficiency is comparable to that of other young massive clusters in the Milky Way. We observed significant changes in the cluster's mass distribution during the star's travel and noted the presence of less massive stars that had not yet undergone the star's mass range. This is consistent with a mass turnover period for the cluster. In contrast, the cluster's outer layers have already experienced massive-star ejection, while internal regions have not yet seen this process. This internal mass can eventually be ejected in the future. Based on this analysis, we suggest Westerlund 2 is around half-way through its life. Like other young massive clusters, it will eventually disperse its stars into the field, altering the region's stellar population characteristics. This work highlights the value of observing the movement of individual stars within a cluster to understand massive-star ejection and stellar population evolution. This research can inform the development of more accurate population synthesis models in the future. This research combines the capabilities of handwritten Text Recognizers (TRs) and
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to enhance the quality of degraded document
images. First, a handwritten TR is adapted to work with degraded images by using
pre-processing techniques. Next, a GAN model is created to generate high-quality
handwritten text based on degraded images provided by the adapted TR. The
integration of these models improves the visual clarity of degraded images, making
them more readable for the TR. However, using real handwritten samples for the
discriminator in the GAN training process is impractical due to the need for vast
collections of handwritten samples. This research overcomes this limitation by
using the output of the adapted TR as input to the discriminator in the GAN training
process. The results show that the quality of degraded images is improved, but the
gain tapers off after a certain point, and introducing noise to the degraded images
results in poorer recognition rates. This contrasts with previous findings that text
recognition performance can improve with added noise. A possible explanation for the
discrepanies is the difference in the type of degradation and hand-written text used
in the studies. This research presents a novel application of TRs in conjunction
with GANs, and the resulting improvement in degraded image quality opens up new
possibilities for enhancing handwritten text recognition in real-world scenarios. 
Additionally, this research demonstrates that TRs can be adapted to work effectively
with multiple image formats, and the study provides new insights into the effects of
image degradation on text recognition performance. The study also showcases the
potential of TRs in generating text along with its layout in various formats, 
such as paragraphs and tables. This research serves as a foundation for exploring the
use of TRs in conjunction with GANs in handwritten text generation. As a result of
this research, several new datasets were created, including one for visual
verification of text recognition and another for generating handwritten text. These
datasets are available for public use. Lastly, this research highlights the
possibilities of using TRs in conjunction with GANs to improve handwritten text
recognition, and the study paves the way for future research in this area. 
Additionally, this research is the first to use the generated text from TR along with
GAN to improve the visual clarity of degraded images which can further lead to
improved accuracy of TR. This research is significant in the field of handwritten
text recognition

Accurate text extraction from ID cards is crucial for a wide range of applications, including law enforcement, border control, and customs. Despite significant advancements in Natural Language Processing (NLP), extracting ID card text remains a complex task, especially when the cards are distorted, faded, or written in handwriting. To address this challenge, we propose an end-to-end approach that combines the strengths of both deep learning and traditional image processing techniques. Our approach leverages a convolutional neural network to extract ID card features, which are then fed into a recurrent neural network trained on a word-level language model. To further improve performance, we incorporate the means of morphological analysis and a language model's likelihood of seeing given n-grams. Our approach has been successfully evaluated on the AccessID 2020 challenge dataset and achieved exceptional results, surpassing state-of-the-art benchmarks by a significant margin. This study examines data-driven channel estimation in millimeter wave (mmW) systems, employing narrowband waveforms with wideband modulation for high mobility scenarios. We integrate a LSTM neural network into a data-driven channel estimator to optimize performance. Our findings indicate that, upon being trained with simulated channel data, this integrated approach yields improved estimation accuracy, particularly in situations of high mobility, surpassing conventional channel estimation methods. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of channel model parameters on LSTM performance and assess its capability to generalize to untrained scenarios. Additionally, we compare LSTM with randomization techniques in a real-world channel environment, revealing that both methods are susceptible to deviations from assumed signal models, but randomization exhibits better generalizability. Lastly, we contemplate the potential of applying LSTM to real-world channel estimation scenarios. To achieve this, we created an mmW testbed on a high-speed vehicle, simulating both LSTM-assisted and conventional channel estimation methods. Our results show that LSTM outperforms conventional methods in actual channel conditions, validating its efficacy in practical applications. This research lays the groundwork for the utilization of deep learning in data-driven channel estimation for mmW systems. To further explore this topic, we suggest designing a testbed that integrates deep learning-based channel estimation, which can be used to investigate various factors such as generalizability across different signal models and environments. Moreover, we propose that this testbed could be employed to investigate the impact of numerical issues on deep learning-based channel estimation, which is a significant area of study. Lastly, we aim to contribute to the development of a comprehensive channel estimation methodology that incorporates both conventional and deep learning-based techniques. To achieve this, we plan to design a testbed that integrates an adaptive LSTM-based system, allowing it to adjust the model's complexity in response to changes in the system's environment or parameters. This research has the potential to make a significant contribution to the field of channel estimation, offering a novel and efficient approach to parameter-free deep learning-based channel estimation. Moreover, we plan to investigate the potential of applying a Bayesian approach to combine LSTM and conventional channel estimation methods, with a view to leveraging their respective strengths in a unified framework. This research aims to address key challenges such as the need for large training datasets, the potential for overfitting, and the requirement for generalizability across different signal models and environments. To overcome these challenges, we suggest designing a testbed that integrates a Bayesian-approached deep learning-based channel estimation system, which can be used to investigate the efficacy of this approach in practical applications

During training, neural networks may become overly specialized on their training data and fail to generalize well to new cases, a limitation known as overfitting. A novel algorithm is proposed, combining a common regularization technique with an adaptive data selection approach and a neural network damping mechanism, to address overfitting and enhance generalization. This method initially uses random data to stabilize the neural network, before gradually introducing the full training set. During training, the algorithm regularly switches to a damping phase, freezing the network's parameters and forcing them to converge to a stable state. Meanwhile, only a subset of the training cases is selected based on a margin score, with overfitting cases excluded to promote generalization. To prevent over-specialization, the algorithm also uses L2-regularization and the adaptive data selection mechanism. The algorithm has been successfully applied to 13 difficult image classification problems, achieving accurate results on three datasets. Notably, the algorithm achieved a top-1 accuracy of 78.18% on the ImageNet dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art models at the time of writing. Thorough ablation studies confirm that each component of the algorithm contributes significantly to its performance. The proposed method represents a groundbreaking approach to deep learning, addressing a key limitation and achieving state-of-the-art results on a range of classification tasks. The development of novel and efficient methods for manipulating light and sound in the optical and acoustic domains is of great interest for creating innovative photonics and acoustic technologies. Recent research has demonstrated the ability to precisely control graphene-based patch antennas to produce line waves through sound-generated photodetection, yet these protocols are limited to micrometer-scale precision. We have devised a innovative approach that allows for the design of graphene patches to generate line waves at will, while also maximizing their propagation velocity and efficiency. By formulating an electrical current equation based on the principles of perturbation theory and combining it with numerical simulations, we can accurately determine the optimal graphene size and shape to achieve the desired line wave propagation. Notably, our method can also produce multiple line waves with distinct frequencies and velocities by shaping the graphene patch accordingly. When applied to a triangular shape, our algorithm produces an asymmetric pattern that produces line waves with higher velocities than traditional monolithic photonic crystals. Furthermore, our results show that our approach can achieve line wave velocities approaching the theoretical limit, while also exhibiting robust resistance to perturbations and optical leakage. We believe that our method will enable the development of new and efficient graphene-based photonic and acoustic technologies. Moreover, our approach can be adapted for use with other meta-materials, such as meta-molecules and meta-patches, thereby holding great potential for future applications in light and sound manipulation. To establish a collaborative, dynamic, and interactive learning environment between multiple humans and multiple robots, we present FedLMI, a Federated Learning-based framework for multi-robot teams. FedLMLI leverages the combination of a) a novel communication system that enables human-to-robot and robot-to-robot data exchange, and b) a specialized representation of local models that combines individual robot-specific knowledge, allowing the team to learn and adapt collectively. Empirical results demonstrate that FedLMI surpasses existing benchmark approaches in both single-human and multi-human settings, and has the potential to improve the performance of robotic swarms in dynamic tasks such as navigation, control, and seach and rescue operations. The code for FedLMI is publicly available at https://github.com/alexandremath/FedLMI. For further details on the project, please visit https://alexandremath.github.io/FedLMI/.

We introduce a new approach to achieve efficient bias-reduced estimation in nonparametric models by leveraging Fourier series. This novel method assembles an initial estimate, obtaining a corresponding frequency-based representation, and then uses the smooth nature of the bias to downsample the frequency domain, thereby enhancing estimation efficiency. The proposed estimator is versatile and can be applied to a range of established techniques such as the classic De Walque estimator and more recent proposals like the Bell-Brown and Buis Bell-Brown estimator. By incorporating our estimator, the conventional De Walque estimator is improved by achieving a more substantial $n^{2l}$ rate of convergence, where $l$ is a positive integer representing the smoothness level. Furthermore, our estimator is shown to be compatible with various measures of smoothness such as the sup-norm, mixed norms, and Besov spaces. The proposed estimator is also integrated with alternative frequency domain downsample methods, like the orthogonal basis systems and the Fourier series for data with periodic structure, to yield more efficient results. Through simulations and real-data analyses, the enhanced performance of our estimator is demonstrated. The associated R code is available upon request. This paper presents a novel knowledge graph link prediction approach, termed RE-LP, that leverages relation extraction data to identify missing object links. Unlike traditional methods that rely on generalized knowledge graph structures, RE-LP utilizes specific relation data to predict object links. The proposed method is straightforward yet effective in incorporating additional data, and it can be applied to various techniques for object link prediction. Experimental results on multiple benchmark knowledge graphs demonstrate that RE-LP achieves notable improvements when paired with a generalized knowledge graph structure. Additionally, RE-LP performs exceptionally well on the Wikidata entity linking task, which involves a more challenging and real-world scenario with less generalized knowledge graph structures. The source code for RE-LP is available at https://github.com/flashblue/RE-LP.

Many machine learning models are beneficial when high-quality training and inference data share the same data distribution. However, the situation changes when we consider generalization, specifically when there's a discrepancy between training and testing data conditions. In this research, we explore an alternative to traditional parametric models by representing learning tasks locally using functionals, rather than parameters, resulting in improved generalization for low-dimensional signals. Our method involves representing both data and the underlying signal using a combined Gaussian process and enforcing similarity between the underlying manifolds representing training and testing data through functional correlations. This framework is scalable and can be applied to various learning tasks, including supervised regression and classification, as shown in our experiments which demonstrate improved generalization performance and accurate prediction capabilities. In a semi-generative model, the target variable is conditioned upon in a conventional sense, yet its effects are accounted for through an unconditioned prior distribution on possible causes, resulting in a conditional (effective) prior for the target once those causes are identified. This approach is taken further in a new class of models where, unlike traditional Bayesian methods, the optimal model given the data is not necessarily one that assumes the data is error-free – instead, a best-fit model is chosen that takes into consideration the potential for measurement errors within the given information. Additionally, a novel semi-supervised learning technique has been devised, where the target variable's effects are balanced against the potential for the data to be incomplete – an issue addressed by introducing a new type of regularization. This approach leads to the development of unique optimization problems, whose solutions are shown to have meaningful interpretations in line with expectations in statistics and machine learning. By applying this framework to well-known models, as well as developing new ones, it is demonstrated that the proposed semi-generative model outperforms traditional probabilistic models in various scenarios where the data may be limited or prone to errors. As a testament to its utility, the proposed model successfully accounts for common issues in the analysis of real-world data, such as missing values, noisy observations, and the reliance on external sources of information. We establish a general theory for describing systems defined on a finite-dimensional, smooth, compact Riemannian manifold. The set of possible momenta and the set of possible positions are both represented by the points on the manifold, with the relationship between them determined by the de-Broglie wavelength, which serves as the maximum resolution of momenta, and the geodesic distance, which serves as the maximum resolution of positions. The geometric structure of the manifold is independent of its coordinate system, and the same description applies to both free and interacting systems. When the manifold is approximately flat, as in the case of Cartesian space, our theory reduces to standard position and momentum operators. Additionally, we illustrate a system defined on a two-dimensional sphere that demonstrates wave-particle duality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any system can be described both classically and quantum mechanically by mapping the set of possible momenta to the set of possible classical momenta and defining the inner product such that Liouville's theorem is preserved. Finally, we show that any system can be described either by a partial differential equation or by a Fock representation of a von Neumann algebra, and that these two descriptions are equivalent when the manifold is approximately flat. However, these two descriptions are generally non-equivalent for complex geometries. Notably, the lack of equivalence between these two descriptions has significant implications, including the possibility that a future understanding of reality may necessitate a description that surpasses both the quantum mechanical and the geometric framework. In particular, geometric operations that preserve the manifold may have inherent uncertainties, which could potentially resolve long-standing debates about time translation invariance and system dualities in string theory. In conclusion, our theory offers a novel and general approach to describing physical systems, and it holds significant potential for contributing to our understanding of the world. Some of the ideas presented in this article are reminiscent of earlier proposals, such as the proposal of M. S. Marinov for describing a free particle using a single geometric object, and the proposal of R. J. Glauber for describing light as a geometric soliton. However, our theory is significantly more comprehensive, and it has the potential to be more useful, as evidenced by its application to a two-dimensional system and a non-relativistic hydrodynamics model. In the future, we plan to expand the scope of our geometric framework to include relativistic systems, and to use it to investigate fundamental problems in physics, such as the origin of the universe and the nature of matter and charge. The increasing importance of social media in modern life has made it a key platform for voice expression and dissemination of information. As a result, it has become a significant source of information, influencing people's knowledge and perceptions. The narratives shared on social media shape public opinion, yielding a wealth of information for researchers to explore. Exploring this information can provide insights into societal issues, enabling more informed debates and discourse. Nevertheless, social media posts are often characterized by informal language, abbreviations, and grammatical errors, making them challenging to comprehend. To unlock the full potential of social media information, there is a need for machine learning models that can effectively process and interpret this data. To address this need, we developed a novel approach, SocNar, for extracting and analyzing social media narratives. SocNar leverages a transformer-based architecture and a pre-trained language model to accommodate the unique features of social media language. Additionally, we annotated a large dataset of Twitter posts, comprising 48k narratives, to facilitate the development and testing of machine learning models. This research presents a novel event detection system capable of processing event data with varying spatial resolutions, by projecting them onto a unified grid based on their geographical coordinates. Each data point is represented as a vector combining its own metrics and those of neighboring locations, before being fed into a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) model. The proposed system can handle multiple data series (e.g. sensor readings, weather forecasts, population estimates) with different resolutions, and is capable of learning a unified metric to combine them. Unlike previous approaches, this method does not require synchronization of datasets with different temporal resolutions. The system can handle real-time and historical data simultaneously, and is scalable for large datasets. The performance of this method was demonstrated in two practical applications, namely (1) predicting crowd density from sensor readings and weather forecasts, and (2) estimating crowd density from weather forecasts and population estimates. Experimental results show that this approach outperforms traditional methods and machine learning algorithms in both scenarios. Furthermore, the proposed system achieves a high Area under the ROC Curve (92.0%) and has a good F1-score (88.0%), indicating its strong classification performance. By combining this with data from the Planck satellite, we derived the fraction of matter in the universe that consists of cold dark matter, finding it to be $0.8139 \pm 0.0274$ within the framework of the six-parameter LCDM model. Deep learning has become a powerful approach for solving inverse problems, but its applications are often limited due to its susceptibility to adversarial attacks. A novel framework, called the Adversarial Robustness through Variable dependence on external sources (ARVES), has been developed to enhance the robustness of deep learning models. This framework employs an additional neural network to identify key variables that can withstand perturbations in deep learning models. By doing so, ARVES consistently produces stable results, as these key variables can accommodate and counteract potential attacks, thereby safeguarding the model's accuracy. Experiments have been conducted on image denoising, super-resolution, and video de-mosaicing tasks using neural networks, and the results show that ARVES significantly boosts the robustness of these models against various perturbations, whether they are small, medium-sized, or extreme. Notably, ARVES achieves this robustness without compromising their original performance. Building upon ARVES, several variations of the framework have been explored to further improve the robustness, including incorporating regularization and constrained optimization. These variations demonstrate the effectiveness of arming key variables with adversarial capabilities to boost robustness. As such, ARVES represents a pioneering approach in using adversarial machines to boost the robustness of deep learning models. This methodology can be applied to a wide range of deep learning techniques, such as those employing adversarial networks, and even extend to other machine learning methods, potentially opening up new avenues for enhancing their robustness. Furthermore, ARVES has potential applications in safety-critical systems, where reliable performance under adverse conditions is crucial for human life and property, and could potentially be useful in systems related to healthcare, image processing, and law enforcement. In conclusion, the proposed framework of ARVES represents a groundbreaking approach to bolstering the robustness of deep learning models through the use of adversarial machines. This methodology has far-reaching implications for the future development of deep learning techniques, and could potentially have a significant impact on systems requiring high reliability, such as those involved in the diagnosis of diseases, the analysis of images, and the investigation of crimes. In the future, the framework of ARVES could be used as a basis for investigating the use of adversarial machines in various applications, and exploring alternative methods for enhancing the robustness of deep learning models, such as the use of uncertainty-based methods or generative adversarial networks. Ultimately, the potential applications of ARVES are vast and it has the potential to significantly contribute to the development of deep learning techniques that are both accurate and robust.

The dynamics of a rumor's spread can be complex, with factors like early promotion affecting its peak popularity and location influencing its decline. A nonlinear, nonlocal model is developed in this study to analyze the dynamics of a rumor based on its characteristics and the information about its dissemination. The model examines how a rumor's peak intensity and attenuation coefficient are affected by its properties and the impact of spatial factors. Compared to a purely temporal model, the novel model shows more realistic and localized rumor behavior, with greater variation in its patterns. Furthermore, the model's results are applied to a real-world example, illustrating the significance of both precursor information and spatial factors in determining a rumor's spread. The model's outputs can be utilized to identify early indicators and potential sources of a rumor. The findings suggest that a rumor's characteristics and spatial factors have a substantial influence on both its peak intensity and attenuation coefficient, with early promotion often leading to a greater and longer-lasting impact, and localized dissemination resulting in greater and more prolonged variations in the rumor's spread. This research investigates the effectiveness of different dimensionality reduction techniques, including PCA, ICA, and AE, in a hyperspectral pixel classification task. Using three public datasets, we found that these methods can enhance signal reconstruction while improving classification accuracy. Specifically, AE was shown to offer better results than PCA and ICA when combined with supervised classifiers, particularly when working with larger datasets. Notably, the use of reduced-dimensional data also resulted in improved reconstruction errors and a more stable training process for the classifiers. While supervised PCA and ICA achieved comparable performance to their unsupervised counterparts, supervised AE consistently outperformed them, highlighting its benefits in a semi-supervised setting. Our findings suggest that using a combination of AE for dimensionality reduction and supervised classifiers is a viable approach for hyperspectral pixel classification. Moreover, the reconstructed images resulting from this method displayed better visual quality and fewer artifacts compared to those obtained with other reduction techniques. With its superior performance and signal reconstruction capabilities, supervised AE is recommended as a promising technique for hyperspectral pixel classification. Based on these results, we propose the potential of utilizing this method in real-world applications, such as remote sensing. Deep neural networks have exceptionally high storage and computational requirements, which has led to various compression methods being developed to tackle these challenges. A comprehensive review of deep neural network compression is provided, covering recent advances in model pruning, quantization, compact architecture design, and efficient inference frameworks. This article also examines the interconnected relationships among existing compression methods and suggests potential future directions for further improvement. Moreover, a detailed analysis of the application of deep neural network compression to different platforms and scenarios is offered. Finally, the main challenges and limitations of current compression-based approaches are identified and possible areas for improvement. Nonetheless, it is crucial to acknowledge the significant progress made so far; hence, this review is intended to facilitate future research and development in the field. Experimental results demonstrating the efficacy of different compression methods on image classification, object detection, and segmentation tasks are also demonstrated, highlighting the diverse applications of deep neural network compression. A novel approach, ProCS, utilizes refined protein sequences to improve structure prediction accuracy by constraining overall protein shapes, specifically through assessment of contact maps. Integrating ProCS with the ROSETTA structure prediction tool, we developed a protein structure refinement method that leverages native contact prior knowledge derived from high-resolution protein structures. ProCS refines contact maps by filtering out long-distance contacts and establishing a distance-based constraint, while also maintaining the map's overall density. In structure refinement, ProCS significantly outperforms the existing ROSETTA tool in terms of conformational similarity and overall structural accuracy, as verified by the High Accuracy Protein Structure Prediction (HAPSS) benchmark. Notably, ProCS achieves top-tier results in multiple assessment criteria across various target protein size and resolution groups. Although ProCS was primarily designed for given sequences with high accuracy, it still demonstrates substantial improvement for sequences with lower accuracy. Our study demonstrates that enhancing contact map accuracy through a filter-like procedure contributes to better structure prediction and refinement. Based on these findings, we propose ProCS as a valuable addition to structure refinement tools and anticipate its potential applications in various fields, such as protein design and structure prediction. The ProCS method can be accessed through our website at https://salilab.org/procs/. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/salilab/procs. The contact map prior can be downloaded from the ProCS website as well.

In our study, we demonstrate that training on a subset of predictions, tailored to the target loss function, can effectively bridge this gap, resulting in performance comparable to conventional methods. Notably, our approach allows for the discovery of novel, highly effective loss functions, such as a simplified MINE variant, which outperforms CE and MINE on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Our technique is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of under-represented loss functions, opening up new avenues for optimization. We have investigated the intermediate- and low-temperature electronic properties of monolayer TiSe2 by employing angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Our study revealed the emergence of a charge-density-wave state below 250 K, accompanied by clear signs of exciton condensation at 225 K, as seen in the evolution of the condensate-weight parameter obtained from the many-body corrections to the band structure. The exciton condensation gives rise to a significant lattice distortion at 200 K, as evidenced by the formation of a heavy Fermi-like state, and the excitation of phonons in the real and momentum spaces. The strong coupling between electrons, photons, and phonons in this exciton condensate result in the observation of distinct Raman scattering signals at 82 and 14 cm^-1 at 200 K, which are indicative of intra and inter-layer phonon modes, respectively. Our research demonstrates that the exciton condensation gives rise to a new class of many-body states that couple with phonons, photons, and other bosonic modes, thus offering a broader understanding of electron-boson interactions. Our findings also open up new avenues for the creation of new bosonic states through electron-boson coupling in two-dimensional van der Waals materials. Moreover, we have successfully developed a new theoretical framework for exciton-phonon coupling, which we have applied to a general class of multi-component Fermi systems interacting with bosons and phonons. Our approach allows for the determination of many-body corrections to the band structure, dynamical structure factors, and Raman scattering spectra with unprecedented accuracy, as seen in the case of TiSe2. Our research demonstrates that our theoretical framework is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of materials exhibiting exciton and/or phonon condensation, such as TiS2 and VSe2. Our study on TiSe2 also offers a new perspective on the concept of superconductivity, as it reveals that exciton condensation can lead to the emergence of a heavy fermi liquid state that is compatible with superconductivity. Our research thus suggests the potential for the realization of a new class of heavy fermi liquid superconductors that originate from exciton and/or phonon condensation. Our work also highlights the significance of electron-boson and electron-phonon interactions in two-dimensional van der Waals materials and superconductors, as exemplified by MgTe2 and few-layer SnSe2. This research addresses two key issues in active learning algorithms: ensuring diversity in selected samples and dealing with noisy labels in the data. We present a semi-supervised minimax entropy-based active learning approach, drawing on the minimax fair income distribution model. This method seeks to optimize the trade-off between entropy-based uncertainty and diversity in selected samples, while accounting for class imbalance and noisy labels in the data. We evaluate our approach through comprehensive experiments on various real-world datasets, comparing it to established active learning methods. The results demonstrate that our proposed technique outperforms the baseline methods, with particular improvements in datasets with high label noise. Furthermore, we investigate how label noise affects the performance of active learning algorithms and the diversity of selected samples. Additionally, we develop a theoretical framework to analyze the label noise and its impact on the minimax entropy-based active learning approach. Based on our findings, we make several practical recommendations for active learning algorithms. The proposed approach and associated code are available online for replication purposes. We expect this work to contribute to the ongoing discussion in active learning research. Moreover, we anticipate that our study will benefit researchers working on semi-supervised active learning tasks. This study analyzes the similarity of musical instrument sounds in popular songs from the 1950s to the 2000s. By treating songs as points in a multidimensional space, researchers created a map of song characteristics and calculated the distances between them. The results show that songs with similar instrument sounds appear clustered together in this map, exhibiting decades-based groupings. The arrangement of points in space reveals an evolving pattern of instrument sound profiles across different time periods. Additionally, the study discovered that songs using the "wall of sound" production technique, prevalent in the 1960s, occupy a distinct region of the map, characterized by bright and treble-dominated sound qualities. By transferring the decade-based patterns in song characteristics to music genres, researchers were able to create a predictive model that accurately classifies genres based on era, achieving a high success rate. The study's findings contribute to an understanding of how music production techniques and instrument sounds evolve over time. Furthermore, the study's results can be used to create predictive models of music style based on time period, which can inform the creation of future music compositions. This paper is centered around a discrete-time Markov chain with a finite state space, where each state is assigned a positive reward value. We investigate how the structure of the process changes over time, specifically how the number of distinct blocks within the process evolves. We demonstrate that, as time progresses, the cardinality of these blocks inevitably becomes comprehensive, encompassing every state in the chain, provided that the process's expected block size remains finite. Furthermore, under the condition that the process has a bounded relative entropy rate, we establish a lower limit on the process's complexity, measured as the average number of bits required to express a block, relative to its length. We also examine how these results generalize to the setting of stationary ergodic processes sharing certain similarities with Markov chains. Importantly, the concepts explored in this study are applicable to processes lasting any duration, be it finite or extending indefinitely. Additionally, we illustrate the significance of these findings through examples. Lastly, we highlight an area where future research could be directed. Overall, the findings contribute valuable insights to our understanding of discrete-time processes.

This work proposes a novel, flexible approach to understanding the meaning of mathematical assertions through their proven relationships with other statements. In this framework, the meaning of an assertion is encoded as a collection of weaker, inferable statements with unique properties. The semantics of our system are founded on three key axioms, which enable the reliable interpretation of commonly employed logical operations and allow for a clear distinction between the original assertion and its various weakening forms. By analyzing these axioms, we identify correspondence relationships between different logical frameworks, while also revealing an inherent order among them. Ultimately, our approach is grounded in a novel, analysis-free representation of provability, which reframes the notion of provability as a series of containment relationships with maximal and irreducible forms. This formulation is contrasted with other, related concepts in proof theory. Specifically, we observe that the maximal containment relationship aligns with the notion of weakly maximal provability and that the irreducible forms correspond to strongly minimal provability. Additionally, we show that the standard provability relation is sandwiched between these two forms, thereby establishing a chain of containment that accurately reflects the relationships between commonly employed provability notions. By adopting a reliable interpretation of the provability relation, we gain insight into the meaning of universally quantified assertions and, through an analysis of their behavior under weakening, identify correspondence relationships between universally weakly maximal provability and other, related concepts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach enables a reliable interpretation of existential assertions, while also revealing an intrinsic order among universally weakly maximal provability, existentially weakly maximal provability, and universally and existentially weakly maximal provability. A highly efficient training method called reward learning utilizes human feedback by assigning rewards to general comparisons, such as "which of these actions is more effective?" Instead of requiring numerous individual comparisons, we investigate batching these comparisons to a limited number of options, e.g., "which of these three actions is the best?" Batching has two key advantages: it lessens the burden of human labor and often yields more precise training data. We draw on the principles of statistical analysis to determine the optimal batching strategy and demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments on a navigation task and an autonomous driving application, where batching comparisons lead to a 2-4 times faster training process without compromising performance. Our work provides a systematic approach to batching comparisons and identifies a balanced strategy between data quantity and accuracy. We also offer a straightforward tool to guide practitioners in selecting an appropriate batching method given specific circumstances. Ultimately, our research reveals batching as a practical and efficient technique for awarding humans more general comparisons to enhance the efficiency of reward learning. We investigate a fluid flow defined on a loop in 3D space, assuming it follows a perfect rotation. To study the loop's dynamics, we map its configuration, where a key point is fixed, to a corresponding point in a 2D space, taking into account the area it encloses and the orientation of a defined vector when projected onto a plane. A novel metric is established for this mapping, which reflects the distance between loops based on the area they enclose and the difference in their vector configurations. In the context of this metric, we demonstrate that the space is neither entirely Euclidean nor Riemannian, instead falling into a category of spaces that are neither simply connected nor of a constant curvature. We derive an equation for the geodesic distance between loops and, by analyzing a specific motion pattern, verify that the loop's configuration evolves along a geodesic path. These findings provide a framework for understanding vortex ring behavior and their dynamics in terms of a defined manifold structure. Additionally, we identify key features of this space that influence its connectivity properties. As a notable consequence, we find that loops with different configurations cannot be connected by a straight line, which has implications for their generalization to other dynamical systems. Furthermore, we explore the conservation of a specific quantity in this system and, based on numerical simulations, illustrate the complex behavior of vortex rings as they traverse this space, involving both simple and intricate path trajectories. These findings demonstrate the richness and uniqueness of vortex ring dynamics. As an extension of this study, we consider a related space based on a different mapping of their configurations and, through metric analysis, identify a key difference that distinguishes this space from the original one. As a practical application, our understanding of the metric space of vortex loops can be utilized in approximating their behavior over extended time periods, thereby facilitating predictions through Monte Carlo simulations. To illustrate this, we demonstrate a hypothetical scenario involving the prediction of a vortex ring's behavior. Ultimately, our research provides a comprehensive theoretical framework for the study of vortex rings, their dynamics, and the space in which they move, as well as provides a useful tool for their analysis. To address this, a novel AIPW+REG estimator is proposed, which combines the original AIPW formula with a specially designed regularization technique. The research demonstrates the distinct advantages of this new estimator over traditional AIPW and Wright-type estimators through both theoretical analysis and practical applications. Additionally, key aspects regarding the choice of regularization method and potential bias in the predictive accuracy are explored. This project's primary goal is to create highly precise predictions for the mass of the tau lepton, a subatomic particle. Lattice QCD offers a promising approach to achieve this level of precision, given its established and accurate results for the masses of other particles. However, the tau's mass poses a significant challenge due to the limitations of perturbative QCD, a theoretical framework used to understand particle interactions. To overcome this issue, we employ a more direct method of determining the tau's mass by simulating its behavior in a virtual environment and applying a theoretical correction to ensure accuracy. Our approach involves two distinct methods of matching the virtual and real worlds to validate the precision of the results obtained. In this study, we present the details of these methods, the simulations performed, and the steps taken to ensure the accuracy of the results, including a thorough analysis of systematic errors. Our preliminary findings based on an incomplete dataset reveal a mass for the tau lepton of $1177.91(74)$ MeV, a level of precision nearly two orders of magnitude higher than the current experimental standards. This study marks a major breakthrough in the application of lattice QCD to the tau's mass, a first in the field's history. Our study's results will soon be updated with the inclusion of the full dataset, an improvement that is expected to significantly reduce the errors and lead to a highly precise prediction of the tau lepton mass in the near future. In particular, we expect the errors to be limited to a small fraction of a millionth (10^-6), a level of precision that is comparable to the experimental measurements of other subatomic particles. Once confirmed, our prediction will be the most precise of its kind, a testament to the power of lattice QCD in understanding the behavior of subatomic particles. Our study's results will also have far-reaching implications for the field of particle physics, an area of study that is central to our understanding of the universe and its fundamental constituents. In particular, our prediction will contribute to the ongoing efforts to create highly precise predictions for a wide range of subatomic processes, an area in which lattice QCD plays a vital role. These predictions are crucial for the ongoing and future experiments such as the proposed Belle II experiment, a particle accelerator that is expected to significantly improve our understanding of the universe and its fundamental constituents. Our study's results will also have an impact on the future experiments such as the proposed PANDA experiment, a particle accelerator that is expected to significantly improve our understanding of the universe and its fundamental constituents

In a rotating, differentially heated annulus of fluid, baroclinic waves develop at the surface, influenced by variations in temperature and the strength of the outer and inner walls. These waves can be studied using a surface-based diagnostic technique, which generates time-series data by projecting the vertical velocity field onto a specific pattern. This data is then analyzed using methods like Fourier transform, to identify the frequency and wavenumber of the dominant wave; and other techniques like spectral analysis, to understand the distribution of energy across different frequencies and modes. This diagnostic provides a way to quantify the movement and behavior of baroclinic waves over time, and their relationship with the walls of the annulus. By applying it to a series of numerical simulations with varying outer wall strength, we demonstrate how the technique works and identify its ability to quantify high-frequency noise. Additionally, we use this diagnostic to understand how the frequency and amplitude of barcllinic waves change in response to the strength of the outer wall. These results are comparable to previous studies using other methods, such as measuring the time it takes for a wave to circumnavigate the annulus. By applying spectral analysis, we find that the energy of these waves is typically concentrated around a specific frequency and mode, and that the distribution of energy across different frequencies and modes does not show a clear trend with outer wall strength. Finally, we find that the amplitude of these waves does not show a clear relationship with the strength of the outer wall, and that the presence of baroclinic waves is observed across a wide range of strengths, from weak to very strong. This suggests that the formation of these waves is not solely the result of a particular strength of the outer wall, but rather of the overall differentially heated and rotating environment of the annulus. By applying this diagnostic and analytical technique to a series of numerical simulations with varying parameters, we can gain a deeper understanding of the behavior of baroclinic waves, and their response to changes in the conditions that drive their formation. This research demonstrates the value of combining numerical simulations with analytical techniques to identify and quantify complex phenomena in fluid dynamics. Additionally, the diagnostic and analytical methods employed here can be adapted for use in future studies of other fluid dynamic phenomena, such as geostrophic vortices and wave modes. This could involve modifying the diagnostic technique to project the time-series velocity data onto different patterns, such as a simple sine wave or a complex function, and using spectral analysis to identify the energy distribution across different frequencies and modes. This study develops a Bayesian approach to estimate the parameters of models describing extreme events, such as the likelihood and probability density functions for the generalized Pareto, lognormal, and logistic distributions. The models rely on a tuning parameter'm', which is part of a weighted likelihood estimation and is determined by minimizing a weighted version of the loss function. The optimal'm' values vary depending on the prior distributions assigned to the model parameters and are typically specific to each model. Therefore, instead of using a universal'm', we investigate the properties of Bayesian posterior distributions given the maximum a posteriori estimates of the model parameters, as well as the behavior of the models for small'm' values. Simulation experiments and a case study using real data from wind speed observations are used to evaluate the performance of the proposed Bayesian models. The optimal number of data points to use in the estimation process, as well as the potential for the models to be extended by introducing new latent parameters, are also investigated. The posterior distributions of the model parameters are estimated using Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, and the results show that the Bayesian approach can provide accurate estimates of the model parameters and their uncertainty when'm' is small. Our goal is to develop an efficient policy search method that can find a nearly optimal policy under corruption while also being resilient to various levels of corruption. To achieve this goal, we have leveraged a corrupted version of the advantage function and established a connection between the corrupted and clean reinforcement learning problems. Based on this connection, we have developed a novel algorithm using a corrupted version of the policy gradient method. Our results show that the expected regret of our algorithm is O(epsilon^(-2) sqrt(T) log(T)/beta) when the policy is corrupted, and O(epsilon^(-2) T log(T)/beta) when the environment is corrupted. These results demonstrate the dependence on epsilon, a known quantity, leading to improved regret bounds compared to algorithms that estimate corruption levels. Our study has also explored the challenges of unknown corruption levels and the limitations of using corrupted versions of value functions. Our work contributes to the development of robust reinforcement learning algorithms, particularly in environments that are susceptible to corruption. Our experimental results have validated the efficacy of our algorithm in scenarios with known corruption levels. This study examines the approximate controllability of the impulsive heat equation, a model that incorporates discrete impulse effects and stochastic noise, using a single control input. We address the issue of impulse controllability and find a sufficient condition for approximate controllability around a specific time period, specifically at impulses and a short time interval following them. Furthermore, we investigate the control required for approximate controllability and establish a key inequality involving the difference between bounded and unbounded impulsive effects. Additionally, we generalize our results to multi-dimensional impulsive heat equation models. Our analysis is supported by various numerical examples that verify our theoretical findings on approximate controllability. Notably, we discover that the high-frequency control impinges upon the high-frequency perturbation with a frequency inversely proportional to the spatial dimension, a behavior influenced by the nature of the impulsive effect. We also explore the application of our results to continuous heat equation models, a case that is found to be uncontrollable under a specific high-frequency frequency threshold, whereas the impulsive effect can facilitate approximate controllability down to a much higher frequency. Lastly, we explore the approximate controllability of stochastic impulsive heat equation models, a case that requires a sufficient condition on the control parameter and impulsive effect and yields a controllability result within a shorter time interval compared to deterministic models. Our analysis is further generalized to multi-dimensional stochastic impulsive heat equation models, a case that presents an upper limit on the control parameter due to the interplay between stochastic noise and impulsive effects. We verify our theoretical findings through numerical examples and observe that the impulsive effect can facilitate approximate controllability even when the stochastic noise fails to do so, a case also applicable to stochastic partial differential equation models. Our study offers a new perspective on the approximate controllability of these models, a field of study that has garnered significant interest in recent years. We investigated the interaction of a motor protein fueled by electric current in an optical trap, and found that electric current can produce forces strong enough to drive the motor's movement, even in the absence of a gradient. Our results demonstrate that electric current can propel a motor protein through a biological system, and potentially provide a means to control the motor's movement. Moreover, we discovered that electric current can produce a force large enough to overcome the motor's static load, and observed the motor escaping from an optical trap to reach a target. The use of electric current to power a molecular motor offers a new means of controlling the motor's movement, and potentially allows for the development of more efficient molecular machines. This research focuses on the computational efficiency of the f-Convolution, an advanced convolution operation between two arbitrary functions f and g, typically resulting in a high-dimensional polynomial expression. Computing the entire convolution output is often unnecessary, as only a single entry might be required. To address this issue, this study proposes a symbolic factorization method to directly evaluate a specific entry of the convolution without computing the entire convolution polynomial. The factorization technique is based on a fundamental mathematical concept and can be validated analytically. This approach has been validated through high-performance coding in the SymPy symbolic mathematics framework, achieving a notable speedup of several orders of magnitude in comparison to the standard convolution calculation. The proposed method reaches near-linear scalability when applied to large-scale problems, as demonstrated in the provided benchmarks. To the best of our knowledge, this factorization-based efficiency enhancement represents the first application of symbolic factorization to optimize computational convolution. The associated code is freely accessible on the SymPy GitHub repository for further exploration. Our analysis utilized the DOOPy code, which analyzed data from the VOSPIRIS instrument and the Keck AMOS telescope, operating at wavelengths between 0.8 and 2.4 $\mu$m. We introduce a novel method to examine the QCD ground state's spectral properties, allowing for a detailed analysis of hadronic contributions. This formalism is applied to two problems: (i) we investigate the potential existence of tetraquark states, discovering that the $0^{+-}$ channel in $\pi\pi$ scattering is influenced by tetraquark formation, yet also receives significant contributions from corralled mesons and, in quark model languages, Dibaryon formation; (ii) we re-evaluate the kaon loop contribution to the pressure of QCD, identifying a previously unreported effect that significantly impacts the results. Additionally, our study highlights the importance of including the quark's intrinsic momentum in the ground state and the limitations of the quark model when trying to understand the results. Both of these findings have important implications for ongoing research in the relevant fields. Finally, the spectral density analysis is compatible with ongoing lattice QCD simulations that aim to directly sample the QCD ground state. A refined version of dynamic mode decomposition, capable of analyzing nonlinear problems, has been created through a kernel-based approach. By utilizing a kernelized version of the Gram-Schmidt process, this method integrates multiple measurement techniques to solve complex nonlinear problems without needing the underlying equations that govern the system's behavior. A key advantage of this method is its ability to handle diverse data sets, differing in form and structure, to identify the underlying patterns in a nonlinear system. A crucial step in the method involves the effective integration of multiple kernels to enhance pattern extraction, and a determination of the optimal number of modes required to accurately represent the system. The method's effectiveness has been demonstrated through its application to multiple nonlinear problems, including a simplified Rayleigh-B\'enard system and a more complex laser-induced fluorescence data set. The results show that this method can accurately identify the system's states and dynamics in both cases. Furthermore, the method has been compared to other low-dimensional representations and dynamic mode decomposition variants to showcase its superior performance. The exoplanet HD 80606b, orbiting a G-type star in a near-circular orbit, is notable for experiencing one of the largest temperature fluctuations among hot Jupiters. In our study, we analyzed data from multiple instruments on the Spitzer Space Telescope, taken at different points in the planet's orbit, and found that HD 80606b's equilibrium temperature drops by approximately 500 K (from 1273 to 773 K) as it orbits its star. By modeling these observations, we determined that the planet's size and curvature of its orbit contribute significantly to the temperature change. Notably, our findings indicate that HD 80606b's atmosphere is characterized by strong winds of at least 5 km/s and a thermal expansion rate of 1.1+/-0.2 km/s per degree Kelvin. Additionally, we estimated the planet's size to be approximately 1.03+/-0.13 times the size of Earth, and our analysis suggests that HD 80606b's atmosphere is likely dominated by iron and magnesium compounds. Our results are consistent with a hydrodynamic model of the atmosphere, and we discuss the implications for future studies, including those using the James Webb Space Telescope. Ultimately, our findings highlight the significance of accurately understanding the uncertainties in exoplanet size and orbital distance for the field of exoplanetary science. Specifically, we derive the following results: Firstly, we conclude that Fixed-Source Reachability in directed acyclic graphs can be resolved in linear time parameterized by the treewidth. This conclusion enhances the findings of Elbassioni, Kout, and Wahl (ICDT'14) and Bozzato, Vardi, and Viglietta (IJCA'20). Secondly, we prove that Fixed-Target Reachability on directed acyclic graphs can be resolved in linear time parameterized by the treewidth, thereby improving the algorithm from Elbassioni et al. (ICDT'14) which had a time complexity of O(k^|V|). Finally, we note that these conclusions use algorithms parameterized by the treewidth, yet this parameter can be restricted to just one for various problem instances where the treewidth is fixed. This observation yields linear-time parameterized algorithms for general graphs under fixed treewidth conditions, comparable to the best known parameterized results for general graphs (e.g., see Chen, Kout, and Wahl, ICSM'15; Bozzato, Vardi, and Viglietta, IJCA'20; and Iglesias, Giordano, and Vardi, LICS'21). The key to our conclusions lies in an efficient algorithm for computing the set of sources reachable by a given path, which can be derived from the works of Elbassioni et al. (ICDT'14) and Lammich and Wiese (FSTTCS'14). Moreover, we introduce a new data structure - the 'forward abstract representation' - to facilitate the rapid calculation of the set of sources reachable via a given path. This data structure comprises a forest derived from the directed acyclic graph along with its 'forward' abstract representation, enabling the determination of a set of sources in O(|E| + |V| \log k) time. The algorithm optimizes power allocation, subchannel assignment, and beamforming weights by utilizing a DCA method. We investigate a simple model of two coupled populations, where one population is affected by a long-ranged mean field interaction and the other is affected by diffusive coupling. This model is inspired by the Goodwin model, a fundamental model in Michaelis-Menten kinetics that underlies oscillating solutions in biological systems. Our analysis reveals that the presence of the long-ranged mean field interaction and diffusive coupling leads to the emergence of spatially heterogeneous solutions, which are stable in a specific range of parameters. This heterogeneity gives rise to patterns of one population being dominant in a particular region and the other being dominant in another region. This phenomenon is further enriched by the diffusive coupling, which causes waves of one population to trigger changes in the other population, ultimately resulting in the formation of diffusive shocklines. This study provides a foundation for understanding the origin of spatial patterns in systems of coupled populations through mathematical modeling. It also has implications for systems where interactions are limited to local areas, such as in the Goodwin model, which we verify through numerical simulations. Ultimately, this research contributes to the broader field of pattern formation in biological systems. It is also relevant to various fields where such patterns occur, including ecology, cell biology, and immunology. In the SemTab 2022 track at ISWC 2022, we presented SEM-TAB-FACTS, a dataset and competition that combines semantic web knowledge acquisition with data annotation guidelines. The competition attracted 18 team participants, who submitted 33 valid entries for the knowledge acquisition task and 23 entries for the data transformation component. The outstanding performance of the top-ranked team in the knowledge acquisition task revealed a significant gap between automated and human-based approaches, indicating that there is still considerable potential for improvement in knowledge acquisition through automated methods. The top-submission achieved a 71.9% accuracy in relation to the annotated data. The data from this competition have been made publicly available to enable further research. Additionally, we introduced a new sub-task focused on justifying data transformation operations with web-based explanations, which garnered interest from three participating teams who submitted a total of six entries. The outstanding performance of the top-ranked team in this sub-task reached 66.67% by accurately explaining the most frequent data transformation operations. The data from this competition have been made accessible at https://sem-tab.org/2022/track/sem-tab-facts/ for the purpose of enabling further research. The technical papers presented at SEM-TAB-FACTS have been published in the SEMTAB proceedings volume, and the research methodology can be found in a companion publication at CEUR-WS. The dataset used for SEM-TAB-FACTS has been updated to incorporate the results from the competition, and it can be accessed via the SEM-TAB-FACTS website. The dataset has been updated to reflect the outcomes of the competition by incorporating the annotated data along with the explanations and justifications for the selected samples. The code utilized for participating in the competition has been made publicly accessible via the SEM-TAB-FACTS website. The updates to the dataset and code aim to facilitate the replication of the study and to provide future researchers with opportunities to improve existing methods by learning from the published results and code. The knowledge acquisition task has been integrated into the knowledge graph embedding evaluation framework, which has been made available on GitHub. The knowledge transformation task has been incorporated into the PyKEEVL framework, which is also hosted on GitHub. The knowledge transformation task can be accessed via the PyKEEVL interface by running the command 'pykeevl semtab_facts_2022', which enables the execution of existing validation cases along with the development of new ones. The knowledge acquisition task can be accessed via the command 'pykeevl semtab_facts_

Utilizing the expectation value, as defined by Dirac, of Hermitian operators, and adhering strictly to unitarity, it demonstrates that all necessary physical properties can be quantified with complex measurements. Further, building on the principles of scattering theory, it shows that Mirror Quantum Mechanics can be defined, and reflection and transmission coefficients are readily derived from first principles. This value of $t$ can be estimated in O(n^(2.5)) time and, in some cases, can be computed exactly in O(n alpha(n)) time, where alpha(n) is the Ackermann function's asymptotic value. By studying this problem, the relationship between shortest paths, distances, and metric dimensions is explored. Additionally, two variations of the problem are considered where the distance matrix is restricted to exact geodesic distances and where the distance matrix is approximated. It's found that these issues have different complexities and are influenced by the graph's properties, such as being a circle graph, a chordal bipartite graph, or a sparse random geometric graph. The research also identifies open questions and potential areas for further investigation. This problem has potential uses in developing efficient distance estimation protocols and has connections to graph labeling problems, particularly where labels are subject to a limited memory constraint. This study investigates the performance of an O3-UV reactor in removing sulfur dioxide (SO2) as a proxy for VOCs. SO2 was mixed with oxygen and water in a quarts reactor and exposed to a low-pressure UV lamp emitting at 254nm. The reactor's efficiency in destroying SO2 was evaluated under various conditions, including variations in oxygen concentration, initial SO2 concentrations, and reactant flow rates. A first-order kinetic model was used to analyze the data and determine the reaction rate constants. The study found that reactor size and residence time significantly impacted the removal efficiency of SO2, with higher residence times resulting in greater destruction rates. Additionally, the research indicated that the reaction rate constant increased with increasing oxygen concentrations, but decreased as initial SO2 concentrations rose. A possible explanation for these observations is that SO2 acts as a catalyst in the reaction, consuming oxygen and reducing the destruction rate as its concentration rises. A mass balance model was also developed to predict SO2 concentrations and simulate the reactor's performance under different operating conditions. Comparisons between theoretical and experimental results showed good agreement, suggesting that the models accurately capture the chemical reactions occurring in the reactor. However, the research noted that the models do not account for mass transfer limitations, which become apparent at higher gas flow rates and lower oxygen concentrations. As a result, the destruction efficiency of the reactor is lower than expected under these conditions. Based on these findings, the research recommends increasing the reactor size or reaction time to enhance its ability to remove pollutants using the O3-UV technology. Alternatively, the study suggests that supplementing the reactor with an scrubber could effectively remove pollutants in smaller, more efficient systems. Finally, the research proposes that future investigations into UV-oxidation systems focus on the role of mass transfer and chemical kinetic interactions in determining reactor performance. By understanding these interactions, designers can optimize chemical engineers to achieve higher efficiency and destruction rates in UV-based air pollution control systems. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach to segment and isolate various components of a virtual platform, enabling the creation of customized architectures for testing and benchmarking. By employing this technique, we identify the distinct impacts of different hardware modules on the speed of neuromorphic accelerators during both synaptic operation and data movement. Furthermore, we introduce a device under test, DUT-16, a 16-bit RISC-V based SoC with integrated neuromorphic cores, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our segmentation method during training and inference experiments on both synaptic operation and sparse convolutional workloads. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the design of neuromorphic accelerators, encouraging the integration of data movement components into the synaptic operation pipeline to optimize overall performance.
