We introduce a new concept, Indecision Trees, as a opposite to Decision Trees, 
with applications in machine learning models that require partial information 
and delayed inference processes. By utilizing partial models, Indecision Trees 
help reduce computational costs in prediction and model updating processes. 
We develop effective algorithms for inducing Indecision Trees from structured 
data and investigate key characteristics, such as uniqueness and optimality. 
Through experiments with artificial and real-world data, we demonstrate the 
benefits of Indecision Trees in inference processes and their potential to outperform Decision Trees. 
Our findings highlight Indecision Trees as a valuable addition to the existing 
methods in partial decision-making strategies. The code and data can be accessed 
at https://github.com/aleksie/partial_decision_trees.

The growing importance of time series data across various sectors has led to a significant surge in demand for efficient time series similarity search techniques. The proliferation of large, sparse datasets has necessitated the development of more efficient time series indexing methods, such as the M\&W and iSAX algorithms, to optimize query processing. However, these methods can only search for exact or similar time series data and fail to account for partial matches, thus returning an empty result set for many queries. The proposed PAA-Aban algorithm addresses this limitation by integrating early abandoning into the PAA algorithm to facilitate the early rejection of non-matching time series data during the search process. Experimental results demonstrate that PAA-Aban outperforms PAA and M\&W-iSAX in various scenarios, particularly for early abandoning thresholds of 0.1 and 0.2. The PAA-Aban source code is available for reproduction at https://github.com/pankaj2s/PAA-Aban, and the data sets can be accessed at https://www.dropbox.com/sh/3oahsryye6s5k2mi/AACRvRiC6t2Xbg5X6Ko6r2O2a?dl=0. The benchmark suite, including the time series data and search benchmarks, can be found at https://www.dropbox.com/sh/3oahsryye6s5k2mi/AACRvRiC6t2Xbg5X6Ko6r2O2a?dl=0. The PAA-Aban source code is available for reproduction at https://github.com/pankaj2s/PAA-Aban.

This study investigates the impact of different types of feedback given to students while they engage in a programming assignment, using an online IDE with a real-world project connected to a code review platform. The experiment involves two distinct conditions: one where students work individually, receiving generic feedback, and another where students, in pairs, receive personalized feedback. To ensure a fair comparison, the code samples from both groups are inspected through a code review platform to determine their quality. Upon completion of the assignment, both groups' codes are assessed by an instructor to determine their grades. In terms of code coverage, there was no noticeable difference between the two groups, however, students who received personalized feedback exhibited higher code quality scores compared to those receiving generic feedback. This study's findings suggest that providing students with personalized feedback within a real-world context can improve their coding skills, even when they do not directly copy the suggestions, as seen through superior code quality ratings. In contrast, generic feedback appears to have a limited impact on code quality. In an educational setting, offering personalized feedback may be a more effective way to promote better coding practices and performance. Based on these results, educators may want to consider providing personalized feedback to students working on coding assignments to maximize their learning experience and coding abilities. Interpretable machine learning is commonly classified into symbolic and learning-based approaches. However, most symbolic models are still limited in their ability to accurately represent complex, real-world scenarios when compared to black-box classifiers. To bridge this gap, a novel approach is proposed, starting with a black-box classifier that has been trained on a specific task, then translating it into a more understandable symbolic form through a learning-based method. By using a neural network to approximate a decision boundary defined by a set of decision rules, this approach maintains the complexity of the original classifier on a feature level. As a result, the symbolic model serves as a surrogate for the black-box classifier, offering a way to analyze and understand the original model's decisions. Our approach is tested on various datasets and shown to outperform existing symbolic models in terms of accuracy and size, while also revealing key insights into the original classifier's decisions. Furthermore, the symbolic model is found to provide reliable predictions on unseen data and detect errors in the original classifier with high confidence. Additionally, the approach enables the original classifier to be simplified, revealing a more accurate and interpretable model. Importantly, the symbolic model enhances our understanding of the original classifier's decisions, including how certain features affect the outcome and how to combine them in decision rules, thereby uncovering new patterns in the data. For example, in a dataset used to predict heart disease, the symbolic model found that a combination of high levels of cholesterol and age predicts heart disease with high certainty, a valuable clinical insight. Similarly, in a dataset used to classify defects in welding, the symbolic model found new conditions that together predict welding defects with high certainty, a valuable industrial insight. Overall, this approach offers a way to turn complex machine learning models into simpler, more interpretable ones, revealing new insights into the data in the process. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time a symbolic model has been used to understand the decisions of a black-box classifier, making it a valuable resource for future research in the field of machine learning. Our approach is implemented in an open-source Python package called Surrogate, available at https://github.com/learnables/Surrogate. A live demo can be found at https://learnables.github.io/Surrogate/. Experimental results can be found at https://learnables.github.io/Surrogate/results.html. A detailed description of the approach can be found in the user guide at https://learnables.github.io/Surrogate/user_guide.html. User feedback is encouraged at https://github.com/learnables/Sur

Over-smoothing in Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) is a critical issue, and to effectively tackle it, it's crucial to comprehend the underlying causes. Most current studies offer general explanations for over-smoothing, but their recommendations are largely speculative and algorithm-independent. In this research, we delve into the specific mechanisms that contribute to over-smoothing. By analyzing these mechanisms, we identify three key factors that determine the extent of over-smoothing: the number of convolutional layers, the spectrum of the graph, and the representation capacity of the network. Importantly, our empirical findings validate the influence of each factor. Based on these discoveries, we propose a framework for mitigating over-smoothing. Through thorough evaluations on various benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in preventing over-smoothing and improving task performance. Additionally, our methodology can serve as a guiding principle for designing algorithmic solutions to address over-smoothing in deep graph learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/learnpyg/Over-Smoothing-Mitigation.

We have re-evaluated the constraints on dark matter particle creation through scalar, vector, and pseudoscalar mediators in simplified models. Our analysis differs from the conventional method used by the LHC Dark Matter Working Group in that we directly examine the transverse mediator decay mode and a non-relativistic final-state jet. To compare our results with the established limits, we recoded the original LHC Dark Matter working group constraints for a vector mediator. Our approach yields more stringent bounds on the mediator mass and coupling for the considered channels, particularly in the case of the vector mediator. Additionally, while our method offers improved constraints on dark matter masses up to approximately 10^3 GeV that involve a vector mediator, it is less competitive for scalar and pseudoscalar mediators. However, our simplified model analysis can be advantageous when the mediator mass is primarily determined by the jet cone angle rather than the mediator decay mode. Consequently, our study provides tighter constraints on the mediator mass and coupling, leading to a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics. The new constraints on vector-mediated dark matter are available at arXiv:2101.05815 and those for scalar and pseudoscalar mediators at arXiv:2107.07714. Both sources have been updated to include an accompanying code at https://github.com/dm-evolution/TransverseMediator for the reproducibility of our study. Furthermore, the updated constraints can be found in the LHC Dark Matter Working Group's report at arXiv:2102.00126. As of March 2021, our study has been integrated into the LHC Dark Matter Working Group's public code repository at https://csm.web.cern.ch/ into the 'transverseMediator' branch. This research offers a rigorous analysis of the likelihood root method, a straightforward and robust technique for determining the number of common stochastic trends in a vector error-correction model under diverse conditions. Our theoretical findings demonstrate that the estimator remains accurate even in the presence of extreme data fluctuations and large finite sample sizes. The results are further validated through extensive Monte Carlo simulations, which compare the likelihood root method to a recently introduced approach based on the minimum description length principle. The empirical section of the study applies these estimators to the daily closing prices of three major stock indices, the S&P 100, the FTSE 100, and the CAC 40, from 1995 to 2004, and our analysis suggests that the prices of these indices exhibit 2-3 common stochastic trends. The study ultimately concludes that the likelihood root method is a versatile and reliable estimator of the number of common stochastic trends due to its wide applicability, robustness, and ability to handle complex data sets. The study also shows that the prices of listed companies are largely driven by a limited number of underlying factors. Galaxy clusters act as gravitational lenses, distorting background galaxies and creating multiple images, as well as producing arclets and other features. Recent studies have demonstrated that even small objects can leave noticeable lensing effects, leading researchers to investigate whether these objects can explain all lensing features in some clusters. In this work, we use data from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 to study the lensing effect on the background galaxy GAMA 272379, caused by the galaxy cluster MACS J0210+5534. Our findings reveal that the images of this background galaxy show multiple distinct arcs, which we analyze using a lensing model. Our results indicate that a small-mass object is required to adequately explain the lensing effect, as moving it away from the center of the cluster affects the appearance of the arclets and makes it harder to fit the data. In fact, the small-mass object adds a statistically significant 5.5σ confidence to our model. We also found that removing all known objects from the center of the cluster still leaves noticeable unexplained features, suggesting the presence of additional, unseen mass that could potentially account for some of the observed lensing effects. Our study highlights the significance of small objects in understanding lensing phenomena and suggests that these objects should be taken into consideration when analyzing all lensing features in galaxy clusters, as required by the 'Omega problem'. Our research also underscores the importance of having high-resolution images of the background galaxies and a precise model of the galaxy cluster to accurately interpret the lensing effect. In the future, our approach can be applied to other galaxy clusters to investigate the presence of similar small-mass objects and their potential impact on the lensing effect. Our data and analysis are available online for public use. Additionally, our study is one of the first to demonstrate that a small-mass object can explain all lensing features in a galaxy cluster, a finding that has significant implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution and the formation of galaxy clusters. Our research is self-consistent, meaning that all the models used to study the lensing effect were created independently, as moving any of these mass components could potentially improve the fit to the data, although the improvement would be statistically insignificant. Our study is an important step towards understanding the role of small objects in galaxy clusters and their potential impact on the lensing effect, a field where further research is necessary to clarify the relationship between the objects and the lensing effect. We investigate the idea of weak naturality within the context of categories. A weakened version of the concept naturality, weak naturality arises from the composition of a family of natural transformations that may only approximately satisfy the criteria of naturality. This notion is closely tied to certain instances of adjunctions, where for any adjunction with a weakly natural unit, an adjoint functor that exhibits universal properties can be constructed. Similarly, any adjunction with a weakly natural counit will result in a coadjoint functor that demonstrates universal properties. Building on these findings, we establish that in the presence of a weakly natural unit and counit, the adjoint functors represent the unique mediating functors in the formation of homotopy limits and colimits. Furthermore, these results serve as the foundational elements in the development of a weakly naturally weakly conservative version of the concept of adjoint functors. This approach is distinct from the standard situation, as it relies on the existence of weakly natural units and counits rather than the stronger condition of 2-naturality. An alternative application of weak naturality is also explored in the context of monoidal categories, where it serves to formalize the notion of weakly natural monoidal natural transformations. Ultimately, these findings contribute to an extension of the concept of weakly naturally weakly conservative adjoint functors to the context of monoidal categories, where they exhibit properties akin to a form of weak equivalences. In the process, we examine the concept of monoidal homotopy limits and colimits and their relationship to weakly naturally weakly conservative adjoint functors. It is demonstrated that under suitable conditions, these can be expressed as monoidal versions of the homotopy limits and colimits of the corresponding components. In the case of monoidal categories with weakly natural monoidal natural transformations, these conditions are met, allowing for an expression of these homotopy limits and colimits in terms of the monoidal structure. We've developed a systematic approach to compute electric dipole transition probabilities between the ground state and excited Dirac-Hartree-Fock states. Our approach breaks down complex nuclear transitions into simpler components, enabling a more intuitive understanding of the underlying physics. In this framework, the total transition probability is the sum of three distinct probabilities: 'Main', 'Core', and 'Tail' contributions. The 'Main' contribution is calculated directly using standard dipole transition rules, while 'Core' and 'Tail' components involve more complex rearrangements that originally were part of the initial or final state, respectively. By applying this formalism to isotopic analog transitions, we found that the 'Main' component is zero, whereas the 'Core' and 'Tail' components can still contribute. This systematic approach is expected to be beneficial for evaluating complex nuclear transitions. As a test case, we used it to calculate isotopic analog transition probabilities in even-even $^{142}$Ce, $^{154}$Ce, $^{186}$Ce, and $^{208}$Pb targets, undergoing an isospin transfer of 2. The results showed that 'Tail' components dominate these transitions, suggesting a significant role of the proton $1p_{1/2}$ subshell in such processes. Additionally, we found that the 'Core' component, stemming from the proton $1p_{3/2}$ subshell, also plays a substantial part in these transitions. This study provides a novel understanding of isotopic analog transitions and highlights the significance of the 'Tail' component in such processes. Furthermore, it underscores the importance of the proton $1p_{1/2}$ subshell in transferring isospin of 2. Finally, the study demonstrates that even isotopic analog transitions with an isospin transfer of 2 can be influenced by the proton $1p_{3/2}$ subshell, contrary to the commonly held belief that only the proton $1p_{1/2}$ subshell contributes to such processes. This work is expected to be beneficial in evaluating complex nuclear transitions in a wide range of processes. Moreover, it can serve as a stepping stone to extend the formalism to other types of nuclear transitions, enabling a more accurate and reliable calculation of nuclear transitions involved in nuclear reactions crucial for nuclear applications. This study is anticipated to contribute positively to the nuclear physics community. This study explores twists in actions of a finite group on a two-dimensional torus. We establish that equivariant cohomology serves as a reliable tool for identifying and classifying these twists by showing it is isomorphic to the cohomology of the group action on the fiber, as a result of Poincaré duality. We also extend our findings to torus surfaces by considering actions of the group G on these surfaces and classifying the resulting twists. The current study aims to examine the academic environment within the Department of Computer Science at Indiana University, focusing on its overall atmosphere. Research on departmental sentiment has been scarce, yet it is crucial for identifying areas for improvement. An online survey was administered to department members, utilizing a 5-point Likert scale to gauge sentiment regarding various topics. Additionally, network analysis was applied to reveal collaborative patterns and perceived climate connections. Our findings indicated a positive overall sentiment, but distinct differences in opinions among distinct groups. Furthermore, our results revealed that community feeling and collaborative efforts are significantly linked to the department's overall atmosphere, and that individual feelings of isolation can negatively impact the collective climate. Higher education departments are encouraged to foster a unified, collaborative environment to improve the overall climate. By promoting community building and collaborative activities, the department can effectively address isolated feelings and contribute to a better academic experience for its members. Based on our research outcomes, several actionable recommendations were provided to the department to improve student and faculty well-being and overall satisfaction. These suggestions can be adapted by other computer science departments to create a more harmonious and collaborative academic environment, thus benefiting their own personnel. Lastly, our research highlights the value of incorporating sentiment analysis and network analysis to understand the complex and often invisible dynamics within a department to inform data-driven decisions. These methodologies can be applied to other academic departments in the future. As a flat spacetime's isotropy gives way to more complex geometries, we establish that isotropy can emerge at later stages through the breakdown of certain physical mechanisms, even if the spacetime remains symmetrical. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, commonly referred to as ADHD, is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by excessive hyperactivity, inattention, and impulsivity in children. Although deep learning models have achieved impressive results in classifying ADHD, they have significant drawbacks due to their need for extensive training data, computational resources, and potential for overfitting. To address these limitations, we developed a novel approach, starting from a pre-trained ResNet-50 model, where the full convolutional layers were replaced with attention-enabling layers. This enabled us to create an attentive deep learning model (ADL) that identifies and prioritizes critical regions of interest for ADHD classification. During training, the model was forced to focus on these key areas by masking the remaining features. As a result, ADL required and was trained on a significantly lower number - just 70% - of the original features, while demonstrating enhanced classification performance and stability. When applied to the OASIS dataset, ADL achieved an impressive 70.46% accuracy, outperforming other models by 3.46%. Furthermore, the model's attention weights accurately pinpointed critical regions such as the temporal lobe for ADHD classification. In a subsequent study, the model was tested on the MCIC dataset, where it showed potential for classifying ADHD with high accuracy across single-site and multi-site datasets. This research indicates the potential for computer-based ADHD diagnosis and highlights the importance of integrating clinical knowledge into machine learning algorithms to improve model interpretability and performance. The increasing use of digital communication has led to a significant rise in acronym usage, with many becoming ambiguous and requiring context for understanding. Previous research has focused on using context from a single text, but this often fails to consider broader information such as domain-specific knowledge. We have developed a dataset with 1,637 acronym-definition pairs that includes not only text context but also domain information, and used it to create two regression-based models that can help identify and clarify ambiguous acronyms in a given text by considering its surrounding words and domain. While our models demonstrate some ability to utilize context and domain information, they also reveal a noticeable limitation in performance, suggesting that additional contextual elements and domain knowledge are required to enhance their capabilities. To aid in future research, we have made our dataset available for public access. Furthermore, we have created a system utilizing the predicted results of our models to assist users in identifying and disambiguating acronyms in written content. We propose a new model, based on edge resonators, which enables heat rectification in quantum Hall systems. This is made possible by exploiting the energy edges of these resonators and their interactions with nearby energy levels. Notably, our design can function even in the absence of external drive power. Additionally, the edge resonators allow for the directional transfer of heat from a colder to a hotter reservoir, while also maintaining a steady flow of charge from the colder reservoir to the hotter one. Our research focuses on creating a DNA template with uniform DNA lengths in each partition, using an algorithm that determines the optimal primer pair arrangement based on DNA length distribution. Additionally, our model includes a management system for DNA sequences retrieved from each partition, which assigns sequences to the partition they belong to upon detection. An experimental demonstration using a DNA synthesizer and fluorescence detection equipment validated our template design, demonstrating the feasibility of creating a DNA-based storage system with multiple storage partitions, each managed independently. Topological phases in condensed matter physics have garnered significant attention, but the concept of nodal lines in momentum space remains poorly understood despite their potential classification as topological states. In contrast to other exotic phases, nodal lines can be easily destroyed by an external influence, leading some to question their relevance in topological physics. However, recent advances have revealed that nodal lines can be stable within certain symmetry conditions, and that Nodal lines and their associated point nodes share a common connection. Furthermore, studies have shown that nodal lines can coexist with other topological features, such as domain walls and surface states, and that they are essential for the formation of these other phases. As a result, the stable incorporation of nodal lines into a Hamiltonian is crucial for understanding the emergence of other topological states. This understanding enables the use of nodal lines as a tool to create and control exotic surface phenomena, making them an essential component of topological phase transitions. Ultimately, the incorporation of nodal lines contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of topological matter. To illustrate the principles outlined above, we examine the example of Bi doped WTe2, in which the introduction of Bi results in the creation of a nodal line loop in the 2D kx-ky plane, associated with a gapped 3D structure. Bi doping causes the movement and possible disappearance of the nodal line, and the appearance of a gap at the k0z axis. By adjusting the chemical doping, the nodal line can reappear while a mass gap appears along the z-axis, and finally, the surface can display a Dirac cone while the nodal line and the mass gap coexist. This study of Bi doped WTe2 demonstrates that the incorporation of a nodal line contributes to the control and understanding of a Dirac cone on the surface, underscoring the importance of nodal lines in topological matter. As a result, the use of nodal lines provides a means to control and create various surface phenomena, including Dirac cones, magnetism, and other exotic phases, and can be utilized to transition between different topological states. Ultimately, the study of nodal lines contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of topological matter. The study utilizes wave speed as an environmental indicator to explore how a medium responds to vibrations. Analyzing the speed of waves propagated by an array of oscillators within a flexible membrane reveals a strong correlation with the distance between the oscillators. Additionally, it is observed that wave speed is influenced by the size and shape of the oscillators, as well as the presence of boundaries, leading to the adoption of a network-based approach to understand the dynamic behavior of the system. This involves comparing wave speeds in different networks to those in a fixed, homogeneous medium to reveal the impact of topological factors on the system's response. The results show that wave speed is directly related to the average degree of neighboring nodes and the presence of clusters within the network, with the most significant influence coming from the distance between the oscillators. This study provides novel insights into the dynamic behavior of complex systems and offers a new approach to understanding environmental responses. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that wave speed can be optimized through targeted modifications to the system's architecture. The findings of this study have implications for a wide range of applications, from the study of planetary systems to the behavior of social networks. This paper provides a detailed analysis of a novel entropy estimation algorithm known as the L^2 Markov algorithm. Our investigation focuses on the scenario where the transition matrix of a discrete-time discrete-state Markov process is perceived as a random variable, subject to certain stochastic correlations. Under this premise, we demonstrate that the transition matrix can be approximated as a correlated version of a uniform distribution, and leverage this conclusion to establish a lower bound on the input entropy of the algorithm. Our results indicate that the algorithm is capable of accurately estimating entropy when the input entropy exceeds a minimum threshold, which is dependent on the strength of the stochastic correlations. Our theoretical findings are substantiated through numerical simulations involving Navier-Stokes equations and a simple weather model, revealing that the algorithm achieves precise entropy estimation in scenarios with high stochastic correlations. However, the algorithm's accuracy is compromised in cases with extremely low stochastic correlations. To address this limitation, we propose an enhanced version of the L^2 Markov algorithm, which incorporates a regularization step to enhance its robustness in the former class of examples. The modified algorithm is validated through numerical experiments on the same examples, resulting in accurate entropy estimation in scenarios with weak stochastic correlations. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the L^2 Markov algorithm and its potential for general use in entropy estimation. Additionally, our investigation highlights the significance of the algorithm's input entropy being greater than zero for effective operation. Our work is further supplemented by a newly created open-source code, L2Markov, which facilitates the use of the algorithm for entropy estimation in various applications. As deep learning continues to evolve, there's a growing need for high-quality, accessible datasets. Current computer vision datasets are often insufficient due to privacy concerns, thereby prompting the development of privacy-enhanced imaging biobanks. This paper outlines essential requirements for creating and implementing effective imaging biobanks, particularly in the context of artificial intelligence applications, and presents a novel biobank design based on quantum computing principles. To protect sensitive information, we integrate a quantum error-correcting code into the biobank's design, while maintaining data usability for machine learning purposes. Notably, our proposed biobank design can be realized using existing quantum devices, even if they're not fault-tolerant, thanks to the integration of a quantum filter circuit. The benefits and limitations of our approach are discussed, and we demonstrate the feasibility of our method through the creation of a simple digital biobank containing X-ray images. This study examines the application of data augmentation to a popular medical diagnosis task, specifically identifying patient diagnoses from electrocardiogram data. By training a model on augmented data, we investigate whether this strategy improves diagnosis accuracy and, if so, under what conditions it occurs. Our analysis reveals that while data augmentation can be beneficial when basic clinical features are lacking, such as signal lengths, it is unnecessary and may even detract from performance when complete context is available. Notably, in our test case, using augmented ECG signals failed to improve accuracy and occasionally compromised it, suggesting that relying solely on data transformation may not always yield optimal results. We hope our findings encourage the development of more sophisticated data augmentation techniques tailored to the specific characteristics of their applications. When executed on a quantum computer, the asymptotic complexity of our algorithm is significantly improved, at $\mathcal{O}\left(R^{3}\right)$, as opposed to the $\Omega\left(2^{n}\right)$ complexity of classical algorithms for data sets of size $n$ and feature dimensionality $d$, where $R = \min\{2^{d/3}, \sqrt{n}/\sqrt{K}\}$. This technique adds a penalty term to the likelihood function to restrict the size of the O-D demand values. However, simply penalizing large values does not guarantee a sparse solution matrix, as it may still contain non-zero values when there is no data. Therefore, a new method is proposed in this study, where a linear transformation of the covariance matrix is regulated using lasso, resulting in a more accurate and sparse solution. Furthermore, a detailed analysis is provided on how the sparsity pattern of the solution matrix changes with varying levels of regularization. This method is tested using data from a real-world transportation network and simulated data, which show that it outperforms the traditional method by providing a more accurate and sparse solution for the specific case where there is limited data on pedestrian traffic. However, it performs similarly in scenarios with abundant data, where both methods produce a non-sparse solution. Consequently, the proposed approach is particularly beneficial in situations where there is limited data and a desire for a more compact and interpretable model. We investigated the occurrence of stable, phase-locked states in pairs of oscillators, one located in a two-dimensional cubic lattice and the other in a three-dimensional cubic lattice, when they were coupled through weak nonlinear frequency dispersion. This type of dispersion causes a slight shift in each oscillator's frequency due to its interaction with nearby oscillators. This mechanism of coupling is distinct from typical direct coupling methods. It was observed that phase-locked states could arise in both dimensions through the existence of linear instability modes. However, we found that while long-lived in both dimensions, the states' stability declined gradually in two-dimensional arrangements. In three-dimensional arrangements, the stability remained robust. The reason behind this difference lies in the availability of a distinct type of boundary condition in two-dimensional scenarios, which facilitates the release of unstable frequency fluctuations into propagating waves, thereby enhancing the states' stability. In contrast, the absence of such boundary conditions in three-dimensional scenarios hinders this process and thus prolongs the duration of the frequency fluctuations. Consequently, the three-dimensional states could maintain their higher frequency than the two-dimensional states, which in turn resulted in a more robust stability. This paper presents an improved hybrid method for creating uniform spanning trees in finite connected graphs, combining the efficiency of Aldous-Broder and Wilson's exact algorithm. The new approach undergoes a dynamic shift between these two methods, utilizing the exact algorithm when the generated tree is likely to be retained as the final uniform spanning tree, and switching to the hybrid Aldous-Broder-Wilson algorithm otherwise. A novel technique is employed to determine the likely success of the exact algorithm, involving a brief examination of the newly added tree. The study shows that the expected overhead of this hybrid method is less than or equal to 5 times that of the original Aldous-Broder-Wilson algorithm, with the efficiency in practice being significantly better. The implementation of this hybrid method in C has been made available under the GNU Public License at arxiv.org. A series of numerical examples demonstrate its remarkable performance, with the gain in efficiency increasing in more complex graph structures. Even in relatively simple scenarios, the hybrid method usually attains overall efficiency within a fifth to a tenth of that required by the Aldous-Broder-Wilson algorithm. A key factor is that the hybrid approach can terminate once a uniform spanning tree is generated, which in most cases occurs long before reaching the desired sample size. The study's worst-case analysis, however, does not rule out the possibility of the hybrid method being less efficient in certain situations. Consequently, further research is recommended to investigate whether a similar worst-case bound can be established for the expected running time of the hybrid method. Nevertheless, the observed efficiency gains in practical terms suggest that the hybrid method represents a viable and valuable alternative to the Aldous-Broder-Wilson algorithm. As a result, this approach can be utilized to efficiently generate uniform spanning trees in a range of graph structures. The accompanying code has been successfully applied to various graphs including random geometric graphs, random nearest neighbor graphs, and a social network derived from the'soc-heros' dataset. The generated uniform spanning trees have then been employed to create random spanning forests by taking a sample of n-1 vertices for each, which can be useful in analyzing connected subgraphs. A series of numerical examples illustrate the effectiveness of this method in practice. The code is available online at arxiv.org for anyone to access and use. A new MusicTM-Dataset has been created through a collaboration between two leading music datasets, combining the melodies from MagnaTagATune with the song titles from Million Song Dataset. This collaborative effort enables large-scale cross-modal music retrieval and provides a challenging benchmark for evaluating the performance in retrieving matching music via different modalities. For instance, given a song title as input, the model should be able to identify the corresponding melody, and vice versa. This comprehensive music dataset comprises 13,786 unique song titles and 19,776 distinctive melodies, totaling 11.9 million unique song-title pairs, along with the corresponding audio features. To assess the effectiveness of different models in retrieving matching music across different modalities, we have developed a custom evaluation framework that calculates precision, recall, and the area under the curve of the precision-recall graph. This benchmark allows for comparing the performance of different models in a standardized manner. Furthermore, our study investigates how the performance of different models varies in terms of the number of available samples, much like how human performance improves with experience. Additionally, we have developed a set of baseline models that leverage both traditional machine learning and modern deep learning techniques to facilitate comparison with other proposed models. This comprehensive resource enables researchers to develop and test their own cross-modal music retrieval models, which can be found in the accompanying code repository at https://github.com/krishanm/MusicTM-Dataset. Finally, our work highlights the potential applications and future directions for further research in the cross-modal music retrieval domain. These could involve using pre-trained models on large-scale datasets like MusicTM-Dataset for downstream tasks, exploring the transferability of models across different datasets, or using the MusicTM-Dataset to investigate the role of side information in enhancing cross-modal music retrieval. By delving into these questions, we aim to contribute meaningfully to the advancement of cross-modal music retrieval and understanding the intricate relationships between music, our emotions, and our perceptions. The manipulation of polarization has far-reaching implications in various fields. Historically, a limited range of control over polarization was achievable through the linear combination of two laser beams with orthogonal polarizations. Recently, our group, in collaboration with Prof. Zhang's at University of Washington, has successfully developed a novel technique to control polarization on a broad scale. This advancement allows for the transformation of a single laser beam's polarization without relying on external beams, breaking previous polarization control barriers. By integrating a micro- or nano-structured metallic substrate into this process, the team achieved substantial control over polarization, demonstrating the ability to map arbitrary polarization states to polarization-locked ones with unparalleled scale and precision. This breakthrough has significant potential to transform fields like spintronics and nonlinear optics, offering a promising path for dynamic and scalable polarization manipulation through advanced micro- or nano-polarization engineering. This research introduces a novel hierarchical fusion strategy, termed as hierarchical fusion (HF), in this study. It diverges from conventional early and intermediate fusion techniques, which combine information at respective initial or intermediate stages of multiple-source systems. Instead, our model recursively merges sources at a macro-level, with each component being a combination of two or more sources at a lower level. This paper presents a novel multi-task pre-training framework, specifically designed for representation learning from spoken language, by combining the goals of both language model and dialog tasks. The framework's design is based on two key components: a large-scale language model, which is fine-tuned to anticipate the next utterance in a dialog sequence, and a span prediction task that focuses on identifying segments within dialogues. To achieve this, both utterance-level and span-level models are optimized using a task-specific loss function. The former is driven by a cross-representation loss, which is enabled by a common embedding space for all training data, while the latter is guided by a cross-entropy loss. The paper showcases the effectiveness of this multi-task model through comprehensive experiments on three publicly available Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) benchmarks from various Asian languages, namely, Mandarin, Korean, and Hindi. The results indicate that our multi-task model yields superior performance on all benchmarks, surpassing the baseline models by substantial margins of 3-6%. In Visual Relationship Detection, a model is optimized to identify the connections and attributes in objects within an image. The area faces a challenge due to the vast number of possible object attributes and relationships. To address this, a previously used approach, Negative Proposal Sampling, was employed, where a model was trained to disregard irrelevant proposals in an image to focus on those that are most likely to contain the objects of interest. Further research found that the optimal proposals for optimization are often difficult to determine without the optimized model itself, resulting in a chicken-and-egg problem. To resolve this issue, a new strategy, Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), has been developed. BNPS uses two separate models to identify both difficult and easy proposals for the model to optimize, by balancing the difficulty of each proposal based on its predicted confidence, without relying on optimal proposals. The results show that BNPS outperforms existing strategies by optimizing models more efficiently and effectively, without the need for optimal proposals. Additionally, BNPS has the added benefit of improving the model's overall performance, as measured by mean average precision (mAP), in comparison to previous strategies. The improved performance of BNPS is most noticeable on complex relationships and attributes, indicating that the model is able to identify these connections more accurately. A novel concept known as "residual quantumness" aims to quantify the remaining quantum properties of a quantum system even after it has been measured. Our study builds upon a recent proposal by Gu et al., which measured residual quantumness using weak measurement and postselection. We extend this proposal to open quantum systems by leveraging the weak measurement postselection method. To illustrate the effectiveness of our findings, we examine two specific cases: a two-level system undergoing spontaneous emission and a quantum oscillator interacting with a warm reservoir. Our results demonstrate that residual quantumness can be extracted from these systems, and we also analyze the influence of measurement strength and postselection probability on the extracted quantumness. Furthermore, we show that the measured residual quantumness is conserved in a manner analogous to the conservation of probability in classical physics. To validate our measurements, we derive a detailed weak measurement correction for the two-level system and a quantum oscillator. Our research provides a framework for analyzing residual quantumness in open quantum systems, which has practical implications for enhancing the efficiency of quantum light sources. In the field of relationship state graph learning, a method known as Relationship State Graph Learning (RSG) utilizes real-world graph data and node attribute information to develop a relationship state graph. This graph represents individuals and their interconnected relationships. The updating of relationship states is managed by Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), specifically Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs). We investigate the possibility of replacing the traditional RNN with a more efficient alternative, a Random Walk-based method. This approach uses random walk data on graphs to update relationship states, eliminating the need for node attribute information. We combine the strengths of both methods, creating a new hybrid model, and conduct experiments on three real-world datasets. The results indicate that the hybrid model outperforms both individual methods on various metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining RNN and random walk-based methods to improve relationship state graph learning. Large graphs in machine learning are inherently expensive to process due to their size, but a new method tackles this problem head-on by applying techniques originally designed for neural network pruning to map large graphs efficiently. This method, adaptive graph sampling, identifies and eliminates unnecessary nodes in the graph, reducing its size and computational burden. In experiments with existing neural graph methods, this approach outperformed the baseline with significant speed gains and minimal accuracy losses, especially on larger graphs. Furthermore, adaptive graph sampling shed new light on how important node adaptations are in maintaining accurate predictions. This method's code is freely available for public use.

Quantum deep learning is an emerging and promising field that seeks to leverage the unique capabilities of quantum systems to enhance artificial intelligence models. Despite its potential, the field is still in its infancy and faces several hurdles, primarily due to the difficulty in building large-scale quantum computers that can support neural networks. To overcome this limitation, our approach involves simulating complex quantum circuits on classical systems using quantum-gated neural networks, which can be trained with existing machine learning techniques on classical data. This quantum-inspired model yields impressive performance in classification tasks for the datasets we tested, even with the incorporation of noisy data similar to that from quantum experiments. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that neural networks with an increasing number of layers tend to perform better, suggesting a quantum analogy. This finding opens up new avenues for the quantum deep learning research, allowing us to explore the quantum effects in the training of neural networks. Ultimately, the success of quantum deep learning will depend on the integration of quantum technology, and our simulation of quantum circuits using neural networks may pave the way for the development of the first practical quantum deep learning systems. A key factor contributing to this success is the pipelined structure of the processor, allowing multiple operations to run concurrently in a continuous flow. However, the application of pipelining to a processor with multiple functional units does not automatically translate to improved performance in field programmable portables. To take full advantage of the processor's capabilities, a coordinated workflow between the units is essential, one that ensures a continuous flow of instructions through the pipeline. In the context of a processor portable, we have devised novel algorithms that capitalize on the processor's multi-unit architecture, thereby optimizing algorithmic efficiency while up to three units remain idle during pipeline operation. These advanced algorithms significantly outperform existing ones in terms of execution speed. Additionally, our approach allows us to adapt and refine existing algorithms in circuit design, resulting in further accelerated performance. Through comprehensive testing, we have demonstrated that our optimized algorithms achieve faster computation times for a substantial range of circuit sizes. Furthermore, when combined with strategic reordering techniques, our results reveal significant speedups in circuit evaluation, averaging 21% and 35% for small and large circuits, respectively, while also achieving average area savings of 13% and 20%. In circuit design, our approach yields impressive area reductions of 16% to 40% for a wide range of circuit sizes, complemented by considerable performance improvements of 21% to 52%. These remarkable gains in efficiency are largely a direct result of the coordinated use of the processor's multi-unit architecture in a coordinated workflow. This paper analyzes the complexity of optimization problems within the general-valued constraint satisfaction family, specifically those defined by a set of crisp constraints. We demonstrate that an approximation algorithm can be designed for this class of problems, yielding a PTAS when the problem's instance satisfies a particular condition known as "extremely sparse high algebraic rank". Furthermore, this approximation algorithm can be applied to a broader range of instances with some algebraic complexity properties, such as "virtually extremely sparse" instances. Additionally, we examine the limitations of this approach and show that it cannot be easily modified to handle instances with more complex algebraic properties, even if the constraints are restricted to linear or quadratic forms. We also establish a more general result, stating that approximation algorithms for optimization general-valued CSPs can be designed for instances with certain algebraic properties, provided that the constraints' complexity is adequately restricted. Specifically, if the constraints' degree is limited to d=2, a PTAS can be developed for instances with exponentially increasing sparsity levels. This approach is also applied to derive approximation algorithms for specific optimization problems, such as Min-XOR and Min-HAMILTONIAN-CIRCLE, resulting in significant performance improvements for various problem instances. Notably, our findings provide significant insights into the complexity of general-valued CSP minimization. Specifically, we observe that while some instances can be solved efficiently using a PTAS, more complex instances may require non-constant time to be approximated. This distinction marks a significant difference in our understanding of general-valued CSP minimization. Furthermore, our results imply the existence of PTAS for various optimization problems, such as Min-XOR and Min-HAMILTONIAN-CIRCLE, on virtually extremely sparse instances, which were previously intractable to approximate efficiently. We also examine the limits of our PTAS-based approach and show that the complexity of general-valued CSP minimization may not be efficiently approximated if the constraints' degree is not restricted to d=2. By integrating a novel iterative few-shot parser with a hierarchical self-attention module, a hierarchical attention module, a hierarchical encoder, and a hierarchical decoder, FPIO surpasses the performance of previous few-shot parsing methods. Additionally, it outshines a range of established parsing models that are trained with extensive annotated data. We evaluate FPIO on various datasets, including the Princeton Treebank, Sembench, and Semeval-2010 tasks, showcasing its remarkable efficacy with reduced training samples and a limited number of annotated trees. Notably, FPIO displays superior performance when trained with just 50 annotated trees, outpacing a strong baseline parser trained with 500 trees. This work develops a Randomized Algebraic Matrix Algorithm (RAM) model that can efficiently perform algebraic operations using random number generators to handle polynomial coefficients. This model is capable of efficiently computing well-known algebraic problems, such as polynomial factorization, isotopic polynomial set, and other problem sets, all within logarithmic space and polylogarithmic time, thus surpassing the capabilities of prior deterministic algebraic matrix algorithms.

A key innovation of our RAM model is a randomized arithmetic circuit algorithm that allows for the generation of exact polynomial integers using random number generators, thus circumventing the need for arbitrary-precision arithmetic. This approach is combined with a new deterministic sparse polynomial factorization method that factorizes a polynomial of degree n and sparsity level k in O(n^3.599)...(k+1) time, significantly improving the efficiency of previous factorization methods.

As a result, our RAM model can solve various algebraic problems, such as evaluating and interpolating polynomial functions, factoring polynomial sets, and solving systems of polynomial equations, all within polylogarithmic time and logarithmic space, thus greatly improving the efficiency of these computations. Furthermore, these results are equivalent to solving deterministic algebraic matrix problems of O(n^3.5)...(k+1) time, which is a significant improvement over prior factorization methods. Additionally, our RAM model can also be used to solve problems involving modular multi-polynomial integers, which is crucial for applications in number theory. Finally, as a significant application of our RAM model, we prove the hardness of deterministic algebraic matrix problems, thus providing an essential theoretical finding. Session-based recommendation systems are designed to provide recommendations one step at a time, often using user session data. Since they lack information on user preferences, they struggle with session completion. To address this, self-supervised learning has gained attention for enhancing session-based recommendation systems. In this research, we delve into how self-supervised learning improves data augmentation, a crucial step in training session-based models. We found that existing data augmentation methods are limited, as they rely on random and repetitive operations, offering no substantial improvement. To address this, we introduce a new data augmentation method called BiSAL, which uses a bidirectional self-attention layer to create augmented session sequences. By capturing long-term and short-term dependencies in session data, BiSAL enables more effective and varied data augmentation. As a result, BiSAL outperforms state-of-the-art methods, delivering improved recommendation accuracy and diverse augmented sequences. However, when the likelihood noise was decreased to lower levels (1% of the magnitude), the learned controller failed, often causing the helicopter to crash. Further investigation revealed that the original evolutionary optimization was biased towards noise-reducing solutions due to its reliance on simulated generations. To address this issue, a new approach was developed where the likelihood noise was explicitly accounted for, resulting in a learned controller that remained effective across a range of noise levels (from 10% to 1%). Enforcing a lower bound on the likelihood noise in the dynamics model was found to be an insufficient solution, as it only prevented extreme outliers and did not guarantee the robustness of the learned controller. In contrast, explicitly addressing the likelihood noise in the search process was found to be a crucial factor in achieving robust learned controllers. To verify these findings, a new evolutionary optimization was conducted under conditions of high noise levels (10% of the system's magnitude), where the likelihood noise was accurately estimated and reflected in the search process. As a result, the learned controller remained effective across a range of lower likelihood noise levels (from 1% to 10%), even when the likelihood noise was artificially increased. In addition, the study found that the distance between the mean trajectory and the surrounding probabilistic envelope played a significant role in determining the robustness of the learned controller. As this distance decreased, the risk of the helicopter's state drifting outside of it increased, often resulting in control failures. In contrast, the risk of the helicopter's state drifting outside of its probabilistic envelope was found to be significantly lower when the distance between the mean trajectory and the surrounding envelope was larger. As such, an increased focus on explicitly accounting for the likelihood noise in the search process is recommended in order to achieve learned controllers that remain effective across a range of lower and higher likelihood noise levels. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of considering the distance between the mean trajectory and the surrounding probabilistic envelope when evaluating the robustness of learned controllers. To facilitate the reproduction of these findings, a new open-source tool was developed to accurately estimate the likelihood noise and reflect it in the search process, as well as a new approach to explicitly account for the likelihood noise in the dynamics model. This set of four notes commenced as a course held at the University of Bergen during the spring semester of 2003, and subsequently evolved into additional lectures delivered at the University of Bergen during the spring semester of 2004 and the autumn semester of 2004-05. The primary objective of these notes was to present research findings on degenerate Eisenstein series, and specifically the study of the space of degenerate Eisenstein series for a particular real reductive Lie group, and the analysis of certain automorphic representations. Furthermore, these notes also explored the application of a particular invariant, which stems from the Weyl group, to both the degenerate Eisenstein series and weight spaces. Additionally, these notes also touched upon the linear degenerate Eisenstein series, an essential aspect of which is that it vanishes across specific weight spaces. Lastly, these notes also dealt with the differential operators acting on degenerate Eisenstein series, and the resolution of certain problems linked to the Rankin-Selberg conjecture for arbitrary reductive pairs. As such, these notes are targeted towards advanced researchers in the field of representation theory, though some foundational knowledge of representation theory, and the associated Hodge theory, is presumed. In particular, it is presumed the reader has prior knowledge of the classical decomposition theory for reductive Lie algebras, as well as the general theory of admissible representations and automorphic forms for reductive groups over number fields. As such, these notes are intended for researchers with existing knowledge in this field, rather than an introductory text. In total, these notes span 124 printed pages. Following is a detailed summary of the contents. Chapter 1 commences with an overview of the reductive pairs and the associated degenerate Eisenstein series, and presents novel findings regarding the absolute value of the central character of a degenerate Eisenstein series for a given pair. Chapter 2 focuses on the application of the Weyl group cosets to both the degenerate Eisenstein series and weight spaces, and establishes the link between these cosets and the degenerate Eisenstein series. Chapter 3 delves into linear degenerate Eisenstein series and proves that a particular differential operator acts on these series. Chapter 4 concludes with an examination of the differential operators acting on degenerate Eisenstein series, and resolves problems linked to the Rankin-Selberg conjecture for arbitrary reductive pairs. A novel radial basis function (RBF) interpolation method is introduced, which combines the advantages of thin-plate splines and well-behaved RBFs. The proposed interpolation function not only preserves properties such as convexity and monotonicity but is also shown to be more stable in terms of its $\mathcal{L}^2$-error estimate, even with a higher rate, than other RBF interpolation methods, including those using Gaussian and polynomial RBFs. The proposed interpolation scheme is quasi-interpolation, meaning it relies on a finite number of data points and can be effectively implemented using compactly supported RBFs, while maintaining its desirable properties. Moreover, we present an explicit dimension-dependent error estimate, which indicates that the error decreases at a rate of $h^{2m+1}$ for smooth functions. The proposed interpolation method is particularly useful for solving nonlinear partial differential equations and dimension-independent approximation problems. Several numerical examples are provided to validate the theoretical error estimates. The code for the proposed interpolation method is available online at https://github.com/lmengxiao/Quasi-Interpolation.git. The test data can be found at https://github.com/lmengxiao/TestData.git. Pulsar halos are large, extended structures formed by the diffusion of high-energy electrons from pulsar wind nebulae into the surrounding magnetic field. Identified so far, they are the largest diffuse sources of very high energy gamma-ray emission in the Galaxy, exceeding a scale of approximately 100 parsecs. Pulsar halos are critical in understanding the cosmic positron anomaly and the diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess, as they are both major contributors. A new class of pulsar-driven pulsar halos has been proposed to explain the diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess, involving the diffusion of electrons from an entire pulsar population. However, this model faces challenges in reproducing the spatial distribution observed in the Fermi gamma-ray bubble. Moreover, a detailed examination of the largest known pulsar halo, PSR J1834-07, has revealed a significant discrepancy between its gamma-ray emission and the diffusion model. This discrepancy is mainly attributed to the incomplete cooling of electrons within the halo. As a result, the low-energy gamma-ray emission from the pulsar halo is underestimated, which in turn affects the high-energy gamma-ray distribution. Ultimately, this hampers the identification of local contributors to the diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess through the comparison of spatial distributions. Consequently, an electron cooling age lower than the diffusion age is essential for accurately determining gamma-ray emission from pulsar halos, particularly those with a low luminosity-to-specific-surface-area ratio. This finding is likely to be applicable to other pulsar halos and has far-reaching implications for the understanding of the diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess and the cosmic positron anomaly. As a result, a re-evaluation of the entire class of pulsar halos is necessary to determine their role in these astrophysical enigmas. Finally, the presence of a large-scale gamma-ray bridge connecting the Fermi gamma-ray bubble and the pulsar halo, PSR J1834-07, has been confirmed, which is likely to be associated with the diffusion of electrons from the Central Milky Way. This bridge may serve as a key structure in understanding the large-scale magnetic field in the Central Milky Way. However, a detailed examination of this bridge is beyond the scope of this study. Instead, future research should prioritize determining the diffusion direction within the bridge and its contribution to the gamma-ray emission. As a result, the diffusion model for the diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess in the Central Milky Way remains uncertain. By generating masked images based on pre-defined delimiting masks, the CNN can learn diverse features. However, creating an optimal mask pattern is complicated. To address this, our study employs a Bilinear CNN in conjunction with a BNS layer to learn an unsupervised delimiting mask. A BNS layer is used to extract a delimiting mask from super pixel regions obtained via a Super Pixel algorithm like Simple Linear Iterative Clustering (SLIC), and this mask is learned from image data via back-propagation during training. To understand the public's climate change awareness, researchers analyzed mentions of climate change in prominent German newspapers from 1980 to 2020, also including relevant policy-related science and economics publications for comparison. Climate change was mentioned in over 30% of German newspapers' articles from 2020, significantly more than in policy or economics publications during the same period. Although climate change is increasingly discussed in German newspapers, it is still less mentioned in policy or economics publications than other prominent scientific or economic topics. Our data from 2020 reveal that climate change is mentioned less often in general interest science journals and economics publications than in smaller or more specialized scientific publications. This discrepancy may be attributed to the differing focus areas or the perceived relevance of climate change among scientists and economists. Furthermore, climate change is mentioned less often in policy or economics publications than in other prominent topics, such as the euro or refugee crises, which might indicate a lack of interest among policymakers in this critical global issue. Our long-term analysis provides data from 1980 to 2020, showing that the mentions of climate change have risen more slowly in policy or economics publications than in German newspapers, and even more slowly than in general interest science journals. Our study's findings are consistent with those of previous research on the United States, showing that climate change is gaining more attention in newspapers and scientific publications but less so in economics and particularly among policymakers. This trend could be driven by the perceived relevance, personal beliefs, or political affiliations of individuals within these groups, which may also be influenced by the perceived effectiveness of climate policies and their expected impact on the economy. To better understand these dynamics, our study also includes a short survey of 50 German economists, examining their awareness of climate change and whether it is perceived as a pressing issue, which could necessitate policy action and thus impact the economy. Interestingly, 82% of our survey respondents acknowledge the significance of climate change, yet only 26% consider it a major economic threat and a need for policy action, which might be an underestimation, given the severe consequences of inaction as outlined in the IPCC reports. This limited recognition of climate change by economists, who are often advisors to policymakers, may contribute to the perceived lack of interest among policymakers in this critical global issue. By leveraging the statistical properties of stochastic gradient descent processes, the Natural Gradient Descent (NGD) method achieves faster convergence. However, the widespread use of Automatic Differentiation (AD) for neural network optimization, which relies on empirical measurements, can impede NGD's potential for rapid convergence. In our research, we bridge the gap between NGD and AD, introducing a novel approach that calibrates NGD using a neural network's local statistical characteristics. This calibration enables us to accelerate NGD's convergence, outperforming traditional AD-based optimization and NGD alone while maintaining unbiasedness. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in challenging optimization scenarios, such as noise reduction in images and text prediction tasks. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/alex1998u/sngd. Further details about the project are available in the technical report by Krzysztof Choroszy et al., titled "Accelerating Neural Network Optimization with Stochastic Natural Gradient Descent," available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.00816. Additionally, a video presentation can be found at https://youtu.be/6Q4Q4Q4Q4Q4. In terms of NGD's potential, a figure-of-merit analysis suggests that significant improvements could be achieved by increasing the number of samples used in the statistical estimation. In our experiments, we successfully applied this approach to the ResNet model on the ImageNet dataset, observing a notable speedup of 2.5 times over the standard SGD method. This speedup is particularly pronounced in the early stages of training, with a notable acceleration of 5.5 times. As a result, our method has the potential to accelerate neural network optimizations by a factor of 2-10 times, with an even greater impact when optimizing larger models. We utilize the MVAmed machine learning tool to develop a comprehensive reconstruction of the cosmic microwave background's power spectrum from simulated non-Gaussian maps generated by HaloPatch, taking into account both temperature and $E$-mode polarization data. By integrating an accurate model of the patchy map power spectrum that accounts for varying wavelengths, our method yields precise power spectrum estimates, especially for shorter wavelengths, where the standard Gaussian-based approach falls short. Notably, we find that temperature and polarization power spectra become increasingly correlated as the wavelength increases. Building upon this, we devise a multivariate learning method that merges temperature and polarization data to produce a more accurate joint reconstruction. This joint approach enhances the retrieval of longer-wavelength signals in both temperature and polarization power spectra. With continued improvements in CMB experiments, such as LiteBIRD, planned for launch in 2021, we anticipate that the reconstruction of higher-order modes will become significant, prompting the need for updates to the Gaussian-based estimators. Given the rising importance of $E$-mode polarization data, our findings suggest that combining temperature and polarization data with consideration of varying wavelengths will be crucial for achieving the LiteBIRD mission's goal of constraining primordial non-Gaussianity at the $10^{-3}$ level. Additionally, we identify an area for further research, investigating how to incorporate the cross-spectra between frequency maps in the MVAmed learning framework. This could potentially enhance the reconstruction by leveraging the distinct properties of different frequency maps. Building upon this foundation, we propose that future research on the MVAmed approach could explore the estimation of one-loop power spectrum modes, such as the $TE$ cross-power spectrum. This would necessitate the integration of relevant signal templates into the learning process, a potential adaptation of the MVAmed technique. This research has the potential to significantly contribute to the recovery of primordial non-Gaussianity signals in upcoming CMB experiments. In addition to its relevance to CMB research, we showcase MVAmed's versatility by applying it to the analysis of simulated cosmic void observations. This application serves as a testament to the broad utility of the MVAmed approach in cosmological data analysis. This research paper presents a twofold classification model that determines both the sentiment of a tweet and its relevance to a startup business. The sentiment classification model leverages Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks, trained on a diverse dataset of tweets gathered from various topics including sports, music, and fashion. In contrast, the startup data classification model employs a combination of LSTM and a Random Forest classifier, utilizing a unique dataset comprising startups gathered from various online sources. The models' effectiveness are evaluated through performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, and F1-score, with the latter achieving higher levels of accuracy in classifying startup data compared to existing methodologies. Furthermore, a novel feature engineering technique called word-masking is introduced to enhance LSTM models' performance when classifying limited and highly variable data. Word-masking involves replacing rare words in a text with more common terms to improve model training and output quality. The proposed approach results in substantial improvements in classification and sentiment analysis precision for both individual and startup-based text classification within our dataset. Additionally, the developed models and associated code are made available open-source for potential application to other datasets. The presence of role specifications in conversational interactions is becoming more prevalent, yet their impact on dialogue systems remains poorly understood. In this research, we examine how role-centric conversation details impact dialogue coherence and relevance. To accomplish this, we create a new dataset of dialogues with specified roles, termed Role-Specified Dialogues (RSD), by extracting information from online forums involving individuals with shared experiences. Our analysis reveals role specifications to be highly effective, significantly improving the performance of a pre-trained natural language model in generating coherent and relevant responses. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that role specifications can be effectively represented using a one-dimensional array of role weights, enabling a pre-trained model to automatically extract role information from input text. The proposed model architecture and RSD dataset are made available at https://github.com/argman/RSD. This paper explores the concept of stochastic gravitational wave memory background for the first time, an idea that arises from the cumulative effect of individual gravitational wave memory events, unlike the conventional non-memory background generated by continuous gravitational waves from spinning bodies. Our investigation focused on the stochastic gravitational wave memory background emanating from second-generation gravitational wave events recorded by the LIGO-Virgo collaboration, finding that it significantly differs from the conventional background in its frequency behavior. Furthermore, we determined that the memory background amplitude is too small to be detectable with current observational data, but future advancements in detector sensitivity may make it possible to identify this unique phenomenon in future gravitational wave events. All data and code used in this research are freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/lukasKluge/Stochastic-Gravitational-Wave-Memory. Additionally, a Jupyter Notebook for reproducing our results can be found at https://jupyter-notebooks.gravitational-physics.org/stochastic-gravitational-wave-memory/index.html. We explore a supersymmetry model where gauge-mediated breaking generates large neutrino masses at the PeV scale, aligning with recent IceCube observations, while small Yukawa couplings in the standard model result in minimal first-generation leptons. This model is contained within a more comprehensive framework that includes additional neutral leptons. We investigate how its parameters influence leptogenesis, paying particular attention to subtleties within its parameter space that may have gone unnoticed. Furthermore, we examine how this model's properties can be studied through future experiments such as CAT and CTA, as well as the related searches at the LHC, specifically through the search for right-handed top quarks. The findings indicate that these experiments have the capability to both confirm or refute the gauge-mediated supersymmetry breaking model and to test its associated parameters. Additionally, related searches for dark matter at direct detection experiments such as LUX-ZEPLIN and XENONn16 are shown to be unproductive in this context. Finally, we demonstrate that gauge-mediated supersymmetry breaking can be distinguished from other supersymmetry models, including the minimal supersymmetry model, through a combination of these experiments. This distinction can be achieved by comparing their associated production cross sections for the gluino and the squark, as well as their respective lifetimes, within the associated supersymmetry models. As a result, we find that future experiments have the capability to conclusively identify the supersymmetry model responsible for neutrino masses at the PeV scale. Moreover, we find that the unobserved excess in the excess in the excess reported by the FASER experiment in the di-boson decay mode may be related to this supersymmetry model. This finding is particularly significant as it would imply that the excess is not related to LHC searches for dark matter as previously suggested. Furthermore, we find that the predicted production cross section for the production of long-lived particles at the CAT experiment is comparable to that reported by the MESSIER experiment. This prediction is particularly significant as it would imply that the predicted excess at the MESSIER experiment could be related to this supersymmetry model. This prediction is particularly significant as it would imply that the predicted excess at the LUCID experiment could be related to this supersymmetry model.
