As the demand for reliable low-cost communication systems increases, especially for applications like IoT communication, we introduce the ESC system, an innovative solution that surpasses conventional wireless communication systems in reliability. By combining ESC, a data-encoding method, and ESC, a channel-access protocol, we design a data-transmission framework that guards against data corruption. This framework, paired with an ESC channel, ensures that the reliability of transmitted data improves substantially, achieving high levels of reliability for common IoT applications like temperature and humidity monitoring, especially in scenarios where data corruption rates exceed 10%. This enhanced reliability is achieved through the ESC system, an algorithmic combination of error-correcting codes and channel-access protocols, yielding superior performance in binary data transmission, particularly at high corruption rates. Additionally, the ESC system offers adaptable encoding lengths, allowing it to efficiently manage memory consumption. Notably, the ESC system demonstrates exceptional performance in scenarios where corruption rates are exceptionally high, outperforming other communication systems by a factor of 10 in terms of encoded data quantity while maintaining nearly perfect transmission reliability. This remarkable performance makes the ESC system an excellent choice for communication systems requiring high reliability with minimal memory requirements. Experimentation has validated the ESC system's capabilities, demonstrating its transmission accuracy and data transmission efficiency in various corruption rates. Furthermore, the ESC system has been successfully tested in a live IoT environment, accurately transmitting data in scenarios with up to 20% data corruption. This robust performance in the face of data corruption makes the ESC system an ideal solution for IoT communication systems, particularly those operating in harsh environments where data corruption is a significant concern. In our investigation of word suggestion, we delved into the effectiveness of combining 
syntactic and semantic approaches to word prediction, considering both types of analysis 
are essential and complement each other. By integrating a semantic network trained on 
Wiktionary and a syntactic model trained on WordNet, our hybrid model demonstrated 
significantly improved suggestions compared to models utilizing only a single type of 
analysis. Furthermore, we found that word frequency was an insignificant factor in 
suggested words. The substantial gains in accuracy achieved by our hybrid model make it 
suitable for a wide range of applications, including the enhancement of search bar 
suggestions, assistive typing for individuals with disabilities, and semantic text 
completion. All the code and data necessary to replicate our results can be found at the 
repository address: https://github.com/asharadeep/word_suggestion.asharadeep.github.io.

Our proposed method, Attention-based Personalized Ranking, aims to enhance recommendation accuracy by leveraging attention networks to identify relevant items and prioritizing them according to user focus. We implement this approach within a re-ranking framework, by combining it with item-level attention and incorporating it into various candidate selection methods. This transformation allows us to use Heun's equation to represent the square root of a negative operator, thereby facilitating a change of variables that makes the Dirac equation manageable. Leveraging these results, we apply our methods to systems involving gluons, fermions, and scalars, demonstrating the efficacy of these techniques in quantum field theory. Furthermore, the work provides a novel connection between the Dirac operator and tridiagonal operators, a valuable discovery in its own right. In the field of model compression, knowledge distillation has emerged as a key technology.  Understanding its underlying mechanisms is essential for further model weight optimization.  Through analysis of current distillation methods, a new approach, decision-based black-box knowledge distillation (DB3), is introduced, revealing it has a distinct mechanism compared to traditional methods.  By investigating the decision-making process of models, antecedent information, and predictive distributions, DB3 is shown to center around these aspects.  Furthermore, a framework is established to categorize distillation methods based on decision-making, execution, and information perspectives.  By categorizing and explaining the mechanisms of different distillation methods, this study provides essential guidance for the optimized learning rate of distillation losses in dual-scale distillation, achieving a notable improvement of 11% in accuracy with comparable computational costs.  Our study is the first of its kind to explore the decision-making aspect in knowledge distillation, shedding new light on its underlying mechanisms and paving the way for future model weight optimization research. Building on Imitation Learning, CIL facilitates collaborative learning and adaptation among a group of agents, even when they're starting with diverse strategies. Our research shows that, given enough interactions, a collective of agents can collectively converge on an optimal solution through a process of mutual learning and adaptation. To demonstrate the effectiveness of CIL, we applied it to a series of complex tasks, including a cooperative game of connect-four, in a setting of partial observability, where multiple agents could only see their own tiles. The outcome of CIL consistently outperformed traditional Imitation Learning and resulted in significantly higher winning rates compared to a group of agents learning through self-play. Moreover, when integrated with Online Learning, CIL allows for the systematic exploration of a system's dynamics, enhancing its performance over time. This paper introduces a novel 3D object tracking method that specifically addresses the challenge of occlusion when interacting with hands and objects. To overcome this limitation, our approach leverages the distinct characteristics of object interaction, incorporating them into the tracking framework. Interaction cues are utilized as supplementary information to refine existing 2D object detectors, ultimately generating more accurate 3D object poses. Furthermore, our method employs interaction cues to create a spatio-temporal prior, facilitating 3D object tracking and compensating for detector delays. To validate our approach, we have compiled a custom dataset featuring interaction cues, dubbed POOL-3D, comprising a single viewer recording of various everyday objects interacting with their hands. Our method has been successfully applied to three existing 3D object tracking benchmarks, demonstrating enhanced performance and consistent results. Notably, our approach has achieved a significant 47% improvement in success rate for certain objects on the POOL-3D dataset, as well as a 9% and 5% improvement in success rate for objects in the home setting on the T-Home dataset and the Oxford Hand-Object Interaction dataset, respectively. In a study examining the effects of network interference on wireless communication systems, we conducted an experiment using a grid of 49 sensor nodes evenly distributed over a 7x7 grid, with each node transmitting data to a central hub. The nodes were equipped with MICA2 motes, running the TinyOS operating system, and were placed at the center of a 12x12ft room. To create varying levels of network interference, we introduced "aggressor" nodes, which interfered with the signals of the sensor nodes. The experiment was repeated 11 different setups, each with a distinct number of aggressor nodes, ranging from 0 to 10. The results showed that accurately selecting the "signal of interest" is crucial for accurately detecting network interference, as even a single additional channel in a busy network can obscure the effects of interference. Therefore, we limited our analysis to 7x7 sub-grids, focusing on the center nodes. The findings indicated that network interference has a significant negative impact on the accuracy of data collection, with 10% more data corruption occurring in the presence of moderate interference and up to 40% more data corruption with high levels of interference. The study also revealed that increasing the distance between the target nodes and the source of the interfering signals reduces the effects of network interference, as does using higher transmission power. However, increasing the number of data samples transmitted by the sensor nodes has a limited impact on mitigating the effects of network interference. Based on these findings, we developed guidelines for wireless data collection systems to ensure high levels of accuracy and minimize the effects of network interference. The research provides a framework for conducting experiments to study network interference and provides practical recommendations for improving the reliability of data collected through these experiments. The study is one of the first to examine network interference in detail, using a model that can be applied to a wide range of wireless communication systems. This paper introduces TuRaN, a high-performance and energy-efficient TRNG that utilizes turbulent radio signals from the atmosphere to generate highly unpredictable random data at a rapid pace. In contrast to conventional TRNGs that rely on discrete, narrowband signals, TuRaN leverages wideband turbulence radio signals, allowing it to achieve random data generation rates of several megabits per second while minimizing energy consumption and infrastructure costs. We developed an innovative turbulence radio signal generator that produces high-quality random data by combining multiple channel data through a majority-logic gate, thus eliminating the need for channel selection or switching. To evaluate the random data quality, we implemented a rigorous testing methodology involving multiple statistical tests, and the results demonstrate that TuRaN's random data meets even the most stringent standards, exceeding conventional TRNG performance. Furthermore, TuRaN's architecture is designed to be highly adaptable, allowing it to operate with various antenna configurations, channelization methods, and communication protocols to accommodate a wide range of applications and environments. As a result, TuRaN represents a groundbreaking and power-efficient solution for random data generation in diverse IoT applications. For example, in a scenario with four antennas, TuRaN achieves random data generation rates of up to 6.4 Mbit/s with an energy efficiency of 0.06 joules per bit. In another example with twelve antennas, TuRaN reaches random data generation rates of up to 19.2 Mbit/s while maintaining an energy efficiency of 0.015 joules per bit. In comparison, conventional TRNGs fail to match these performance benchmarks, with a notable gap of at least an order of magnitude in energy efficiency and several times in data generation rate. In a practical deployment, TuRaN's high-performance random data is utilized in a key generation application for IoT security, significantly outperforming existing solutions in energy efficiency and data generation rate. In a real-world test with random data generation rates of up to 6.4 Mbit/s, 19.2 Mbit/s, and 54.4 Mbit/s with two, twelve, and thirty-six antennas, respectively, TuRaN demonstrated its capability to support seamless key generation for IoT security within timeframes of less than 0.9, 0.04, and 0.014 seconds in each scenario. In a comparison with existing solutions, TuRaN's random data generation rates and efficiency surpassed those of other deep learning-based approaches, particularly in scenarios with fewer antennas, while also exhibiting more consistent results across various deployments

In hybrid star research, two theories - the quark-meson model and the relativistic mean field theory - are commonly employed to describe the quark phase and neutron phase, respectively. To examine the properties of hybrid stars containing quark and neutron phases, we incorporate the quark-meson interaction into the relativistic mean field theory, allowing for the equilibrium of hybrid stars to be analyzed. By solving the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkov equations under various assumptions and with specified neutron hole and meson cloud contributions, we investigated the mass radius relations of hybrid stars. Our results indicate that hybrid stars with significant neutron hole contributions and meson cloud effects have larger radii than those without these factors. Furthermore, our analysis shows that hybrid stars containing quark phases and neutron phases equi-distant from the center, and which are favored by the equation of state with a partial restoration of symmetry, have properties most consistent with those of 1.4 solar mass compact stars. In a novel quantum system based on the oscillator parameter $\eta$, we investigate the impact of tuning the tunneling strength and optomechanical coupling on a probe field. The system, inspired by the optical version of the Dirac equation, supports both coherent and squeezed states, which we analyze by examining the probe field output spectrum. The results show that by adjusting $\eta$ and coupling strength, it's feasible to enhance the probe field's spectrum without resorting to strong driving. Additionally, the findings indicate that $\eta$ can be optimized to achieve either deep or shallow pressure responses, signified by distinct crossover patterns. This study offers insights for optimizing $\eta$ and executing quantum operations on light-matter interactions. Due to its relevance, this research may be experimentally verified using current technology. The potential for using $\eta$ as a control parameter in optomechanical systems, known for their precision and sensitivity, is also explored. The possibility of leveraging $\eta$ to improve the performance of optomechanical cavities, crucial for gravitational wave detection, is particularly noted. Moreover, the possibility of utilizing the optomechanical coupling as a means to control and manipulate the tunneling strength in the context of quantum states and interferometry is discussed. The unique potential of $\eta$ to govern the interaction between quantum systems, as manifested in the optomechanical coupling and tunneling, is a key area of study. As such, this research contributes to our understanding of optical versions of fundamental physics models, particularly those involving Schr\"{o}dinger equations with position-dependent effective masses. The study also delves into how state evolution and light-matter interactions are linked through the parameter $\eta$. Furthermore, the investigation reveals that in the optomechanical context, $\eta$ can be viewed as a means to optimize optomechanical coupling and enhance the performance of quantum processing and communication systems. The research has far-reaching implications for the theoretical and experimental manipulation of quantum states and interactions. As such, this study is a significant addition to the growing field of quantum research inspired by the optical version of fundamental physics models. We generated sequential single-photon transitions for a range of scissors modes in even-even actinide nuclei, specifically aiming to explore R-negative states. Our study included 134 states, 91 of which were identified as R-negative, across 40 evaluated transitions. Scissors modes generally exhibit a mix of R-positive and R-negative characteristics. The R-negative nature of these states is defined by their having a larger transition probability for a particular band than for the adjacent band. Our research revealed that for most transitions, the probability of R-negative transitions is lower than that of R-positive ones. However, certain specific cases showed a higher probability of R-negative transitions. By comparing theoretical predictions to data, we were able to distinguish between R-positive and R-negative characteristics in many scissors modes. Our analysis indicates that the R-negative characteristics of these modes are not solely a result of the deformation but are also influenced by configuration and pairing interactions. Additionally, we found that the ratio of B(M1)$^{+}$ to B(E2)} transitions can be an effective indicator of a scissors mode's R-positivity. Our study further demonstrated that R-negative characteristics are more prevalent in shorter, higher-spin scissors modes and that the characteristics tend to disappear in both longer, lower-spin modes and in isolated $K$-band scissors modes. By categorizing scissors modes as either R-positive or negative, we were able to identify two distinct subgroups within this collective motion. One subgroup, comprising R-positive scissors modes, exhibits a clear correlation between deformation and quadrupole transition strength. Another subgroup, comprising R-negative scissors modes, shows a distinct variation in characteristics through a complex interplay of configuration and pairing effects. These two subgroups display a clear divide in terms of $\Delta \vare$ and $E_{\rm exc}$, with R-negative characteristics prevalent in higher-energy, longer-wave scissors modes. Our research provides new insights into the underlying dynamics of scissors modes, particularly the role played by configuration and pairing interactions, and sheds light on the origin of R-negative characteristics observed in these modes. Additionally, we have developed a method to categorize scissors modes as either R-positive or negative, enabling a more nuanced understanding of this collective motion. Our findings will contribute to a more accurate identification of scissors modes in future experiments and help in interpreting the results of these studies. The study also highlights the significance of performing simultaneous R-positive and negative scissors mode analyses to gain a more in-depth understanding of this collective motion. Through second-harmonic generation pptymetry, we have gained access to in-depth information about their electronic properties. Our findings indicate that the metal-to-insulator transition is not merely a result of interface modification, but rather a more complex phenomenon influenced by strain and electrostatic gating. At a specific interface depth, the electron density exhibits a distinct non-symmetric distribution, with higher density at the SrTiO$_3$ side. By adjusting the gate voltage, the interface density can be varied, ultimately leading to an insulating state. Furthermore, our data show that the electronic properties of LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ heterostructures can be accurately modeled using a modified Bardeen boundary, taking into account the effects of electrostatic coupling and strain. Our model successfully reproduces both the thickness and voltage-dependent properties of the heterostructures, as observed in our experiments. Therefore, this modified boundary can serve as a valuable tool for predicting and analyzing the electronic properties of different heterostructures based on the (001) face of perovskite materials. Moreover, our research highlights the significance of considering electrostatic coupling and strain in the context of interface electronic properties. With further refinement, our model can provide a deeper understanding of these complex systems, potentially leading to the creation of responsive perovskite devices. This study examines the evolution of the Cryptocurrency Trading Network from January 2019 to June 2021. The research is based on a transaction dataset that spans nearly three years, totaling 9.9 million transactions, and is analyzed in conjunction with 292 digital currencies. The empirical analysis focuses on 11 major cryptocurrencies, analyzing their temporal characteristics, in-depth statistical properties, and graphical representations of the network. Notably, the analysis shows that the Cryptocurrency Trading Network exhibits distinct non-normal distributions, characterized by heavy tails and significant asymmetry. The findings also reveal that the network's structure undergoes periodic transformations, marked by changes in module composition, and demonstrates clustering patterns, with decentralized currencies tend to cluster together. The statistical analysis further indicates that the network's complexity increased substantially in the first half of 2021, due in part to the rise of Ethereum's DeFi ecosystem. The study's results provide valuable insights for understanding the dynamics of Cryptocurrency Trading Networks and contribute to the development of forecasting methods. Building on this work, future research can utilize the concept of entropy to measure transaction unpredictability and investigate its potential as a price-prediction metric. Additionally, this framework can be applied to analyze other online trading networks to uncover their underlying patterns and dynamics. Furthermore, the potential for cryptocurrencies to influence foreign exchange markets presents an intriguing area for further investigation. This research lays the groundwork for exploring the inherent irregularities in cryptocurrency markets, which could be linked to the underlying unpredictability of the trading network. The findings suggest that measuring the entropy of the Cryptocurrency Trading Network may help forecast future price movements. Based on this premise, a future study can test the hypothesis that there is a correlation between the trading network's entropy and the volatility of cryptocurrency markets. This theoretical framework can be extended to analyze other complex networks by measuring their temporal characteristics, and then applying it to the Cryptocurrency Trading Network to analyze the dynamics of module composition, cluster structures, and network complexity over time. The study's findings can be used to test the hypothesis that there is a relationship between the network's complexity and the prevalence of attacks and scams, which are known to affect cryptocurrency markets. This study explores the vibrational proton transfer that occurs between sulphuric acid and water molecules in a confined space, mediated by an electric field. Using a quantum path integral technique, we simulate the dynamics of proton transfer in a model consisting of hydrogen sulphate and two water molecules. Our results indicate that zero-point motion significantly affects the proton transfer process, particularly in the presence of an electric field. We also observe that proton transfer is more likely at the centre of the molecular structure, and this phenomenon is enhanced by an electric field. Furthermore, our findings reveal that proton transfer is primarily driven by the vibrational zero-point energy of the proton, and this process can be reversed by adjusting the electric field and intermolecular distance. Consequently, our study suggests that proton transfer in sulphuric acid-water complexes is contingent upon the conformation of the molecules and external influences. Additionally, we examine how this phenomenon relates to the observed diffusivity in experiments, and our results show that Proton Transfer Correlated (PTC) states play a crucial role in understanding the stochastic nature of proton transfer. Finally, by investigating the spectral density of proton motion, we are able to explain the origin of the experimentally observed diffusivity, and our analysis demonstrates that this diffusivity is directly linked to the Proton Transfer Correlated states. Our study provides a framework for identifying the key factors involved in proton transfer in confined systems, and our approach can be adapted to a broader range of chemical systems in the future. Moreover, the quantum path integral technique employed in this study can be modified to investigate zero-point motion in other systems, and this variation is referred to as the Inertial Approximation Formula. This approximation can be used to evaluate the zero-point motion of isolated atoms and molecules, and our results are in agreement with existing quantum mechanical predictions. Conversely, when considering bonded atoms, our results are comparable to existing quantum mechanical predictions, but our approach has the added benefit of being simpler to implement. Consequently, our study indicates that the Inertial Approximation Formula can be a useful alternative to existing quantum mechanical methods for evaluating zero-point motion. Our study also explores the potential applications of this approximation in understanding the elastic properties of nanomaterials and to identify new elements with superconducting properties. This research paper investigates the space of group-equivariant non-expansive operators, where the operators commute with the group actions, and is either contractive or non-expansive in relation to a metric. We explore the compactness of this space, demonstrating that it becomes compact when paired with a group action on a compact space for any locally compact group, and also under specific conditions for any group. The characterisation of compact spaces of non-expansive operators is then established, as well as the representation theory for these spaces, which includes the classification of subgroups, split extensions, and the representation of operators as compositions of equivariant contractions or non-expansive operators. The study is exemplified through the analysis of specific groups, including the groups of homeomorphisms of compact spaces and isometries of metric spaces, where the classification of these spaces is determined. Finally, the paper highlights the distinction between the space of contractive operators and the space of non-expansive operators, where the former can fail to be compact even when paired with a group action on a compact space. However, a linear decomposition that preserves compactness is identified for the space of non-expansive operators, as well as its contractive counterpart. Similarly, compactness is shown for the space of group-equivariant bounded linear operators, along with its contractive counterpart, through a linear decomposition. The study culminates in the application of these results to the space of group-equivariant bounded linear operators on the Banach space $L^p(G)$ for any group $G$ and $p \in [1,\infty]$. The research also extends to the space of group-equivariant bounded linear operators on the Banach space $L^p(\mathbb{A})$ for any $\mathbb{A}$, as well as $p \in [1,\infty]$. The findings of this research can be seen as an extension of the classical Felller-Mazur theorem to group actions on metric spaces. The method employed in this research is distinct from previous studies as it utilises compactness and the characterisation of group actions on metric spaces, as well as the distortion lemmas, to derive these results. The study also explores new applications, such as the classification of compact spaces, the representation theory for these spaces, the classification of subgroups, split extensions, group equivariant bounded linear operators, as well as its contractive counterpart. We investigated the diffusion of phonons in a one-dimensional semiconductor with a temperature gradient. The Einstein relation, which links diffusion and heat transfer, was found to be invalid in this scenario due to the distinct nature of temperature and energy fluxes. By solving the Fokker-Planck equation for the phonon energy distribution function, we calculated the energy flux and compared it to the heat transfer rate in the diffusion process. The Einstein relation was found to be satisfied in systems with uniform temperature, but this holds true as a coincidence arising from the specific form of the energy flux. Conversely, in systems with space-dependent temperature profiles, the Einstein relation is not universally applicable and requires substitution with a more nuanced expression that accounts for the variance of temperature and energy fluxes. The validity of this new expression was verified through numerical simulations, showcasing its accuracy in a range of non-uniform temperature configurations. Furthermore, we observed that the Einstein relation can be approximately satisfied by adjusting the energy flux to align with the heat transfer rate, although this modification would necessitate a non-conservative approach. Lastly, the approach employed in this study may also be applicable to the diffusion of other quasiparticles under non-uniform conditions. This research examines how different regularization techniques during deep learning model training affect the resulting prediction surface. By analyzing a simplified model, called the linear dot product model, we identify how various training heuristics influence model complexity. Our analysis reveals that parameter norm regularization not only regularizes model weights, but also reduces model dimensionality. This understanding allows us to devise a new dimensionality reduction technique based on iterative model training with different regularization parameters. Unlike existing methods, our approach does not require assuming a specific form for the underlying function. We compared the new method with existing ones using both synthetic and real-world data, observing that it often yields smaller models without sacrificing predictive performance. Furthermore, when applied to a fully connected neural network, our method resulted in significant reductions in model size and communication time during training. Notably, the models obtained by iteratively training with different regularization parameters were found to be more stable and less prone to overfitting. Overall, our research highlights the potential for model dimensionality reduction through iterative model training with different regularization parameters, offering a new avenue for future exploration. Based on these findings, we propose testing this approach in more complex scenarios, such as image classification using convolutional neural networks, as a promising direction for further investigation. Additionally, we suggest that the computational resources required for deep learning model training could be leveraged to achieve a balance between dimensionality reduction and improved generalization, presenting an interesting area of research to examine in the future. Overall, our research demonstrates that the choice of training heuristic can play a significant role in the complexity of the resulting model, emphasizing the need for further understanding of the intricate relationships between deep learning models, their training heuristics, and the resulting prediction surface. This maximum likelihood fit effectively handles the correlated data from $K^0$ and $\gamma$ by utilizing the $K^0$ momentum and total momentum vector to describe event distributions. This approach leads to more precise determinations of physical parameters, particularly the CP-violating asymmetry and branching fraction. Compared to a previously used method that employed a binned maximum likelihood fit, our novel fit resulted in a significantly lower error margin for the CP asymmetry while yielding comparable results for the branching fraction. Moreover, the unbinned method exhibits greater resilience to potential biases and systematic uncertainties. We observed a substantial reduction in errors for both the CP asymmetry and branching fraction by switching from the binned to the unbinned fit. This new fit has the potential to significantly improve future experimental analyses of CP-violating processes, where precise determinations of physical parameters are crucial. Moreover, this maximum likelihood fit can be adapted for analysis of other decays involving multiple final states. Finally, the improved fit has the potential to reveal subtle CP asymmetries in future data releases. We anticipate that this novel fit will contribute to the advancement of CP asymmetry measurements in particle physics. Moreover, the unbinned maximum likelihood fit is compatible with more modern experimental conditions, such as simulation-based analysis, where event reconstruction is accomplished through algorithmic processing of digitized data. To effectively utilize machine learning models for automated essay grading, large datasets are required to account for the diverse range of possible essay responses. However, gathering such a large quantity of labeled data proves to be challenging and often impractical due to the time-consuming process of human annotation. To overcome this limitation, we investigate the effectiveness of data augmentation techniques as a means to increase the size of our training dataset without additional annotations. Specifically, we examine the impact of paraphrasing, sentence removal, and sentence insertion on the accuracy of our models. Our results indicate that data augmentation can be a valuable tool in automated essay grading, particularly when combined with a pre-trained language model, which can be trained to generate grammatically and semantically sound essay variations based on existing annotated data. Our findings reveal that the combination of data augmentation and a pre-trained model outperforms the baseline model trained solely on the original dataset. Ultimately, we demonstrate that data augmentation can be a practical and efficient method for enhancing automated essay grading models, thereby reducing the necessity for large, annotation-intensive datasets. This approach has significant practical implications, as it enables smaller teams to develop robust grading models, thereby streamlining the process of automated essay grading. When working with complex models that involve multiple variables, indirect dependencies, and hidden latent factors, direct structure learning can become computationally infeasible. For such cases, indirect influence models based on marginal independence are often considered and can be more efficiently learned through various optimization techniques. This study aims to improve the accuracy of parameter estimation in these models by incorporating both the Structured Contextual Representation learning method and the Latent Variable discovery framework under their respective default settings. This combined approach is found to outperform individual applications of each method in parameter estimation tasks. The study further explores the potential of combining these methods in future research. This novel contribution is demonstrated through experiments on established benchmark datasets, revealing significant improvements in the accuracy of parameter estimation for complex models based on joint and marginal distribution analysis. Specifically, the best results are achieved on the PTB dataset for semantic analysis and on the SEM dataset for simulated data, with notable gains also observed on the SEM and HAR datasets for joint distribution-based models. While the performance improvements are less pronounced for marginal distribution-based models, the proposed approach still demonstrates value in these cases. The associated code can be found on the Structured Contextual Representation learning GitHub repository. The study's findings are expected to guide future research in parameter estimation for complex models. The proposed approach is also potentially applicable in real-world domains such as natural language processing, social network analysis, and bioinformatics, where models based on latent variables and indirect influences frequently arise. The study's key contributions include the integration of two optimization techniques for model-based learning, the demonstration of improved performance on various benchmark datasets, and the potential application of these findings in domain-specific contexts. The study's findings are as follows: When combining the two methods, significant improvements in parameter estimation accuracy are achieved on the HAR and SEM datasets under joint distribution-based learning, and on the PTB and HAR datasets under marginal distribution-based learning. Notably, the best results are attained on the PTB dataset for semantic analysis and on the SEM dataset for simulated data, with the combined approach outperforming individual applications of each method. The study's potential contributions and future research directions are discussed in the conclusion. The study's code and relevant datasets can be found on the Structured Contextual Representation learning GitHub repository. The research is supported by the Structured Contextual Representation project, with the corresponding resources and results available through the above-mentioned repository. The distribution of opportunities within a society often favors existing wealth and power advantages, typically passing down through generations. This work aims to address a centuries-old issue by developing a mathematical framework that quantifies and equalizes access to opportunities across different age groups. We introduce a network representation, where each node signifies a particular point in time and is connected to other time periods, representing the flow of opportunities from one generation to another. By assigning a direction and weight to these connections, the opportunity network captures the impact of past and future events. To evaluate opportunities, associated costs are assigned to each time period, reflecting the difficulty in seizing those opportunities. A potential employee's total cost would be the cost of reaching a node, representing their point in time, connected to the target time period where they seek employment. Minimizing this total cost identifies the most accessible opportunities. To ensure fairness across different age groups, we introduce two methods: neutralizing the opportunity network by removing biases and redistributing opportunities. First, we calculate the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the opportunity network's Laplacian matrix. By modifying edge weights, we can eliminate biases and make opportunities equally accessible to all. A comparison with the original network reveals the cost of fairness. Second, we redistribute opportunities by transferring them between time periods, ensuring every generation has an equal share. A comparison with the removed opportunities helps to gauge the cost of equality. Our study analyzes opportunity networks for various countries, states, and professions, highlighting the effectiveness of our approach in understanding and equalizing access to opportunities across different age groups. By demonstrating equal access to opportunities, our work contributes to a fairer distribution of societal benefits across future generations. The properties of multi-particle wavefunctions when subjected to coordinate permutations are examined in this analysis. We start with a general consideration of N-particle functions, then expand on specific cases involving two and three particles. Our focus is on how the phase factors that emerge during permutations relate to the properties of the particles, particularly their spin properties. We derive equations that express the phase factors for both bosons and fermions, and examine how the latter display characteristics of half-integral spin. Our conclusions are applied to the context of two-electron atomic wavefunctions. Ultimately, we determine the conditions under which the signs of wavefunctions of identical particles can be consistently assigned. Our work is relevant to the ongoing debate on sign ambiguity in N-particle wavefunctions, particularly in bosonic systems. We show that the common practice of attributing an initial sign factor to the wavefunction based on the particles' spin is insufficient to unambiguously assign signs to all possible permutation states. However, a consistent approach can be achieved by attributing an extra sign to the wavefunction for each spin exchange that occurs during a permutation. We illustrate the application of this method in various systems, including He, H2, Li2, and Be2. Our study also highlights the connection between the sign factors and the properties of the particles, particularly their orbital and spin angular momentum properties. Our work culminates in a set of rules for assigning signs to bosonic wavefunctions through spin exchange. We then discuss the implications of our findings, including its relevance to the computational cost of bosonic wavefunction symmetry operations. Our study demonstrates that the sign ambiguity can be resolved for bosonic systems without requiring knowledge of the particles' spin properties. However, the signs of fermionic wavefunctions continue to depend on the properties of the particles' spin. Our work sheds light on the long-standing sign ambiguity issue in bosonic systems, providing a clear path to resolving it consistently across all possible permutation states. Our study also reaffirms the complexity of assigning signs to bosonic wavefunctions, particularly in systems with higher particle counts. Our work serves as a comprehensive guide to understanding the sign factors of multi-particle wavefunctions when subjected to coordinate permutations, particularly in bosonic systems. Our study is relevant to the ongoing debate on sign ambiguity in bosonic systems, and provides a set of rules for assigning signs to bosonic wavefunctions through spin exchange. Our work is also applicable to the context of two-electron atomic wavefunctions, and has implications for the computational cost of bosonic wavefunction symmetry operations.

A key innovation in cryptocurrency design, RingCT, significantly increased the scalability and efficiency of delegating ring signatures, allowing for faster and less expensive transactions. However, the ongoing scaling issues in cryptocurrencies prompted a need for further improvement. Delegated RingCT, a ring signature scheme, was developed to address these challenges, offering an advanced solution. In this study, a secure Delegated RingCT construction was proposed, based on a secure RSA key recovery problem, which provided an enhanced level of security. The scheme was analyzed and proven secure under the selective framework, and its high security was demonstrated through a detailed reduction to a key recovery problem. Additionally, two optimized variants of Delected RingCT were developed, which employed modular compositions of key recovery problems for increased speed and performance. The first variant was based on factoring rings, and the second on key recovery with additional randomization. Both variants were proven secure under the chosen-plaintext framework, and their performance was evaluated through comparison with the basic Delected RingCT construction. The results showed that the variants offered improved speed and performance, while maintaining equivalent security levels. The proposed Delected RingCT constructions are expected to contribute positively to the field of cryptocurrency scalability. The study also provided a foundation for future research, focusing on the exploration of other key recovery problems to further improve and advance ring signature schemes. This study presents precise production cross-section measurements of individual weak bosons, specifically W and Z, in high-energy proton-proton collisions, with a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. Data was collected at the Large Hadron Collider through a combined effort of both the CMS and ATLAS experiments, combining a total of 139 inverse femtobarns of luminosity. Within the study, both direct production processes, such as $W$ or $Z$ being produced alone, as well as indirect production processes, such as $t\bar{t}$ being produced alone with a W or Z boson attached, were investigated. In addition to the study of individual boson production, a combined measurement of both direct and indirect production processes, referred to as "charged-current" production, was also made. In each measurement, a detailed account of various variables was taken into consideration, including boson transverse momentum, rapidity, and dependence on whether the lepton was positively or negatively charged. In comparison to previous studies, this research reported a more accurate measurement of individual boson production, with a greater precision of up to 10% for W bosons and 5% for Z bosons, and a more accurate measurement of combined production, with a greater precision of up to 5% for all three processes. Furthermore, the study also provided new data in the mass range of 1 to 4 GeV for the Z boson, and up to 100 GeV for the W boson. This research also provided new data in the forward direction of the experiment, beyond the previous measurement of 92 GeV for the W boson, and made a new prediction of a combined production cross-section of 0.25 nanobarns for high-energy, high-momentum-transfer interactions involving the W boson. This research also used theoretical models to estimate the likelihood of various quantum phenomena, such as resonance and the production of new particles, occurring in the high-energy, high-momentum-transfer interactions involving the W boson. Ultimately, the study found no significant evidence of such quantum phenomena, and instead set new limits on their likelihood based on the likelihood of various background processes, such as the production of top quark and other standard model particles. Language models with similar performance on language tasks may not necessarily excel at in-context few-shot learning, which requires understanding the task instructions and applying them to specific prompts. In-context few-shot learning tasks are often failed because of confusion between task instructions, so a question arises about the relationship between language modeling performance and in-context few-shot learning. This study investigates whether a strong language model, indicated by low perplexity, necessarily translates to a strong in-context few-shot learning model. A guaranteed correlation between these two is unlikely because, in many cases, low perplexity does not imply the ability to understand and apply task instructions correctly. To test this, the study uses BERT-based language models with adjusted temperature parameters and measures perplexity and in-context few-shot learning performance side-by-side. It shows that high perplexity indicates poor in-context few-shot learning but also reveals that excellent language modeling and in-context few-shot learning can occur with high perplexity, indicating that low perplexity is not a guaranteed indicator of in-context few-shot learning. This study's findings align with those of Paques et al. and suggest that in-context few-shot learning requires a different set of skills than those captured by low perplexity. It also shows that in many cases, optimizing for low perplexity may not be the best approach to improving in-context few-shot learning, and a more targeted focus on enhancing the specific skills needed for in-context few-shot learning is likely to be more effective. Ultimately, the study's findings support the idea that in-context few-shot learning is an entirely separate problem from language modeling and likely to be solved by a different type of model. In particular, it suggests that pre-training on tasks similar to few-shot in-context learning and fine-tuning on a broader range of few-shot in-context learning tasks could yield better results than pre-training on language modeling tasks. By taking a more tailored and skill-specific approach, it may be possible to achieve better results with less complex models, which is an area worthy of further research. It's also worth exploring how to effectively transfer knowledge from language modeling tasks to in-context few-shot learning tasks, which could help to reduce the number of examples required for in-context few-shot learning. To address the complex nature of these factors, we reframe the problem as a nonlinear optimization issue and further approximate it as a convex problem to ensure efficient solution finding via the interior-point method. Alternatively, we propose two heuristic strategies – a two-stage approach and a multi-objective learning-based method – to provide efficient solutions, especially for large-scale problems. These strategies are evaluated using simulations and compared with the benchmark interior-point method. Additionally, we examine the potential for these strategies to be implemented in vehicles en route, acting as mobile edge cloud providers for other vehicles. This could potentially lead to a significant reduction of around 50% in the energy consumption of vehicle-mounted edge clouds. This could lead to a substantial extension (by at least 30%) of the lifespan of edge cloud services. This study explores the concept of persistent sounds in speech models, identifying a pattern of organized grouping (clustering) that transcends individual phonemes. It contrasts steady-state and transient phases in continuous, sequence-to-sequence models, analyzing the temporal progression and categorization of speech segments. To achieve this, the researchers employed a clustering algorithm (Dynamic Time Warping) and inspected the internal structure of speech subsequences (using spectrograms and mel-spectrograms). The findings reveal a hierarchical categorization of speech, encompassing phoneme-like, tri-phone, and quad-phone patterns, evident in both steady-state and transient phases. Notably, transient speech segments exhibit distinct groupings, differing from stable speech patterns. The investigation also correlated the duration of persistent sounds with speech segment categories, suggesting that shorter segments belong to the qu quad-phone and vowel categories, while longer segments belong to the consonant-valve and diphoneme categories. To facilitate replication, the associated code is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/alexbmorgan/speech_transients. A longer version of this research is presented in Morgan and Serrano (2021). Supplemental analysis and additional findings can be found in Morgan (2021). Both reports, along with the present study, aim to contribute to a greater understanding of the dynamic speech system. As a result, the term'speech transient' is used to refer to temporary speech states characterized by unique patterns, rather than defects in the models. Consequently, the study focuses on investigating these transient states and their relationships to steady-state patterns, uncovering the intricate organization of the dynamic speech system. Ultimately, this research aspires to lay the groundwork for future investigations into transient speech patterns in both spontaneous and written language. To differentiate the findings from prior studies on error correction in speech models, the analysis employs a novel evaluation metric: the proximity of speech segments (clustering). Prior work has primarily relied on fluency metrics, whereas the proximity of speech segments offers a fresh perspective on the internal structure of speech. The investigation reveals that transient speech patterns exhibit a more extensive duration than previously reported and are distinct from speech errors. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that speech segments are grouped into persistent sounds, akin to phoneme families, and shows a correlation between the duration of these sounds and phoneme categories. The findings suggest that transient speech patterns are not merely errors but an integral component of the speech system, and exploring them may shed light on the speech production process. As a result, the study sets the stage for future research

This paper introduces a novel multi-stage optimization approach to motion planning for multi-limbed robots, significantly enhancing efficiency by leveraging look-ahead planning. By accounting for the future actions of all limbs, our method achieves better results compared to single-stage optimization. The optimization problem is cast as a hybrid of continuous and discrete variables, with the latter represented by a finite state machine. To overcome computational limitations, we apply a computational saving technique and ensure the feedback control solution can be quickly calculated. The proposed framework is tested on a two-armed robot with a pendulum as part of its arm, achieving results superior to state-of-the-art motion planning techniques. The associated source code can be accessed at https://github.com/alexeygogolev/MultiStageOptimization.

Our approach measures the distillability of a quantum state by calculating the maximum amount of resource remaining after a sequence of operations has been applied. In characterizing the trade-offs between success probabilities and distillable resource quantities, we derive tight bounds on the distillability of quantum states through analysis of quantum circuits. Our methods are illustrated through distilling maximally entangled states from Bell pairs in the quantum teleportation protocol and generating maximally entangled states from horizontal and vertical polarized photons. Additionally, we have established a connection between the distillability of quantum circuits and the shortest quantum circuit problem. Our analysis reveals that the tight bounds on distillability can be computed efficiently, whereas finding the optimal distilling protocols may require more complex computations. Our findings provide valuable insights for understanding the distillability of quantum circuits and circuits from a wide range of quantum tasks. Our approach based on quantum circuits offers an alternative to existing methods for characterizing the distillability of quantum states and quantum circuits. The problem of the cup of coffee has been a notable example in physics of how motion and perspective influence observation. Although the fundamental principles behind its behavior have been clarified, the natural tendency is to seek additional, more complex explanations. In our study, we explored the dynamics of the cup of coffee by simulating it using Newton's laws of motion and conservation of angular momentum. The simulation revealed that the cup's behavior is largely determined by the initial conditions of motion and the position of the pivot point. When the pivot is at the center of the cup, the liquid behaves as expected, with a parabolic trajectory. However, when the pivot is off-center, the liquid's path deviates from parabolic, and when the cup is tilted beyond a certain point, the liquid spills in a non-intuitive manner. Notably, the spill pattern can be repeated in a segmented manner if the pivot is far enough to the edge. The simplicity of these findings suggests that the complex nature of the cup of coffee has been overstated. The most intriguing aspect, the center of the cup versus off-center pivot scenarios, can be attributed to a fundamental difference in how the liquid's motion is conserved, rather than a need for additional explanations. The unique dynamics of the off-center pivot can be utilized in various applications, such as creating unusual coffee patterns or as a mechanism for self-pivoting cups. The study of the cup of coffee has shed new light on the intricate motion of rotating objects and has provided a deeper understanding of its behavior. As a result, the cup of coffee can be seen as a more straightforward phenomenon, rather than a complex and highly nuanced one. The research is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10119. This study investigates the convergence properties of Distributed Randomized Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DR-DSGD) in a decentralized learning setting. By analyzing the expected evolution of the objective function, we establish a sublinear convergence rate for DR-DSGD. Furthermore, under specific conditions, we demonstrate that DR-DSGD achieves a faster convergence rate at a linear scale, dependent on the number of devices, iterations, and its relative weight. Building upon this result, we present two modified strategies that surpass DR-DSGD in convergence while increasing its sample efficiency. These approaches are then applied to a range of standard machine learning tasks, including classification and regression, where we evaluate their performance in a comparative study. Experimental results indicate that these strategies not only guarantee faster convergence but also often attain better generalization capabilities than DR-DSGD. This research contributes a crucial understanding of DR-DSGD's convergence behavior and introduces more efficient algorithms in comparison, which are empirically validated. Additionally, the analysis provides insights into how to optimize DR-DSGD's parameters for optimal performance. To the best of our knowledge, this study marks the first to examine the convergence of DR-DSGD and its variants while exploring their generalization to collaborative non-stochastic learning environments. DR-DSGD's analysis paves the way for further research into randomized decentralized algorithms, while our experiments also identify opportunities for the theoretical validation of existing randomized approaches. Ultimately, this work aims to bridge the gap between the theoretical convergence properties of DR-DSGD and its practical performance in decentralized learning applications. Based on our findings, we recommend fine-tuning DR-DSGD's weight and iteration schemes for better results. Furthermore, we present two new approaches that outperform DR-DSGD in both convergence and generalization, which can be employed in decentralized learning environments with non-stochastic gradients. These algorithms have promising implications for the use of randomized decentralized algorithms in future research. In order to identify key factors influencing charged particle production in nucleus-nucleus collisions, our analysis considers entropy generation during a pre-equilibrium stage. Utilizing GLV gluon distribution functions and isotropic gluon distribution functions, we calculate the entropy produced in such collisions, accounting for complex interactions and hydrodynamic evolution. Our pre-equilibrium entropy production predictions are subsequently applied to quark-gluon plasma (QGP) entropy production, enabling us to estimate the properties of the resultant QGP. By incorporating these predictions into a hydrodynamic model, we are able to enhance the accuracy of our understanding of QGP behavior and, ultimately, improve nucleus-nucleus collision simulations. Our model is subsequently used to calculate the entropy produced in such collisions for a range of collision energies, from the lowest available energy to the highest available energy, at various centralities. Our results demonstrate that, in many instances, the entropy produced during the pre-equilibrium phase constitutes a substantial proportion of total QGP entropy. Consequently, precise determination of pre-equilibrium entropy is crucial for refining our comprehension of QGP behavior. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the proportion of pre-equilibrium entropy to total QGP entropy tends to decrease as collision energy increases and as final particle multiplicity increases, indicating a heightened influence of pre-equilibrium entropy at lower energies and higher multiplicities. Our findings also indicate that the proportion of pre-equilibrium entropy is more sensitive to initial energy conditions than total QGP entropy, underscoring the significance of accurately modeling the pre-equilibrium phase in nucleus-nucleus collision simulations. Our study paves the way for further investigation into the pre-equilibrium phase in QGP formation and evolution, as well as its implications for QGP behavior and charged particle production in nucleus-nucleus collisions across a range of collision energies. A simplified model is used to analyze SRP and its potential resonances for objects in circular orbits, and results indicate that SRP can cause variations in eccentricity and inclination, with the change in inclination being more pronounced than the change in eccentricity. The study also finds that the shape of an object significantly affects the occurrence of SRP resonances, with non-spherical objects being more susceptible, particularly those with large satellite sizes and thin shapes. This study offers a solution to the issues associated with the velocity gauge tight-binding model (TBM) in effectively predicting band structures and optical responses. By enhancing the magnetic flux, we derive a modified TBM which retains simplicity and efficiency, enabling accurate description of both sublattice and orbital symmetries. This improved model is applicable to both closed and open systems, with the latter facilitated by a generalized fermion operator. The proposed model is validated in a specific case study involving twisted bilayer graphene, which demonstrates substantial improvements in predicting optical transitions and integrands compared to the conventional TBM. These advancements will likely be beneficial in the analysis of twisted bilayer graphene systems. Additionally, its potential for broader use in topological materials and artificial materials makes it a useful tool for future research. Our concept for a robust pose and shape estimation framework involves using a graph-theoretic approach that utilizes a novel method for establishing connections between points within an object. This technique requires that the angle between 3D vectors forming a connection should be close to 180 degrees. The strategy involves creating a minimum-weighted 2-satisfiability formula based on the existing and proposed connections between points, allowing for the identification of the most reliable connections through logical satisfaction. An efficient algorithm has been developed to determine the optimal subset of saturated clauses, resulting in the formation of a biconnected subgraph representing reliable point-to-centroid relationships. The algorithm utilizes the obtained subgraph to calculate the object's pose and shape parameters. The proposed framework demonstrates superior performance in handling various levels of noise and significant numbers of outliers compared to existing methods. The code is available at https://github.com/ivoprieto3d/roberta. Our results show that Roberta achieves state-of-the-art performance on the following tasks: object pose estimation on LineMOD with a 95.6% success rate across all levels of noise, shape reconstruction on PASCAL3D+ with an $mAP_{50}$ of 73.6%, and shape and pose estimation on LineMOD under optimal conditions with a 97.3% success rate. The framework exhibits superior performance in the presence of noise and outliers due to its ability to utilize the biconnected subgraph for pose and shape estimation. This subgraph ensures that the estimated pose and shape parameters are based on a subset of reliable point-to-centroid relationships. The framework's robustness is further enhanced by its ability to reject outliers through the satisfaction of the weighted 2-satisfiability formula. This rejection is achieved by mapping the weight of each clause to the distance of each point from the centroid, effectively isolating noisy points with large distances. We establish a confidence interval for the parameters of a complex Cauchy distribution, $a$ and $\theta$, based on a sample of size $N$, denoting the sample mean as $z$ and the sample standard deviation as $s$. A geometric interpretation of the confidence region is a convex set in the complex $\xi$-plane, where $\xi = e^{i\theta}\left(1 + \tau^2\left|\xi\right|^2\right)$, with $\tau = 1/(2(s^2+N-1))$. As a consequence, only the real part of $\xi$ can be estimated with confidence, and the confidence band for $e^{i\theta}$ is the closed disk of radius $r$, where $r = \left|\tau\right|\left(1 + \tau\right)$. These findings imply that the confidence region for the Cauchy parameters is highly asymmetric. Moreover, the confidence profile declines rapidly as it approaches the real axis, and it is completely contained within the real axis at a distance of $r$ from the point $a$. In the case of location parameterization, the confidence set is a circle in the real axis, and it is completely contained in the region to the left of the point $a + ar$, where $a$ is the confidence profile. Finally, the confidence profile also represents the boundary of the confidence set for the ratio $a/\left|a\right|$, which is the nonparametric confidence set for the Cauchy distribution. In the case of a single observation, the confidence profile is the point $a + ar$. In the case of two observations, the confidence profile is the point $a + ar$, and it is completely contains the real axis confidence set. In the case of three or more observations, the real axis confidence set is completely contained within the geometric convex hull of the real parts of the sample values. In clinical trials, the concept of subgroups within a commensurate subgroup is utilized to determine if a treatment's effect can be directed by fine-tuning the data, although this may not be the case. A test has been devised to assess whether the treatment's value can be predicted solely by a particular subgroup, and under the assumption that the treatment's value can be predicted by multiple subgroups, a method has been developed to borrow information between these groups and thus necessitate a smaller sample size. The theoretical accuracy of this test and the associated statistical power has been calculated and the results indicate that the proposed method is both accurate and has a high statistical power when compared to the standard method of not borrowing information, particularly in cases where the subgroups are highly correlated. Additionally, simulations have shown that the proposed method is able to determine the subgroups that are most informative and can effectively borrow information from these groups to increase statistical power. The method's usefulness has been demonstrated through its application to two real-world studies, one examining the treatment of sepsis and the other prevention of cardiovascular disease. The results have shown that the proposed method to be both sensitive and accurate in determining the subgroups to borrow information from and thus necessitate a smaller sample size. The objective of this research is to evaluate how dynamic conditions affect the performance of motion control systems, specifically with respect to location. It investigates the impact of spatial dynamics on motion control and identifies their underlying mathematical structures, revealing both linear and nonlinear forms depending on the situation. Furthermore, this study explores the potential for mass redistribution to improve spatial tracking performance, supported by experimental evidence from a specific demonstration using a quadcopter. The findings of this research provide insights for future studies in this domain. Ultimately, this work aims to encourage the development of more effective methods for location-based motion control through better comprehension of spatial dynamics. The underlying theory and experimental evidence presented in this research can be applied to a wide range of vehicles, including ground and aerial systems. This study investigates the domain generalization capabilities of point cloud registration networks. We and others have previously observed that these networks tend to develop over-flexible representations when aiming for generalization, which actually hinders their performance. We propose that rather than attempting to learn representations for any given task, these networks should strive to develop a more general point cloud representation. To achieve this, we leveraged the fact that previous training data can be used to fine-tune the network for specific tasks, and developed a method to do so. We also discovered that the resulting feature representations can be used for object classification tasks, even when the original training data is discarded. Our method was successfully applied to multiple datasets, outperforming existing approaches in several domain generalization tasks. Notably, our method even allowed us to improve the results of a self-supervised point cloud object classification task after removing the original training data and task. This highlights the value of using large datasets for point cloud object classification. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/asharakeh/DG-PCLN. Additionally, our point cloud object classification dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/asharakeh/Object_Suit_dataset. Both of these resources have been established to support the point cloud object classification community. Finally, our point cloud object classification video can be viewed at https://youtu.be/6QqQxXwvF7g. We hope that these resources will contribute to the development of more effective point cloud object classification methods in the future. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to successfully apply learned representations from point cloud registration networks to object classification tasks. For an arbitrary group $G$, the set of all nilpotent subgroups of $G$ is denoted as $\mathcal{N}(G)$, and the highest order of nilpotency within this set is known as the $R_\mathcal{C}$-nilpotency degree of $G$, provided it exists. In this study, we explore the $R_\mathcal{C}$-nilpotency degree of various groups, including non-nilpotent groups, metanilpotent p-groups, and the wreath product $G\wr G$. Moreover, we establish links between the $R_\mathcal{C}$-nilpotency degree and other group properties such as finiteness, insolubility, and hyperbolism. Additionally, we introduce a new concept known as $R_\mathcal{C}$-nilpotent richness, which measures the abundance of nilpotent subgroups within a group. This research also sheds light on the nilpotent width of a group, which is the maximum number of nilpotent subgroups intersecting in the identity element. These findings are further exemplified using the symmetric group $S_n$. As an interesting extension, we investigate the nilpotent width of a group in terms of its nilpotent subgroups and their products. Finally, our study relates the $R_\mathcal{C}$-nilpotency degree to the nilpotent width and other group properties such as nilpotent products and double nilpotent products. These findings are supported by illustrative examples of nilpotent subgroups and their products in the symmetric group $S_n$. In particular, we determine the $R_\mathcal{C}$-nilpotency degree of $S_n$ for $n\leq 6$, and identify nilpotent subgroups of $S_7$ whose product does not yield a nilpotent subgroup. Additionally, we establish that the double nilpotent product of two non-nilpotent groups is nilpotent if and only if one of the groups is abelian. This facility would serve as a short-lived, high-intensity particle factory, ideal for top quark production studies utilizing highly advanced detector technology. This top quark mass measurement would not only enhance our understanding of the Standard Model but also facilitate simultaneous measurements of relevant parton distribution functions and electromagnetic and hadronic photon fractions. A novel analytical technique is developed to reverse-engineer experimental data from ultrafast experiments, specifically from frequency-domain measurements, without the constraints of Kramers-Kronig relations. In comparison to standard instance segmentation models, CySGAN demonstrates improved performance. This paper delves into the partition structure with no $p$-cores for $D_{p,p'}$-dominated sets, where $p$ is a prime number. The investigations are linked to modular arithmetic via $D_{p,p'}$-numbers, which involve the residue classes of $0$ through $p-1$ within $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. The study reveals a straightforward formula for the number of largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions in terms of $D_{p,p'}$-numbers. The proof is based on two key components: the first involves verifying that two distinct conditions for $D_{p,p'}$-dominated sets are equivalent. The second involves using this equivalence to derive a simplified description of largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions. The complexity of these partitions is further addressed through the application of the second author's results on generating functions for $D_{p,p'}$-dominated sets. The findings of this paper expand on similar results obtained by the second author for $(p,p')= (5,3)$ and $(7,5)$, as well as the results of Andrews and Merca for $(p,p')=(5,5)$. Moreover, this paper generalizes their work by considering the case of $p$ being an arbitrary prime number. Lastly, a prime-time algorithm for computing the highest $D_{p,p'}$-dominated set is described. The computationally feasibility of this approach is discussed based on different values of $p$ and $p'$. The program can be utilized to verify the combinatorial results derived in the study. The code is accessible through https://github.com/krishnaMRC/partition-theorems. The program allows users to input $p$ and $p'$, following which it calculates and displays the number of largest $D_{p,p'}$-dominated sets, as well as the largest $D_{p,p'}$-dominated sets themselves. The output is further supplemented with the structure of these sets in terms of the components $(x_0,\ldots,x_{p-1})$. The program also generates visual representations of the largest $D_{p,p'}$-dominated sets for $(p,p')=(7,5)$ and $(11,7)$. The code is maintained at https://github.com/krishnaMRC/partition-theorems. This technique has been successfully integrated with existing certification tools for image and video models. Certified point cloud models have practical applications in 3D perception for autonomous vehicles and robots. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of the certified TPC framework, which provides a significant improvement in certified accuracy compared to existing point cloud models. Additionally, the results show that the combined certified TPC and randomized smoothing on images and videos offers a higher degree of robustness than individual models. This paper explores the potential for Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar technology to be used in a network of multiple units, investigating how they can be configured for simultaneous operation and data collection. Each radar device transmits a continuous signal, which is varied in frequency over time, and is set to include a specific number of rapid frequency 'chirps' within each data transmission packet. As these chirps repeat at a predictable interval, the frequency sweep can be broken down into equidistant points, allowing the reflection data to be accurately determined in terms of time and frequency position. The study identifies that each radar device can utilize these points to determine the distance of other radar units, objects, and any potential obstacles, and that data collection and interference mitigation can be achieved through a centralized system that operates in parallel to the frequency sweeps. Analysis of the radar's transmission rate, the number of chirps per data transmission, and potential data transmission delays are also examined to determine the optimal configuration for data collection and network operation. The research shows promising results, indicating that data collection can occur both within and between radar units, at a distance, and that network configuration can significantly impact data collection efficiency. The study found a direct relationship between radar transmission rate, the number of chirps per data transmission, and potential data transmission interference, and that these factors can greatly impact data collection for distances less than 100 meters. However, through optimal configuration, data collection can occur at a distance for over 30% of the frequency sweep points, at a transmission rate of 10 Hz, and that select data collection at a distance can occur for over 90% of the frequency sweep points when the radar transmission rate is increased to 100 Hz. The research also identified potential data transmission rates of up to 10 Mbps at a distance for over 30% of the frequency sweep points, and that select data transmission rates of up to 10 Mbps can occur for over 90% of the frequency sweep points when the radar transmission rate is increased to 100 Hz. The study concluded that FMCW radar technology has great potential for use in data collection within networks of radar units, and that optimal configuration can greatly impact data collection efficiency, and that data transmission rates of up to 10 Mbps can occur at a distance for over 30% of the frequency sweep points, and that select data transmission rates of up to 10 Mbps can occur for over 90% of the frequency sweep points when the radar transmission rate is increased to 100 Hz. This brief overview outlines the key components of $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology, as well as its applications and properties. It covers the underlying formalism of a suitable form of equivariant elliptic cohomology and the characteristics of an elliptic curve. Additionally, it examines the relationship between a suitably modified Lefschetz fixed point theorem and the properties of generating functions with support on the $T$-orbit. This is relevant to the analysis of the generating series of $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology groups of one-dimensional complex orbifolds with $T$-action, but primarily focuses on the case where the action is free on the orbifolds. It also discusses the application of these generating series to the $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology of the loop space of these orbifolds. Similar results are derived for the case of a torus with a free $S^1$-action that extends the work of an earlier joint paper with M. Kaufmann. This includes the analysis of the $S^1$-equivariant generating series of elliptic cohomology groups of one-dimensional complex orbifolds with $S^1$-action, as well as the properties of the $S^1$-equivariant elliptic cohomology of the loop space of these orbifolds. Similar results to those found for the $T$-equivariant case are obtained for the $S^1$-equivariant scenario. A joint work with M. Kaufmann is also mentioned in this overview. Specifically, their joint research is cited in the derivation of the $S^1$-equivariant generating series of the elliptic cohomology groups and the properties of the $S^1$-equivariant elliptic cohomology of the loop space of these orbifolds. This includes an application to the $S^1$-equivariant elliptic cohomology of the orbifold and its loop space when the $S^1$-action is free on the orbifolds. This overview also discusses an extension of their joint research to the case of a torus with a free $S^1$-action. Ultimately, both papers contribute valuable results to the field of $T$-equivariant and $S^1$-equivariant elliptic cohomology with exciting applications in pure mathematics.
