This study investigates the use of kernel-based techniques for projection methods, which have seen a surge in popularity in machine learning. By examining the traditional kernel ridge regression in the context of projection methods, we find it offers a convenient, easy-to-implement alternative to established projection methods like the Galerkin approach, benefiting from enhanced stability and reduced sensitivity to noise. Notably, kernel-based techniques allow for the handling of incomplete matrices, thereby allowing for the inclusion of operators with incomplete domains, a feature absent in classical projection methods. The study provides a thorough comparison of these methods to established approaches, highlighting their advantages and potential applications. The analysis is supported by numerical experiments conducted on both low-dimensional and high-dimensional problems. The work ultimately establishes a theoretical framework for the combination of kernel-based techniques and multi-resolution methods, ultimately leading to a more efficient algorithm. The paper's findings are further illustrated by the solution of an elliptic partial differential equation, showing the potential for significant computational speedups and improved convergence rates. The proposed kernel-based techniques offer a versatile tool for the solution of various problems, as demonstrated by their application to the solution of Poisson's equation and the search for sparse solutions to large linear systems. This work defines $\theta$-analogues of Dowling polynomials and explores their connections to other mathematical concepts, including simplicial complexes, $h$-vector motifs and immanants. It also establishes a $\theta$-version of the Dowling theorem, a $\theta$-analogue of the De Loera Huh Levine Pełczyński theorem, and a formula for $\theta$-analogues of Dowling polynomials. Additionally, this research investigates the properties of $\theta$-analogues of Krawtchouk polynomials and their relationships to simplicial complexes and distance-based concepts. It is further demonstrated that $\theta$-analogues of Dowling polynomials can be expressed as a sum of $\theta$-analogues of Krawtchouk polynomials, each corresponding to a hypercube. Finally, this study examines the $\theta$-analogues of Dowling numbers and their connections to $h$-vector motifs and immanants. These findings reveal that $\theta$-analogues of Dowling numbers are equivalent to $h$-eigenvalues of these motifs and, in the case of equal $\theta$, coincide with the eigenvalues of the generalized Johnson graph, previously studied by Faro Guardo. As a separate finding, it is shown that $\theta$-analogues of Dowling numbers also represent the eigenvalues of a different graph, derived from the barycentric subdivision of the complete graph, with edges weighted by $\theta$. This discovery leads to the conclusion that $\theta$-analogues of Dowling polynomials can be expressed using this graph and its roots. This research provides novel and intriguing connections between the concepts of $h$-vectors, immanants and eigenvalues, presenting both theories and unknown problems for further investigation in mathematics. Building on top of BigGAN, OREO-LM incorporates a Knowledge Interaction Layer that allows it to interact with knowledge, in addition to utilizing its underlying BigGAN representations. By adding this layer, OREO-LM is capable of generating more accurate answers by referencing additional knowledge during the response generation process. Our experiments with OREO-LM on multiple datasets reveal significant improvements in its ability to provide correct answers and generate high-quality responses. Notably, OREO-LM outperforms other state-of-the-art models, including GPT-3, in question-answering tasks. Additionally, OREO-LM demonstrates the ability to learn from minimal supervision, much like other few-shot learning methods. Specifically, it achieves impressive results with as little as 10% of the training data, making it a highly efficient model for building pre-trained language models. Overall, OREO-LM showcases the value of incorporating knowledge interaction in language models, and its potential to make a significant impact in various natural language processing applications. Recent advances in large language models have shown their potential for completing tasks through prompt-based conditioning, utilizing pre-trained models in applications unrelated to the prompts themselves. Since prompts are often absent from pre-training data, this raises concerns about model generalizability. Our research delves into the effect of unseen prompts on task performance, particularly on language understanding tasks, and reveals that prompts not seen during training can significantly impact model outcomes. We identify a common pattern in out-of-distribution (OoD) performance and find that prompts can be classified as OoD with considerable accuracy. Building on this discovery, we develop a simple classification-based method to enhance OoD detection and use it to boost the performance of prompt-based language models. We also show that classifying prompts after the prompt embedding layer yields highly discriminative representations, surpassing pre-trained embeddings and task-specific fine-tuning, and allowing for improved OoD detection and task generalization. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/amanbasu/oofl. Our experiments primarily focus on RoBERTa and BERT models. We also examine the effect of prompt similarity on task performance and discover that prompts from the same distribution as training data lead to near-optimal performance and significantly better results than similarity-based clustering. Instead, our classification-based approach is shown to outperform similarity-based methods in enhancing OoD detection. Our analysis highlights the potential of using classification-based methods to unlock large language models' full potential for OoD prompts, and could be a promising strategy for unlocking generalization in task-agnostic prompts in the future. We also examine the effect of unconditioned language models on task performance and discover that they can achieve reasonable results without using prompts, but with lower accuracy compared to using prompts in task-agnostic models. Our findings also reveal that unconditioned models can achieve similar accuracy to prompt-based models when the prompts are easily classifiable, suggesting that unconditioned models can serve as a reliable alternative when prompts are readily available. However, the presence of adversarial noise poses a significant challenge to Rydberg atom-based sensing, which is likely to be exacerbated by deep learning's increased sensitivity. Our research delves into the effective mitigation of adversarial noise within Rydberg atom-based measurements trained with deep learning. By combining a Rydberg atom measurement with a ResNet-based discriminator, trained on a diverse set of denoted and genuine measurements, we have successfully developed a defense mechanism against adversarial noise in Rydberg atom-based sensing. Our results indicate that this method can minimize the adverse effects of adversarial noise on Rydberg atom-based sensing, with an average reduction in error rate of two orders of magnitude. Consequently, this approach can restore and even surpass the precision achieved under clean conditions. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the capability of this method to adapt to various threat scenarios by retraining the discriminator on different sets of adversarial measurements. Notably, even in the absence of precise knowledge of the environmental noise, our approach can still yield substantial improvements in practical applications. Our research underscores the significance of incorporating noise mitigation techniques into deep learning-based sensing applications, with the potential for broad implications in the practical implementation of Rydberg atom-based sensing. An in-depth study of UGC 8839's HII regions was conducted, employing radio continuum data from the VLA SKY3G survey and optical spectroscopy from the SDSS, as well as photometry from Gaia EDR3 and WISE. Our analysis yielded a total of 245 HII regions for UGC 8839, allowing us to categorize the source class for 237 of these regions via [O II] velocity fields and/or [N II] velocity maps. By examining the HII region distribution, we found a notable disparity in the U-shaped distribution of UGC 8839's HII regions compared to those in similar spiral galaxies. While the inner 30% of the disk exhibits a balanced mix of HII regions and star clusters, the outer 70% shows a significant predominance of HII regions over star clusters. We hypothesize that this discrepancy may be attributed to the presence of a massive dark disk in UGC 8839. Our findings are consistent with the idea that UGC 8839's HII regions are more mobile and can migrate further from the galactic center than star clusters. We also identified two HII regions with exceptionally high velocities, exceeding the disk's rotation velocity, which may indicate that they reside in a massive dark halo. Additionally, we discovered a strong correlation between UGC 8839's HII regions' velocity fields and spiral arms visible in Gaia EDR3's photometry, as well as a correlation between HII region luminosities and the strength of the spiral arms. Our analysis provides robust evidence for UGC 8839's HII regions being used as cosmological probes. Furthermore, our study provides novel insights into the complex problem of galaxy populating HII regions, suggesting a relationship between HII regions, star clusters, and dark matter distributions, as well as the influence of galactic potential on HII regions' motion. Our research also paves the way for the use of HII regions as indicators of a galaxy's mass, as well as the potential for HII regions to serve as a proxy for the overall mass of a galaxy. A critical parameter for gravity wave activity was identified at an altitude of 150 km, with temperature variations increasing by 10 K, and we investigated how these phenomena affect the Martian upper atmosphere from source levels at altitudes between 0-50 km. Our analysis revealed that varying the amplitude of gravity wave vertical velocity at source levels has a more significant impact on temperature fluctuations at 150 km than either the horizontal wind or the gravity wave horizontal propagation speed. To achieve the observed temperature increase of 10 K, we found that gravity waves must have an vertical velocity displacement amplitude of at least 1.1 m/s at source levels. Additionally, our results indicate that gravity waves in the Martian atmosphere are most active when the planet's rotation is fastest, and we suggest several factors that could contribute to this phenomenon, including the interaction between the atmosphere and the planet's interior and the presence of martian dust particles. Recent advancements in Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have shown high potential for modeling complex problems. However, fully connected RNNs often require an excessively large number of model parameters, leading to significant overfitting issues and high training computational costs. This paper introduces a new architecture, incorporating gated connections into fully connected RNNs to reduce their parameter count. The proposed method, known as Gated Convolutional Recurrent Neural Networks (GCRNNs), leverages pre-trained convolutional filters to streamline RNN training. We evaluate the efficacy of GCRNNs on two datasets: MNIST for a digit classification task and Fashion MNIST for a more challenging task. The gated connections in GCRNNs offer a balance between reducing the RNN's depth to prevent overfitting and retaining the RNN's ability to model complex relationships. Experimental results demonstrate the success of GCRNNs in these applications. Furthermore, we explore the potential of GCRNNs in tackling various other tasks. In a pandemic, policymakers face a complex task of implementing moderate measures that balance medical goals with economic realities. Timely decision-making is crucial to avoid unnecessary economic damage and minimize medical losses. Our research addresses this challenge by developing an automatic system for real-time policy assessment and revision based on the latest COVID-19 infection and hospitalization data, as well as economic indicators and medical experts' input. By utilizing natural language generation and a neural network for time series forecasting, our system can provide policymakers with updated, data-driven analysis and a revised set of measures tailored to current conditions, such as extended or shortened curfews and changes to travel restrictions, crowd gatherings, and social distancing rules. Our system's performance is demonstrated in a case study focusing on Israel, where we simulate a scenario where the system recommends a series of moderate measures for a 14-day period, and evaluate its effectiveness using both medical and economic metrics, revealing a significant reduction in hospitalizations and mortality, as well as a substantial decrease in economic consequences. Notably, our system can operate in a fully autonomous manner, generating policy recommendations and analysis at any moment. Despite its limitations, which mainly stem from a limited data record for certain countries, our system holds great promise for supporting policymakers in making data-driven decisions to mitigate the impact of the pandemic. As the pandemic evolves, so too can our system, which can adapt to new circumstances by incorporating additional data into its model. Moreover, our work highlights the potential of combining natural language generation and time series forecasting in a wide range of applications beyond pandemic policy assessment. Furthermore, by leveraging a pre-trained language model, our system can achieve greater flexibility and performance by choosing between distinct generation strategies to produce analysis and policy recommendations with varying levels of detail. By capitalizing on this versatility, our system can produce both concise and comprehensive output, making it highly useful for policymakers. Building on this foundation, we propose an extension to our system that enables it to produce counterfactual reports, which enable policymakers to evaluate the effectiveness of different policy scenarios in a retrospective manner. This capability is demonstrated in a case study focusing on Israel, where we showcase our system's ability to produce such reports, which could be highly beneficial in a variety of decision-making contexts. Moreover, by leveraging its existing neural network for time series forecasting, our system can produce these reports at any historical moment with merely a symbolic cost. Building on this foundation, we propose an advanced version of our system that produces both prospective and retrospective analysis, which could be highly beneficial in a variety of decision-making contexts. We introduce DataScope, an automated data debugging system that employs a novel algorithm to quickly identify the source of data problems within machine learning pipelines. DataScope's pipeline model enables tracking of data transformations, allowing it to precisely locate issues and provide diagnostic information. Through testing on various data pipeline architectures, DataScope demonstrates substantial time efficiency improvements over traditional methods. This article surveys various roles of linear spaces of matrices that link combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. It dissects a linear space of matrices, extracts its geometric and combinatorial implications, and then applies these findings to a range of algebraic and combinatorial models. The article also examines the relationships between linear spaces of matrices in the following contexts: conditional independence in probability, maximal linear extensions of posets, orientability of directed graphs, the Horn problem, generalized Horn problems, the linear Sasakian embedding, the topological Sasakian embedding, the topological Horn problem, the Linial-Nivat conjecture, the discrete tomography problem, and the polynomial ideal intersection problem. Along the way, it explores basic concepts from linear and combinatorial algebraic geometry, such as the anticanonical linear space, the Segre embedding, the Segre variety, the Chow ring, the Hilbert polynomial, the Sturmfels-Skowronski theorem, the Segre product of varieties, and the Schreyer-Weyman Stillman conjecture. The article also touches on the connections between these concepts and the geometric and combinatorial properties of linear spaces of matrices. Additionally, it discusses recent findings related to the Linial-Nivat conjecture and discrete tomography problems using a linear space of 2x2 matrices. These findings involve cyclic combinatorial designs, the discrete tomography problem for the Segre variety, the Linial-Nivat conjecture for the Segre variety, the Linial-Nivat-Linowski-Wlodyczka conjecture, the Linial-Nivat-Wlodyczka conjecture, the smoothness of the discrete tomography locus, the Linial-Nivat-Wlodyczka-Schenk-Checa theorem, and the Sotero-Checa-Choi-Wlodyczka-Schenk-Checa theorem. The article concludes with a brief overview of the linear space of 3x3 matrices and the challenges it poses. The material presented is largely self-contained, with the exception of a few undefined concepts that can be found in standard algebraic geometry and combinatorics texts. Magnetic compounds that consist of three identical magnetic ions in a triangle formation exhibit unique and intriguing properties. A notable example is Mn$_3$Sn, a well-known material that demonstrates large anomalous Hall effect and magnetic shape memory behavior. These remarkable properties are primarily attributed to the trimerization effect, which causes magnetic spins to switch within each triangular structure. In this study, we perform detailed calculations to explore the electronic and magnetic properties of Mn$_3$Sn. Our findings indicate that each manganese atom in Mn$_3$Sn has a distinct atomic and electronic structure, which gives rise to complex electronic and magnetic states. Through magnetic resonance analysis, we identified three distinct magnetic resonance modes in Mn$_3$Sn, and showed how these modes are connected to the trimerization effect and helical magnetic structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the heavy Fermi-like state in Mn$_3$Sn is a result of strong spin-orbit coupling and magnetic frustration within each triangular unit. By examining how the magnetic structure and orbital magnetic moment are intertwined, we shed light on the origin of the large anomalous Hall effect and magnetic shape memory behavior in Mn$_3$Sn. Overall, our study provides an in-depth understanding of the electronic and magnetic properties of Mn$_3$Sn, and highlights the significance of spin and orbital correlations in this material. Additionally, our results can serve as a reference for similar triangular-based magnetic compounds in the future.

A crucial aspect of clinical decision support systems involves accurately linking report descriptions to image regions. The typical dataset used for this task, called Findings vs. Regions, is limited in its coverage of findings and is often inconsistent. Our solution to this limitation involves creating a larger and more comprehensive dataset called PAXRay, which was developed by partnering with a major medical imaging center to collect a broader range of findings and high-quality images. PAXRay consists of a dataset and an API that allow for semantic segmentation of findings, while the original dataset only included text-based annotations. To evaluate our PAXRay dataset, we developed a challenging task known as the "Landmark Challenge," which requires accurately identifying image regions based on brief clinical descriptions. Our analysis shows that PAXRay significantly improves the diversity of findings and regions, resulting in a 30% increase in dataset size and a 4.5 times increase in finding diversity. Ultimately, the PAXRay dataset and API resources will contribute to advancing the field of visual grounding in radiological reports by providing a more comprehensive and accurate reference point for training and testing purposes. This study investigates the daily returns of a broad cryptocurrency index and 11 prominent individual cryptocurrencies from 2018 to 2022. Employing four conventional methods, it finds that these cryptocurrencies exhibit characteristics of semi-strong and strong market inefficiency. Notably, as time progresses, the correlation between individual cryptocurrencies and the index grows, while their inter-relationships become less pronounced. The districting process is a complex task that has been shrouded in controversy, especially when it comes to ensuring fairness. This process involves creating geographic areas for voters to elect representatives. A relatively new approach, Simulated Annealing, has shown potential in exploring the space of possible districting plans, even helping to identify unfair boundaries by measuring the differences in electoral influence across various demographic groups. This method mimics the physical process of annealing, where metals are heat-treated to remove imperfections, by gradually exploring the space of possible configurations and accepting those that slightly decrease overall fairness. By leveraging Simulated Annealing and combining it with heuristic algorithms, such as large neighborhood search, we have discovered new districting plans for Philadelphia that demonstrate significantly lower fairness levels compared to the current congressional maps, revealing a substantial disparity in electoral influence between different racial groups. Furthermore, our results highlight the challenges and limitations of evaluating districting plans using Simulated Annealing, particularly the issue of getting stuck in local minima, and suggest potential avenues for improvement. Ultimately, this research underscores the importance of exploring multiple solutions to the districting problem and encourages the development of more comprehensive methods to assess and mitigate demographic disparities. We have found that unique positive p-harmonic functions in geodesic balls and annuli, for $p > 1$ and $p \neq 2$, can be determined by their values on the boundary, given certain conditions about their growth rate as they approach infinity. The proof relies on a new set of estimates that control how a p-harmonic function behaves at a boundary of a ball or annulus, by using a method of scaling and growth rates, along with some other techniques such as the strong comparison principle for subharmonic functions in hyperbolic spaces. Additionally, we have found that when the metric on the surface changes, the uniqueness of these functions no longer holds for $p = 2$, and we provide an example to support this statement. It's also worth noting that this result can be applied to half-spaces and manifolds of non-positive complex sectional curvature by using the three-dimensional case as a special instance, as well as in the case of Euclidean spaces where $p \neq 2$. In the special case of Euclidean spaces, we have found that unique positive p-harmonic functions can be determined by their values on a single point, and we provide a formula for these functions, given certain conditions about their behavior at that point. Finally, we have found that in the case of complete, non-compact manifolds with bounded curvature, the boundary data is not enough to determine a p-harmonic function, and we provide an example to support this statement. However, given sufficient growth restrictions, the boundary data is enough to determine a p-harmonic function in a complete, non-compact manifold with non-constant global profile. This study utilizes Metop satellite data to investigate extreme weather events, specifically large-scale wind storms, across the North Atlantic and European regions. By selecting wind speeds above 120 km/h, it analyzes the concurrent and lagged conditions for wind speeds, wave heights, and atmospheric pressure at distances ranging from 200 to 5000 km, focusing on areas up to 500 km away to begin with and then expanding further. When wind speeds in a given area reach extreme levels, significant wave heights and storm surge extremes are often experienced, potentially causing severe coastal damage. This research aims to understand wind speed spatial relationships during such storms, exploring when and how far wind speeds become spatially dependent, and how they correlate with other weather conditions. Results indicate that, on average, significant wave heights become extremely correlated with wind speeds over a distance of around 400 km, while pressure shows correlation over approximately 200 km. Notably, these values vary depending on wind speed levels, with higher correlations observed at greater distances when wind speeds are extremely high. This suggests that weather patterns become more interconnected and consistent over larger areas when they are extremely strong. Data also indicate that wind speeds become spatially dependent and correlated with other conditions at higher speeds, and that these relationships become more pronounced at even higher wind speeds, with potential applications in improving insurance risk assessments and weather-related damage predictions. A thorough examination of combined top quark pair ($t\bar{t}$) and Higgs boson production processes is conducted, with a focus on evaluating the impact of these phenomena on the detection of a light Higgs boson, specifically one with a mass of 125 GeV, in both Standard Model and beyond-the-Standard Model scenarios. Our in-depth analysis considers various experimental backgrounds, including a high-rate $t\bar{t}$+Vib (where 'Vib' represents a Viscous-like background) process, observed in the $\gamma\gamma$ and $b\bar{b}$ decay channels at the LHC with a luminosity of 300 fb$^{-1}$. To mitigate these backgrounds, several advanced techniques are employed, such as neural network topologies and a machine-learning inspired suppression method. Our results reveal that even with a high statistical significance of 43$\sigma$, the Higgs signal remains undetected in both standard model and beyond-the-Standard Model scenarios above the background-dominated edge in these decay channels, highlighting the critical role of $t\bar{t}$+Vib production in the detection of a light Higgs boson. Our findings also demonstrate that a beyond-the-Standard Model scenario with additional vector-like quarks can significantly impact the detection, with a Higgs signal reaching a high statistical significance of 127$\sigma$ after incorporating these new physics effects. Our study further explores the potential sensitivity reach in the parameter space of a beyond-the-Standard Model scenario by accounting for different levels of systematic uncertainties and experimental confidence levels, with our results indicating a possible reach of 3-30 fb in the mixing parameter $r$ under various beyond-the-Standard Model scenario assumptions. By analyzing the 2021 data in conjunction with previous observations, we determined that Algol C maintains a consistent orbital period over at least the past 375 years. Furthermore, our research indicates that Algol C exhibits detached binary characteristics during most of its orbital cycles, whereas contact data is observed in nearly half of these cycles. Additionally, we discovered that Algol C's contact epochs coincide with increasing mass exchange between its components, suggesting a W-subtype W UMa binary system. An extrinsic color change was also identified in historical records, which we speculate might be attributed to a thermal interaction due to the accumulation of mass and resulting changes in the component stars. Our study further suggests that Algol C is an overcontact binary system with a derived mass ratio of approximately 3.95, and we speculate that it may evolve into a semi-contact system within the next 1-3 million years. Moreover, we note the necessity of updating Algol C's parallax measurement due to potential systematic errors associated with its past measurements. Our research also highlights the value of long-term monitoring for understanding binary star systems like Algol C. Lastly, we note that Algol C remains an intriguing system requiring continued observational data to refine our understanding of its behavior and evolution. This article explores the classical evidence for the blow-up of solutions to the Schrödinger equation under a real-valued potential with a positive sign, confined within a bounded domain. The boundary influences the solutions, rendering them distinct from those of the equation in unbounded spaces, for which blow-up proof methods rely heavily on the unique properties of the initial data and solutions near the origin. In contrast, this article examines how the presence of the boundary changes the proof of blow-up, utilizing energy estimates and compactness arguments that respect the boundary. The findings indicate that solutions up to a certain threshold in energy will be bounded, while those above that threshold will eventually experience blow-up. Crucially, this proof does not rely on the specific details of the boundary conditions, making it applicable to a range of topologically distinct domains. Two variants of the equation are investigated: one with a real-valued potential and the other with a complex-valued potential, for which a slightly modified proof is required due to the presence of complex coefficients. The article concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for the corresponding wave equation. The boundary evidence for the blow-up of solutions to the Schrödinger equation may also be extended to address scenarios where the nonlinearity in the equation takes on a different form, namely when it is of the form $|u|^{1+\4}u$. Similarly, this proof can be adapted to investigate the scenarios in which the potential in the equation is not limited to being positive, but instead may switch between positive and negative values. The article also explores the extension of these findings to understand the behavior of solutions to the Schrödinger equation in scenarios where initial data are localized near the boundary, rather than being confined to the interior of the domain. A novel training technique, Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation (RANG), has been introduced to accelerate the training process of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). RANG dynamically adjusts the node generation strategy based on the residual error and its gradient during training, prioritizing the inclusion of challenging nodes. By concentrating pinsning efforts on difficult nodes, RANG enhances training efficiency. Experimental results on both a simple problem and two real-world examples demonstrate substantial reductions in training time while achieving comparable or improved accuracy compared to traditional PINNs and existing node selection strategies. Furthermore, RANG shows promise in integrating with various optimization methods to remain effective, even when the node distribution does not consistently reflect challenging nodes. Due to its versatility and performance, RANG presents a promising alternative to traditional PINNs for training neural networks that solve partial differential equations (PDEs) efficiently. Additionally, a pre-trained model for the two real-world examples can be found at https://smwjiang.github.io/RANG/pretrained.html.

This research explores the physical foundation of ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs), examining both the domain wall and periodic texture behaviors of ferroelectric materials. Through the solution of a quantum conduction band equation, it determines the conduction band profile in the presence of domain walls and compares it to the case with uniform ferroelectric orientation. The analysis shows that domain wall textures produce localized quantum conduction states, whereas periodic textures result in a weighted average conduction band shift. This understanding lays a necessary groundwork for the development of more accurate models of FeFETs. Additionally, this study investigates how the device's performance can be optimized by adjusting the thickness of the ferroelectric layer. The results indicate that domain wall textures are beneficial for thinner ferroelectric materials, while thicker materials are preferred for optimal device operation with periodic texture patterns. Ultimately, this work provides valuable insights to guide the design and operation of FeFETs. Recent studies have shown that Gabor filters' (GFs) diverse responses are due to different orientation rather than location. Building on this insight, a novel set of Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), an extension of traditional GFs, is proposed. By incorporating an additional dimension of Landmark (LMB) data, LGFs are learned in an end-to-end manner using a multi-task network, combining Gabor and LMB prediction tasks. The incorporation of LMBs enhances the robustness of image representations across various orientations, while the middle-frequency Gabor filters excel at combining low-frequency base features with high-frequency details. However, the underlying reason for this successful ordering was not well understood. In an effort to clarify this, researchers presented an alternative GCN model where the feature gathering order is randomly varied. Interestingly, this variant performed just as well as the traditional model and, more importantly, was more resilient to faulty data configurations. Furthermore, they found that their shuffled model was capable of producing task-specific predictions with either the original or modified feature ordering. Deep neural networks are susceptible to various forms of attacks that significantly degrade their performance. Existing attacks often rely on internal agents with full access to the target model, which is rarely the case in real-world applications. To address this limitation, we propose a novel, imperceptible Trojan attack that can be executed by multiple agents, each with access to a separate target model parameter. The Trojan, embedded in a trained neural network, triggers a pre-defined response when any of these parameters are manipulated within a limited 'trigger zone'. The trigger zone can be pinpointed even with individual attacks, and the Trojan can be designed to activate a specific response on multiple parameter groups. Moreover, we demonstrate that the Trojan can be utilized for various objectives such as data poisoning, forging model signatures, and manipulating trained models to fulfill specific requirements. We introduce a new framework for semantic studies in modal logic by exploring topological categories, where domains are replaced by categories featuring 'topological' properties. This leads to a natural interpretation of formulas as subsets of domains, satisfying specific conditions, thus yielding a meaningful topology on the domain's underlying set. This topology can be derived from the modal operator, prompting the development of a topological category structure on the domain, where the underlying set's topology is preserved under the domain's preorder. This framework empowers us to examine various families of modal logics, like intuitionistic and basic modal logics, by constructing topological categories from specific topological spaces or categories. Moreover, we investigate a 'compactness' property for modal logics, demonstrating its validity for both intuitionistic and basic modal logics, but potentially flawed for other systems within this framework. Additionally, we adapt a topological category approach to represent graded modal logics, employing graded subsets to define truth values for formulas as 'degrees of inclusion' between, e.g., domains and'super-domains'. This representation allows us to derive a generalised version of our compactness result for graded modal logics. Finally, we establish a connection between topological categories and'relational products' – a construct used to represent products of domains in a functorial manner – thus providing a new perspective on the representation of modal logics through relational products. This connection provides a topological category analogue to the relational product's properties, offering further insights into the underlying semantic structures of modal logics. In particular, it reveals that every topological category with a relational product is equivalent to a subcategory of a presheaf category over a suitable site, defined by a specific coverage on a particular category of topological spaces. Moreover, we demonstrate the existence of relational products in every topological category that is locally compact and has compact objects, thus generalising a previous result on modal logic and relational products due to Allaire and Loiseau. In turn, this generalised result implies the validity of a compactness property for modal logics with relational products. Finally, we show that every graded modal logic can be represented by a graded relational product on a topological category with compact objects, thus establishing a graded analogue to our compactness result for modal logics. Illustrated with two practical examples, the proposed approach demonstrates superior performance, with significant cost reductions of 80% to 90%. This innovative technique offers a flexible and extensible framework for various simulator modules, with its source code and test scenarios freely available online. Further research is recommended to explore the application of parallel projection techniques in simulator tuning. Additionally, the study suggests several promising areas of exploration for future projects. A potential solution to this challenge is presented, involving the utilization of high-performance computing facilities. The feasibility of this approach is demonstrated through the successful application of the proposed simulator tuning method to a complex model, involving 348 model states and 21 variables, which was efficiently tuned within 2 minutes using a computational grid composed of 10 nodes and 20 cores. Our research investigates the production of protons and deuterons in high-energy collisions from 1 GeV to 13 TeV, based on the latest data from the BARILETTE, SICA/E, and ALICE experiments. By analyzing these new results alongside existing information, we gain insight into the collision process at various energy levels. The ratio of $d/p$ decreases with increasing energy in central Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC, while remaining stable or experiencing minor changes in smaller system collisions and $p$-$p$ collisions over a broader energy range. As the size of the collision system grows from $p$-$p$ to $d$-$d$ to Pb-Pb, the $d/p$ ratio exhibits an energy dependence, with the effect becoming more pronounced at lower energy levels. This trend is observed in both intermediate- and semi-central collisions. By considering the possibility of density effects influenced by the Avogadro constant $\mathcal{N}$, the data become consistent across different systems at $\mathcal{N} \simeq 3$ in a range of 1-100 GeV. The significance of this finding, along with its potential implications, is discussed. Additionally, our research explores the behavior of $d/p$ ratios in collisions involving nuclei and includes a comprehensive comparison with theoretical models. The findings presented can provide valuable insights into the properties of particles in high-energy collisions. Finally, our analysis delves into the possibility of nuclear interactions taking place in $p$-$p$ collisions, where a detailed analysis reveals the level of nuclear interaction in $p$-$p$ collisions to be equivalent to that in $d$-$d$ collisions at the LHC energy level. This result is consistent with the notion that $d/p$ ratios in $p$-$p$ collisions are largely influenced by a non-zero density effect. As a result, the level of nuclear interaction in $p$-$p$ collisions is not as low as previously suggested, but rather is comparable to that in $d$-$d$ collisions at the LHC energy level. This information can be useful in refining our understanding of nuclear interactions in low-energy collisions. Furthermore, our research reveals that density effects in high-energy collisions are subject to the constraint of the Avogadro constant $\mathcal{N}$, where the value of $\mathcal{N}$ is found to be approximately 3 in a range of 1-100 GeV. This discovery opens up new avenues for investigating density effects

The review also touches on the proper treatment of parton transverse momenta and its implications on the understanding of DPDs. Finally, the reviews discuss the current and planned experimental situations involving the measurement of DPDs. Several recommendations for future experimental measurements are provided. We evaluate the Prospector Bayesian analysis pipeline on a collection of 13 galaxy datasets, with a focus on $\beta$-disk galaxies, by comparing its predicted values to those obtained through traditional non-Bayesian methods. The analysis utilizes a stellar evolution model that incorporates solar metallicity stellar spectra and spans 0.1 Myr to 10 Gyr, paired with a $\beta$-disk galaxy model that accounts for stellar formation and star formation rates. The Prospector framework handles uncertainty in observational data, individual stellar parameters, and other variables. Our study finds that the Prospector pipeline accurately matches star formation rates within a factor of 1.3 across all 13 datasets when compared to non-Bayesian methods, with a stronger correlation when considering luminosity measurements. The analysis reveals a slight underestimation of ages and metallicities less than solar, along with ages and masses generally being underestimated. The Prospector pipeline tends to provide tighter constraints on parameters compared to non-Bayesian methods, with the exception of stellar formation history parameters. The comparison highlights the importance of utilizing full spectral energy distributions in stellar population spectral analysis and the potential for the Prospector pipeline to improve analysis of future space-based missions, such as the Roman Spatial Telescope, by accurately predicting star formation rates at red near-infrared wavelengths. The objective of the UbiComp 2021 Challenge was to establish a sensor-based approach for distinguishing between daily activities and their generation mechanisms, using time series data from a single sensor. We tackled this problem by training a model to identify written activity from the pressure patterns created by a pen on a touchscreen, specifically on a tablet device, and then defining a theory to explain how written activity is recognized by analyzing the pressure time-series data. This pressure pattern data reflects the physical properties of the pen, such as its mass and friction, which influence the writing process, resulting in distinct pressure patterns for each written character, partly overlapping in time, that vary in intensity, and often involve pauses. We used these pressure patterns to identify written activity and proposed a solution to clarify the mechanism by extracting key features from the pressure patterns that distinguish different written characters. This extraction process enhances the model's performance by automating the feature selection process, and demonstrates that the pressure patterns themselves can serve as character features, identified through similarity analysis of the pressure patterns, without the need for further processing or engineering. This approach resulted in high accuracy in identifying written activity, and a notable improvement in the model's performance when using pressure pattern features versus engineered features. This approach can be adapted to other activities, such as drawing, signing, and gesture recognition, which produce similar pressure patterns, and can be applied to other domains, such as graphics and signal processing, where these pressure patterns can be generated. This research introduces a novel technique for modeling duration, incorporating decision theory to handle non-parametric situations. Unlike traditional methods, this approach models decision-making processes separately for durations above and below a specified threshold, allowing for dynamic treatment of left and right tail behaviors. It differs from parametric models that distribute entire durations or use different parameters for different segments, or assume certain decision-making strategies. This technique is based on the idea that a decision-maker with a desired target in mind will choose a shorter duration if the situation suggests it's urgent or make a longer wait if it's beneficial to prolong the time until a better opportunity arises. This model can be applied to second-best situations by assuming a decision-maker's goal is to maximize expected duration based on their beliefs about how long different actions take. Our analysis shows that this duration model is consistent with economic principles and can be estimated using available data, outperforming the standard approach in a real-world test. This model's primary limitation at present is its reliance on prior subjective beliefs, although we propose a method to refine these beliefs iteratively. This technique has applications in various fields, such as studying how people respond to treatment or how they navigate decision-making situations. One such application is in analyzing how long it takes patients to switch between psychiatric services and self-care. A Bayesian framework is employed to enhance the efficiency of occupancy modeling in species occupancy studies by integrating multiple data sets. This approach is tested using 16 species from a long-running study in a tropical ecosystem, where four surveys spanning 28 years are analyzed to determine occupancy and demographic trends. The results indicate significant changes in occupancy for several species over time, while others exhibited distinct trends in site occupancy. Demographic analysis revealed various species exhibit different responses to long-term site occupancy, with some demonstrating increased or decreased dependence on sites over time. Additionally, species groups exhibiting similar ecological characteristics displayed similar occupancy and demographic patterns, suggesting a potential association between these groups and long-term species dynamics. This research demonstrates the value of Bayesian multi-data analysis in providing nuanced insights into species dynamics and the potential for using a priori species group information to inform hypotheses about species behavior in ecological research. Furthermore, our findings highlight the importance of considering the underlying ecological relationships among species when interpreting the results of Bayesian occupancy models. The computational efficiency of our approach makes it well-suited for the multi-data analysis of long-term surveys in a large number of species. This article introduces the Skincare project's diagnostic tool, a web-based system that aids general practitioners and dermatologists in diagnosing and treating skin conditions. Leveraging a dataset of 3D skin surface maps and clinical information, the deep learning-powered algorithm was trained to reproduce diagnoses made by experienced dermatologists. To model the intrinsic scatter in type Ia supernovae, the supernovova community has employed Gaussian Process Regression since the early 2000s. Previous studies used individual supernovae to train and predict specific snIa models, but these methods were limited by the relatively small sample size. In contrast, our study utilize a cohort of 102 snIa to develop and evaluate various assumptions about intrinsic variability, incorporating both host galaxy information and magnitude measurements. By incorporating a correlation penalty term into the regression framework, we find that snIa luminosity can be accurately modeled with a normal distribution centered on the Hubble constant, with an intrinsic dispersion of 0.25 mag and a correlation coefficient of 0.6. Additionally, our results suggest a moderate correlation between magnitude and variability, with a standardized regression coefficient of -0.4, implying that snIa luminosity decreases as variability increases. However, further supernovae are required to confirm this finding. Based on these findings, we predict a relationship between variability and magnitude that can be used to correct future snIa data and potentially streamline supernovae sample selection. Our study also highlights the potential for future snIa data to refine this variability prediction and magnitude relationship, ultimately enhancing cosmological analyses reliant on snIa data. Ultimately, our research underscores the significance of accurately modeling snIa variability in understanding the diverse nature of snIa events. In an accompanying paper, we demonstrate how to leverage the variability model developed here to make precise predictions about individual snIa magnitudes, with an average error margin of 0.13 mag. In turn, these predictions enable the utilization of snIa data in a cosmological analysis, with a finding snIa Hubble constant of 74.8 km/s/Mpc and a fit to Lambda-CDM parameters indicating a universe that is young and matter-rich. Using data from the SAMI galaxy survey, a study has investigated how mass outflows in star-forming galaxies relate to their supermassive black holes. The research identified 35 galaxies with both stellar outflows and supermassive black hole activity, and found that outflows in these galaxies occur along axes aligned approximately with their spin axes. The findings suggest that star formation in these galaxies may be regulated by a feedback process involving both stellar outflows and energy released from the supermassive black hole. This research investigates the electrostatic discharge capabilities of silicon wafers with different surface treatments, specifically those that have been etched in buffer oxide or chemically processed to remove a thin layer of the oxide. Through experiments and simulations, we examined the electrostatic discharge phenomena on these treated surfaces and revealed that the carrier concentration in etched silicon is significantly lower than in buffer oxide etched silicon. This distinct difference results in distinct electrostatic discharge behaviors, notably a more pronounced delayed electrostatic discharge in etched silicon. Moreover, the simulations accurately replicate the experimental results, thereby validating the underlying physical mechanisms involved. By understanding the carrier concentration and its influence on electrostatic discharge, this knowledge can be utilized to optimize surface processing techniques for improved electrostatic discharge robustness. Conversely, this knowledge can be leveraged to analyze and identify the causes of delayed electrostatic discharge in silicon wafers. Ultimately, this research provides a foundation for further investigations into the electrostatic discharge phenomena in silicon wafers with varying surface treatments. Additionally, this research has practical implications for enhancing the reliability of microelectronic devices subjected to different surface processing methods. Based on these findings, we suggest that the delayed electrostatic discharge is not an intrinsic fault but rather can be attributed to specific surface processing conditions. As such, this phenomenon offers a means to diagnose and identify the underlying surface processing parameters. A widely accepted notion holds that systematic extrapolation is inextricably linked with being able to generalize beyond the initial training limits, with many theories and experiments conforming to this narrative. We demonstrate this by means of a straightforward example, in which a systematic extrapolation is achieved through the utilization of a simple template, without the need for additional neural network capabilities. Furthermore, our findings are reinforced by the observation that, in comparison to an unsupervised form of extrapolation, a supervised form may yield more accurate predictions, yet their associated representations may exhibit lower levels of accuracy. Our research highlights the need for a more subtle distinction between extrapolation and generalization, as well as the value of conceptual clarity in evaluating the performance of AI systems. This paper introduces a pioneering, federated approach to personalizable, context-aware recommendation systems. Our methodology, FLVoogd, is a collaborative, privacy-preserving system that relies on a technique to de-identify data in real-time, allowing for both enhanced fairness and personalization without compromising individual privacy. FLVoogd is unique in its ability to maintain both client-side data anonymization and server-side de-identification, thus safeguarding personal information while enabling accurate cluster assignment. Our approach also ensures that only harmless data is utilized in the clustering process. Furthermore, FLVoogd is designed to be adaptable to various data types and can be applied to various machine learning algorithms. Our experiments, which analyzed both real-world e-commerce transactions and synthetic data sets, demonstrated that FLVoogd achieves fair, efficient, and scalable results in practical settings. Additionally, our source code is freely available for public use.

1. Client-side: Each user runs a local program that collects data, applies a transformation technique to anonymize the data in real-time, and aggregates it into a group using a machine learning algorithm.
2. Client aggregator: A centralized entity collects and aggregates the transformed data from users and sends it to a central aggregator.
3. Central aggregator: This entity processes the aggregated data and distributes it to a central server.
4. Server-side: The central server receives the aggregated data, distributes it to users, and runs an optimization algorithm to determine the group assignments. 

Our experiments focused on two types of data:
1. Real e-commerce transactions from a retail company.

top-down approaches, but it remains unclear how these perform in real-world scenarios.
A recent benchmark, the NeurIPS 2021 Autonomous Driving Dataset Challenge, 
offered a large collection of real-world data along with corresponding labels, 
derived from the NuScenes dataset.
Our team contributed two approaches to the challenge: a method that leverages 
self-supervised learning in simulated data and another that utilizes a top-down 
approach based on semantic scene segmentation.
These techniques achieved notable results, with our self-supervised method ranking 
3rd or 4th in most categories and our top-down approach placing 2nd in several tasks. 
Notably, our self-supervised method demonstrated a 10-20% improvement in object 
detection accuracy when compared to traditional supervised pre-training on real-
world data. 
Our findings suggest that simulated data can be effectively utilized in real-world 
applications, and we intend to share our challenge entry with full code and model 
repositories to facilitate future research. 
In addition, we highlight potential areas for improvement in future work. 
In particular, we note that current self-supervised pre-training strategies may not 
be optimal and might be enhanced by incorporating additional auxiliary tasks. 
Furthermore, despite the advancement of self-supervised pre-training, our results 
suggest that real-world data requires be supplemented with top-down knowledge to 
achieve high performance in object detection tasks. 
Lastly, we observe that top-down approaches continue to play a crucial role in object 
linking and tracking, underscoring the need for further research in this domain. 
In light of these findings, we propose several promising research directions for 
the community to explore in the future.

research grant for this project.

We investigated the atmospheric compositions of temperate planets with masses significantly smaller or larger than Earth using exoplanet models that account for the planet's evolution, stellar radiation, and atmospheric interactions. Our analysis reveals distinct atmospheric profiles for low-mass and high-mass planets, with low-mass atmospheres characterized by high N2/CO ratios and weak magnetic fields, and high-mass atmospheres marked by high CO2 levels, strong magnetic fields, and a greater likelihood of the atmosphere being stripped away. We observed a missing region in our model predictions around 1.5 to 2.5 times Earth's mass, which could be attributed to the atmospheric retention efficiency being heavily influenced by the planet's mass at this scale. This efficiency increases exponentially with decreasing planet mass. We also found that atmospheric compositions can be accurately determined through transit spectroscopy for planets with low-mass atmospheres or those orbiting late-type stars, with other methods such as photometry or transit spectroscopy failing to accurately predict atmospheric compositions for high-mass planets due to the influence of energy input from the host star. Our study identified the need for future observations to target a broader range of planets, particularly those with high masses, and for the development of improved models that account for atmospheric dynamics, chemistry, and interactions, as well as the potential impact of other astrophysical processes. Based on these advancements, we anticipate that future observations may reveal atmospheric compositions for high-mass planets that are consistent with model predictions. Additionally, the study highlights the potential for future space missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope, Habitable Exoplanet Imaging Mission, and future large telescopes to significantly expand our understanding of exoplanet atmospheres, covering a wider mass range and potentially revealing new atmospheric features. By combining these future observations with exoplanet models, we can gain insights into the physical and chemical processes occurring within exoplanet atmospheres, ultimately shedding light on the intrinsic properties of the planets themselves. Ultimately, the study underscores the significance of integrating theoretical models and observational efforts to achieve a more comprehensive understanding of exoplanet phenomena. A two-layer McCulloch-Pitts network, built upon the foundation of a one-layer Hopfield network, is explored in this paper for its potential in pattern recognition tasks. By expanding the capability of the Hopfield network, the M-P network is found to successfully identify both memorized and novel patterns, with its learning ability significantly enhanced. Additionally, the study analyzes the computational complexity and time efficiency of the forward pass and backward propagation processes in the M-P network. Compared to deep neural networks, the M-P network is shown to have a more efficient forward pass process, but similar computational costs in the backward propagation process, as exemplified in the 3-SAT problem. Furthermore, the investigation finds that the number of neurons in the first layer of the M-P network roughly corresponds to the square root of the number of features in the input data. Based on these findings, the M-P network is posited to be a promising new approach to designing neural networks that balance efficiency and generalization capabilities. The research is supported by numerical experiments conducted on MNIST datasets, highlighting the advantages of the M-P network in achieving high accuracy rates and generalizing new pattern features. Specifically, the study demonstrates that the M-P network can effectively identify new pattern features in the MNIST dataset, resulting in a 99.1% test accuracy rate, outperforming various state-of-the-art deep neural networks. The M-P network is also found to achieve superior results in the research of specific objects in the CIFAR-10 dataset, an achievement not seen in the Hopfield network. The study further reveals that the M-P network can effectively tackle the problem of binary classification by adjusting the weights of neurons, resulting in a 94.7% test accuracy rate on the CIFAR-10 dataset, outperforming several prominent deep neural networks. The M-P network is also found to achieve superior results in the research of specific objects in the CIFAR-100 dataset, an achievement not seen in the Hopfield network. The study further reveals that the M-P network can effectively tackle the problem of binary classification by adjusting the weights of neurons, resulting in a 73.1% test accuracy rate on the CIFAR-100 dataset. The emergence of Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based models for scene text recognition has been remarkable, with some models demonstrating exceptional performance on standard training and testing datasets. However, a significant challenge lies in handling Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) words, which are frequently encountered in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we created a comprehensive dataset of OOIV words by combining images from various sources, including Google Books and Street View, with a dictionary of missing words. This joint collection totals over 88K, yielding a significantly enlarged dataset. Furthermore, we introduce the OOIV-AWN challenge, a benchmark that focuses on recognizing rare words in the wild. Given the absence of accurate word-level ground truth in real-world street view images, we employed image-based information retrieval to obtain word-level annotations. This innovative approach enables us to leverage the power of search engines to generate a substantial number of word-level annotations. Ultimately, we invite researchers to participate in the OOIV-AWN challenge, aiming to achieve breakthroughs in scene text recognition for both general and rare words. You can access the dataset at https://github.com/Chen-Eric/OOIV-AWN-Challenge. Additionally, please visit https://awn-challenge.github.io/ for more details about the challenge. Leveraging massive self-supervised pre-trained models has become an essential strategy for various vision and language tasks. To this end, we introduce a new self-supervised paradigm, named Self-supervised Large-scale K-means with extended Edges (S-LKE), to derive effective features from massive scene text images. By integrating edge information into the traditional K-means pipeline, S-LKE is capable of learning more robust text image features that are beneficial for various downstream tasks. As a result, we achieve superior performance on the newly proposed OOIV-AWN challenge, demonstrating the remarkable efficacy of S-LKE features in scene text recognition tasks, particularly for recognizing rare words. You can access the code at https://github.com/Chen-Eric/S-LKE. The goal of validated numerics is to generate reliable, error-bounded solutions to mathematical systems, which can then be used to analyze the resulting discrete data. In this context, we explore the potential of validated numerics to compute separate branches of solutions for continuous parameter values in systems of differential equations. By incorporating parameters into the systems, we can examine how the solutions change and often split into distinct branches, a process that can be difficult to track numerically. We provide a method to combine validated numerics with parameter continuation, ensuring that the solutions generated are accurate and come from distinct branches. A significant advantage of our approach is that it allows for the detection of solutions that may not be connected, such as those in the vicinity of bifurcations, and can identify new branches arising from them. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method with several examples, highlighting its ability to compute isolated branches of solutions correctly. Furthermore, we show that these error-bounded solutions can be used to compute topological invariants, such as Brouwer degree, and even predict the number of solutions on certain branches. We conclude by outlining possible modifications to our method that could enhance its performance and accuracy. Ultimately, the goal is to make validated numerics a valuable tool for computing and studying the resulting discrete data in the context of parameter-dependent systems.}

Detecting abrupt changes in patterns and pinpointing the cause can be crucial for anticipating and mitigating disorders. Currently, identifying the source of these changes is often impractical due to limited data availability. A new method has been devised that uses a regularized version of the online uniform change point detection algorithm to maximize signal detection accuracy without the need for excessive false alarms. By integrating this with a novel isolation technique based on sparse recovery, we can precisely locate the triggers behind individual failures at a significantly reduced computational cost. This approach enables us to accurately identify over 90% of changes and 75% of their causes using only 5 data points, a performance that surpasses state-of-the-art techniques by at least 10% across various parameter settings. Furthermore, simulations have demonstrated that this strategy is resilient to noise and statistical fluctuations, maintaining high effectiveness across a range of signal-to-noise ratios. The improved efficiency of this method reduces the computational time to analyze a single real-world dataset from several hours to just a few minutes. Available at https://github.com/alexdixon/cpd_fmi/tree/main/cpd_fmi. Applied to over 500 industrial systems from the open PHACTS project, we have observed a 20% average improvement in failure detection and isolation rates, coupled with a 50% reduction in false positives. This has the potential to accelerate diagnosis by up to a factor of five in real-world scenarios. Experimental results show that this approach detects failures more quickly, on average by at least one time unit. Available at https://github.com/alexdixon/cpd_fmi/tree/main/cpd_fMI. You can run the code using Python 3.7 or later with the following command: python -u cpd_fmi/main.py --help. A detailed description of the methodology can be found in the accompanying technical report. All source code and simulation data are publicly accessible through the above link. Feedback and suggestions are welcome via email at alex.dixon@ed.ac.uk. This will involve selecting specific time points for active monitoring to optimize prediction, using previously collected data to inform future diagnostic decisions. A common challenge in training machine learning models lies in obtaining a large, costly, or time-consuming dataset of labeled examples. The selective labeling method addresses this issue by identifying the most informative instances, which require the least labeling effort. In this study, a comparative review of existing selective labeling techniques is presented, along with a new method to derive a simple model, which can be trained quickly. This comparative study examines the performance of the methods in scenarios with limited available labels, using synthetic datasets and real-world datasets. The findings indicate that the proposed simple model consistently outperforms the other methods, particularly in scenarios with extremely limited labels. This study also provides open-source code for the methods to facilitate reproducibility and future research on the topic. The code can be accessed through the following link: https://github.com/learn4fog/selective-labeling. Based on the results of this study, a general recommendation can be formulated for choosing a suitable method depending on the specific circumstances of the project. If a model can be trained quickly, it is advised to use it to derive a label predictor. Then, use the confidence of the predictor to select instances for human labeling, either by assigning labels to all instances above a certain threshold or by optimizing the selection through an iterative process. If a model cannot be trained quickly, an offline approach can be employed, where a label predictor is trained in advance using a large, pre-existing dataset and then applied to select instances for human labeling. It is also possible to use the label predictor to estimate labels for a pre-defined subset of instances that were not used in the training process. However, it is essential to note that these approaches are subject to the limitations of the chosen dataset and may not generalize well to other scenarios. An alternative approach is to use an offline method that trains a label predictor on a large, pre-existing dataset and then applies it to select instances for human labeling based on their difficulty, such as semantic difficulty. However, it is once again important to note that these approaches are subject to the chosen dataset and may not generalize well to other scenarios. An interesting area for further research is the development of new methods that can adapt to changing distribution of data over time. An example of such a method is online selective labeling, which trains a label predictor using a stream of data in real-time. However, it is subject to the limitations of being sensitive to data class imbalance and requiring a fixed class distribution. A comprehensive theoretical examination of the interface electronic structure of EuS/InAs heterostructures has been conducted through density functional theory, highlighting the significance of dispersion states at the InAs valence band maximum in shaping the overall electronic profile. These dispersion states, derived from the sp-z orbital combination on InAs, interact with the empty 4f orbitals on EuS, and our calculations demonstrate that they can give rise to a range of anomalies in the InAs spectrum, including a pronounced peak and a shoulder, when considering various interfaces with both clean and oxygen-contaminated surfaces of EuS. Notably, a comparative analysis between the clean and oxygen-covered interfaces reveals distinct features in the interface electron density and a significantly reduced interaction at the latter, indicating that oxygen acts as a surface passivant. Furthermore, our calculations of transport properties across the interface reveal both hole and electron conduction, with associated energy barriers in both cases, having magnitudes of approximately 0.23 and 0.17 eV for the clean and oxygen-covered interfaces, respectively. Overall, our findings provide a thorough understanding of the interface electronic structure in EuS/InAs heterostructures. Additionally, to account for possible inaccuracies in static calculations, our results from a non-local, non-empirical spin-orbit coupled calculation show minimal differences, thereby validating our theoretical framework. Moreover, to address the issue of the inaccurately positioned InAs valence band maximum in the pseudopotential calculation, our results from a structural relaxation with a monolayer thick InAs overlayer, where the InAs surface relaxation reaches saturation, indicate minimal discrepancies, thereby underscoring the necessity of performing such relaxations to ensure precision in the predicted interface electronic structures. Finally, as the interface electronic structures are found to be sensitive to the choice of interface boundary, our study suggests the importance of maintaining the same atomic configuration across the interface in both the clean and oxygen-covered cases, highlighting the limitations of the empirical based Monkhorst-Pack scheme in predicting interface electronic structures with precision. Conversely, the use of the Pauly-Künnmann scheme, which is free from such assumptions, shows promise in predicting such structures with accuracy. Nonetheless, as the scheme is known to be computationally intensive, our study suggests an alternative method based on the automated k-gridding technique. Consequently, our results from this technique indicate minimal discrepancies with the Pauly-Künnmann scheme, thereby validating our theoretical framework. We investigate different variants of Wadge determinacy for subsets of Borel or Suslin sets, and corresponding implications on second-order arithmetic theories, such as $\mathbf{AFCP}_2$ or ${\mathbf{ACA}_0^0$. Our analysis reveals that a particular form of Borel Wadge determinacy, which is equivalent to second-order arithmetic with countable choice and quantifier-free induction over countable partial orders, is the weakest of these theories in terms of coding theory. We also examine the relationship between open sets, closed sets, and complementation, and demonstrate that determinacy for these classes is separate from second-order arithmetic with function or set comprehension. Furthermore, a form of finite Wadge determinacy does not imply $\mathbf{AFCP}_2$. We provide an alternative characterization of the theory of arithmetic with function comprehension using projecta of minimal sets, and show that it is equivalent to a strictly weaker theory. We also explore other themes, such as the connection between projecta of minimal sets and the fundamental theorem of Borel determinacy, as well as the relationship between coded graph determinacy and the indescribability of $\mathbf{\Delta}_2^1$-true sentences. Additionally, we examine a form of second-order arithmetic with choice over minimal sets, and consider its relationship with other existing arithmetical theories. We find that this theory is not necessarily implied by any of the other considered determinacy notions, but is also not weaker than any of them. We provide an alternative characterization using projecta of minimal sets with limited complexity, and show that it is equivalent to a form of Borel Wadge determinacy for sets with $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^1$-complement. Pruning has been a prominent technique for reducing model size to speed up inference. However, the common approach of pruning model weights does not directly translate to accurate results, as reported by \textit{PruneTrain} in 2020. To overcome this limitation, ClickTrain prunes the input data distribution, yielding a more reliable outcome by aligning the model's behavior on the pruned dataset with the pruned dataset itself. In contrast to PruneTrain, ClickTrain focuses on a pre-training stage, employing a probabilistic model to characterize data distributions. The experiment demonstrates that ClickTrain achieves superior results on both quantitative and qualitative metrics when compared to existing pruning methods. Moreover, ClickTrain's design allows for the flexible selection of pruning strategies, such as aggressive or conservative approaches, by adjusting the complexity of the probabilistic model. The code for ClickTrain can be found on GitHub at the link: https://github.com/aleclee20/ClickTrain. This paper presents a relational semantics for substructural modal logics by adapting the relational models originally designed for positive intuitionistic logic to fit substructural and modal requirements. It demonstrates the completeness of this semantics for each of these logics by showcasing a sound and complete axiomatic proof, and further explores an algebraic counterpart using the variety of coreducible algebras. The paper also investigates an expansion of the relational semantics to encompass negation, developing a framework for negative substructural modal logic and examining its completeness in relation to the deep inference calculus of hypersequent calculus. While the deep inference system is proven to be sound with respect to the proposed semantics, establishing the completeness of this semantics remains an area for further research. Additionally, the paper explores an alternative cut-elimination strategy for a negative substructural modal logic through the application of the relational semantics. Relational methods in this context offer advantages over traditional cut-elimination techniques, particularly by facilitating the use of preorders rather than equivalence between proof, and by enabling the incorporation of additional semantic properties such as depth-monotony. The preorders employed in this method are derived from the relation between hypersequents, which is shown to be well-suited for these applications. Consequently, this approach may serve as a useful tool for cut-elimination in other substructural and modal logics. The paper ultimately provides an order-theoretic interpretation of these logics by combining preorders with orderings through the application of upsets and downsets. This allows the representation of substructural and modal rules at the level of preorders and the identification of upsets and downsets as more refined relations reflecting additional logical properties. The integration of order-theoretic elements in this manner contributes to a deeper understanding of the underlying logic. In particular, this framework reveals that coreducibility and depth-monotony are inherent properties of positive substructural modal logic when expressed through relational preorders. The study of relational semantics offers an appealing approach to the study of substructural and modal logics, offering a distinct perspective on these systems that can contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying principles. Furthermore, this methodology may be particularly beneficial when combined with other relational approaches such as nominal logic to handle quantification, or other relational frameworks such as resource logic to handle resource semantics. Consequently, this approach may serve as a useful tool for the relational treatment of other logical systems. The use of relational semantics also presents opportunities for the development of computational algorithms, particularly through the application of relational preorders and order-theoretic elements.
